questions.stem:
63M w/ 3 wk fevers, night sweats and fatigue. Dental extraction 6 wk ago. New apical holosystolic murmur, splinter hemorrhages.

T 38.4, BP 128/74, HR 96.
WBC 12.6 × 10⁹/L, CRP 88 mg/L
questions.explanation: In a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected (subacute) IE, draw at least three blood culture sets from separate venipuncture sites, spaced apart, before antibiotics; premature antibiotics are the commonest cause of culture-negative IE. Then echo (TTE, TEE as needed). If septic/unstable, draw cultures rapidly and start empiric therapy without delay.

questions.stem:
76M w/ HFrEF on furosemide 80 mg BID for 1 wk has a persistent R pleural effusion. Thoracentesis:

Pleural protein 36 g/L (serum 66)
Pleural LDH 120 U/L (serum 260; ULN 250)
Pleural albumin 20 g/L (serum 35)
Cells: 400/µL, mostly lymphocytes; glucose normal
questions.explanation: Light's criteria: exudate if pleural/serum protein >0.5, pleural/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural LDH >2/3 ULN. Here only the protein ratio (0.55) is met. Diuresis concentrates pleural protein, so Light's misclassifies ~25% of transudates in treated HF. A serum–pleural albumin gradient >12 g/L (here 15) supports a transudate.

options.explanation: Correct: albumin gradient 15 g/L (>12) → transudate.

questions.stem:
72F w/ new ascites and leg edema. Elevated JVP, no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Diagnostic paracentesis:

Serum albumin 34 g/L; ascitic albumin 20 g/L
Ascitic total protein 34 g/L
PMN 40/µL, cytology pending
questions.explanation: SAAG = serum − ascitic albumin = 14 g/L (≥11 → portal hypertension). Ascitic total protein then separates causes: <25 g/L suggests cirrhosis; ≥25 g/L suggests cardiac ascites (or Budd-Chiari). Low SAAG (<11) suggests carcinomatosis, TB, pancreatitis or nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: 27F nurse sustained a deep hollow-bore needlestick 2 h ago from a patient w/ known HIV; source's current viral load and ART adherence unknown. She is HIV-negative at baseline.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Testing alone doesn't prevent infection after a high-risk exposure.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.explanation: Regimens are 3 drugs for 28 days.

options.label: E

options.explanation: Delay reduces efficacy; start now and reassess when results return.

Na 138, K 3.0, Cl 114, HCO3 15 mmol/L

Hb 92 g/L
Plt 38 ×10⁹/L
Cr 118 µmol/L

references.title: EULAR fibromyalgia recommendations (RheumNow)
references.supports: Exercise strong for; graduated approach

issues: Distractor B is inaccurate: EULAR 2017 rates tramadol 'weak for', so 'Opioids not recommended' is wrong for tramadol. Strong opioids and corticosteroids are 'strong against'; NSAIDs are 'weak against'. Explanation's 'avoid opioids, NSAIDs' overstates.

questions.topic: Knee OA with CKD and GI risk
questions.stem:
74F w/ bilateral knee OA; pain limits walking despite exercise program and weight loss. h/o upper GI bleed 2 y ago. CKD G3b.

eGFR 40 mL/min/1.73m²

options.label: A
options.explanation: Oral NSAIDs best avoided with CKD and prior GI bleed.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Opioids not recommended for OA.

options.label: C
options.explanation: ACR strongly recommends against.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Still nephrotoxic; renal and CV risk.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: strongly recommended for knee OA; minimal systemic exposure.

questions.explanation: ACR/AF 2019 strongly recommends topical NSAIDs for knee OA and suggests using them before oral NSAIDs to limit systemic exposure, which matters most in older adults with CKD, CVD or GI risk. Oral NSAIDs, duloxetine and IA steroids are other options; avoid glucosamine and opioids.

references.title: ACP MKSAP: topical NSAIDs for knee/hand OA
references.supports: Topical NSAIDs first; avoid oral NSAIDs with CKD, CVD, PUD

references.title: Guiding osteoarthritis management (US Pharmacist 2023)
references.supports: ACR/AF 2019: topical NSAIDs strongly recommended for knee OA

questions.topic: Creatinine rise after starting an ACEi
questions.stem:
63M w/ T2DM and albuminuric CKD (UACR 85 mg/mmol). Ramipril 10 mg started 2 wk ago. No NSAIDs, no diuretics, euvolemic.

BP 128/76
Cr 118 µmol/L (baseline 100)
K 5.0 mmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Same hemodynamic effect; no reason to switch.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: an 18% rise is an expected hemodynamic effect; continue and monitor.

options.label: C
options.text: Halve the ramipril dose to 5 mg
options.explanation: Unnecessary; the rise is within the accepted range.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Consider if Cr rises >30%; not needed here.

options.label: E
options.explanation: A rise <30% doesn't justify stopping a kidney-protective drug.

questions.explanation: A stable Cr rise of up to ~30% after starting or up-titrating an ACEi/ARB reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure, not injury: continue and recheck Cr and K in 1–2 wk. Reassess (volume status, NSAIDs, renal artery stenosis) if the rise exceeds 30% or keeps climbing.

references.title: NephJC Freely Filtered 73: KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline
references.supports: Continue ACEi/ARB unless Cr rises >30% within 4 wk

references.title: Interpreting creatinine and potassium changes after RAAS inhibition (Drug Topics 2026)
references.supports: Tolerate stable rise up to ~30%; reassess if >30% or worsening

issues: Content accurate (18% rise; KDIGO 2024 PP 3.6.4 continue RASi unless Cr rises >30% within 4 wk), but both references are weak: an exam-prep site (open-exam-prep, not affiliated with KDIGO) and a trade-magazine commentary (Drug Topics). Neither is the guideline.
Minor: KDIGO suggests checking Cr/K within 2-4 wk; '1-2 wk' is acceptable but not the KDIGO wording.

questions.stem:
68F w/ nonischemic cardiomyopathy, NYHA III despite 6 mo of target-dose sacubitril-valsartan, bisoprolol, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. Sinus rhythm.

TTE: LVEF 28%
ECG: LBBB, QRS 162 ms

options.label: A
options.explanation: Already on optimized GDMT for months; delay isn't warranted.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not before CRT; requires sinus HR ≥70 and has smaller benefit.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Symptomatic only; doesn't address dyssynchrony.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Misses resynchronization benefit given LBBB and QRS ≥150.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB, QRS ≥150 ms on GDMT.

questions.explanation: CRT is strongly indicated (Class I) for symptomatic HFrEF (NYHA II–ambulatory IV) with LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm and LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms despite ≥3 mo of optimized GDMT. It improves symptoms, hospitalizations and survival. Benefit is weaker with non-LBBB or QRS 120–149 ms.

references.title: 2012 ACCF/AHA/HRS device-based therapy focused update (ACC)
references.supports: Class I: EF ≤35%, SR, LBBB, QRS ≥150, NYHA II–IV

references.title: When to choose CRT in chronic HF (Eur Heart J Suppl 2019)
references.supports: CRT for LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II–IV despite OMT, LBBB ≥150 ms

source.book: ACC/AHA/HRS Device Therapy Guideline; ESC 2021 Pacing/CRT

questions.topic: Acute pulmonary edema days after inferior MI
questions.stem:
71M, day 4 after delayed presentation with inferior STEMI (RCA occlusion, PCI done). Suddenly dyspneic and hypotensive.

BP 82/50, HR 118, RR 30, SpO2 86% on 6 L.
New soft apical holosystolic murmur radiating to axilla
CXR: bilateral pulmonary edema

options.label: A
options.explanation: Presents with tamponade/PEA, not a new MR murmur.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Hypotension with clear lungs and raised JVP.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Wouldn't explain a new holosystolic MR murmur.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: posteromedial papillary muscle (single PDA supply) → acute severe MR.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Harsh LLSB murmur, often thrill; more with anterior MI.

questions.explanation: Papillary muscle rupture (usually posteromedial, supplied only by the PDA) typically occurs 2–7 d after inferior MI and causes acute severe MR: flash pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock. The murmur may be soft or absent. Confirm urgently by echo (TTE/TEE); treatment is afterload reduction/mechanical support as a bridge to emergency surgery.

references.title: Papillary Muscle Rupture (StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf)
references.supports: Posteromedial; days 2–7 after MI; acute MR, shock; emergency surgery

references.title: Papillary muscle rupture after acute inferior MI (Texas Heart Inst J 2021)
references.supports: Shock and pulmonary edema; TEE; emergency surgery

questions.stem:
44F, smoker, w/ 2 mo of early-morning chest pain at rest lasting 10 min, relieved by SL nitroglycerin. Normal exercise tolerance.

ECG during episode: transient inferior ST elevation
Coronary angiography: no obstructive disease

options.label: A
options.explanation: Triptans provoke coronary vasospasm.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Nonselective beta-blockers can worsen spasm (unopposed alpha).

options.label: C
options.explanation: No ACS or stent; DAPT doesn't prevent spasm.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: CCBs are first-line to prevent coronary spasm.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not first-line with nonobstructive disease.

questions.explanation: Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina: rest angina, often early morning, with transient ST elevation and nonobstructive coronaries. First-line prevention is a CCB (diltiazem, verapamil, or a dihydropyridine), adding a long-acting nitrate if needed. Stop smoking and avoid triggers; avoid beta-blockers, especially nonselective ones.

references.title: Vasospastic Angina (Merck Manual Professional, 2026)
references.supports: CCBs first-line; beta-blockers not recommended; nitrates second-line

references.title: Vasospastic angina: ED summary (Emergency Care BC)
references.supports: CCBs first-line; avoid beta-blockers; avoid triptans

source.book: ACC/AHA Chronic Coronary Disease 2023; JCS VSA 2023

questions.stem:
58M w/ HTN, 3 episodes of symptomatic typical (counterclockwise) atrial flutter in 1 y despite metoprolol; cardioverted each time. No documented AF. On apixaban.

TTE: normal LVEF, mild LA enlargement

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: cures >90% of typical flutter; superior to drugs for recurrence.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Last-resort rate control, not rhythm control.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Less effective and more toxic than ablation.

options.label: D
options.explanation: AF ablation; typical flutter is a right-atrial circuit.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Class IC drugs are less effective than ablation; IC alone risks 1:1 conduction.

questions.explanation: Typical flutter depends on the cavotricuspid isthmus; ablating it cures >90% and is preferred over antiarrhythmics for recurrent episodes. Anticoagulate flutter exactly as AF (same risk scores), including after ablation, since AF later develops in up to 60%.

references.title: Atrial Flutter (Merck Manual Professional)
references.supports: CTI ablation more effective than drugs; anticoagulate as AF

references.title: 2023 ACC/AHA AF guideline: anticoagulation of typical AFL (PMC table)
references.supports: Anticoagulate AFL by AF risk profile; ≥4 wk after ablation

issues: Answer correct: Merck states CTI ablation cures typical flutter in >95% and prevents recurrence more effectively than antiarrhythmics + AV nodal blockade; anticoagulation guidelines don't distinguish flutter from AF; AF occurs in up to 60% within 10 y.

Option 'Flecainide + metoprolol long term' explanation is inaccurate as written: the co-prescribed AV nodal blocker is what mitigates 1:1 conduction, so the explanation implies the regimen itself causes 1:1 conduction.
'continuing >=4 wk after ablation' was not verifiable in the opened sources (PMC table returned CAPTCHA); long-term OAC is decided by CHA2DS2-VASc, which is the more important teaching point.
Second reference (PMC table) could not be opened (CAPTCHA).

questions.stem:
70M w/ COPD, ex-smoker (quit 5 y ago). On LAMA/LABA/ICS single inhaler w/ good technique and adherence; completed pulmonary rehab. 3 exacerbations needing prednisone in the past year.

FEV1 42% predicted
Eos 0.2 ×10⁹/L
ECG: QTc 430 ms
No hearing loss

options.label: A
options.explanation: CTS recommends against: little benefit, narrow therapeutic window.

options.label: B
options.explanation: De-escalation; would lose LAMA benefit.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: reduces exacerbations in frequent exacerbators on maximal inhaled Tx.

options.label: D
options.explanation: No role in COPD.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Maintenance systemic steroids are recommended against.

questions.explanation: For patients still having exacerbations on optimized triple therapy, CTS 2023 recommends add-on azithromycin (best evidence in ex-smokers), or roflumilast for chronic bronchitis with FEV1 <50%. Before azithromycin, check ECG for QTc, hearing and exclude nontuberculous mycobacteria. Avoid theophylline and maintenance oral steroids.

references.title: 2023 CTS Guideline on Pharmacotherapy in Stable COPD (PDF)
references.supports: Triple for high risk; azithromycin/roflumilast/NAC for specific populations; against theophylline, oral steroids

references.title: GOLD 2023 report summary (SFHP)
references.supports: Azithromycin for exacerbations despite therapy, especially non-smokers

questions.stem:
34M, asymptomatic. Preemployment CXR shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, clear lung fields. No skin, eye or joint findings.

Spirometry and DLCO normal
Ca 2.35 mmol/L
ECG normal
IGRA negative

options.label: A
options.explanation: No role as initial or maintenance therapy here.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Steroids aren't indicated without symptoms or organ threat.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: asymptomatic stage I disease remits spontaneously in most.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Steroid-sparing agent; no indication for treatment.

options.label: E
options.explanation: More invasive than needed; biopsy optional in this presentation.

questions.explanation: Asymptomatic stage I pulmonary sarcoidosis (hilar adenopathy, normal lungs and PFTs) needs no treatment: most (60–90%) remit spontaneously. Screen for extrapulmonary involvement (eye exam, ECG, Ca, Cr, ALP) and follow with CXR/PFTs. Treat for symptoms, declining lung function, or cardiac, neuro, ocular or hypercalcemic disease.

references.title: MKSAP quiz: asymptomatic stage I sarcoidosis (ACP IM Matters 2024)
references.supports: Observation; no biopsy needed; prednisone not indicated

references.title: Sarcoidosis (5-Minute Clinical Consult)
references.supports: No treatment for asymptomatic stage I–III with normal/mild PFT; treat for cardiac, neuro, eye, hypercalcemia

issues: Answer correct and supported by ACP MKSAP (observation; neither steroids nor MTX indicated; biopsy not required for asymptomatic stage I) and 5-Minute Consult (no treatment for asymptomatic stage I-III; treat hypercalcemia, cardiac, neuro, eye disease).
'~90% remit spontaneously' overstates the figure; 5-Minute Consult gives ~50% overall resolution within 2 y; stage I remission is usually quoted as 60-90%.
Related to bank im-261030-66 (Lofgren: NSAIDs/follow-up) but distinct teaching point.

questions.stem:
29M, recently arrived from the Philippines, w/ 3 wk fever, night sweats and pleuritic pain. CXR: moderate right effusion, no parenchymal lesion.

Pleural fluid: protein 52 g/L (serum 70), LDH high
Lymphocytes 85%
Glucose 4.1 mmol/L
Gram stain and AFB smear negative
questions.lead: Most useful next test on the pleural fluid?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: ADA >40 U/L in a lymphocytic exudate strongly supports TB.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Low yield; fluid is lymphocytic, not neutrophilic.

options.label: C
options.explanation: For HF transudates, not a lymphocytic exudate.

options.label: D
options.explanation: For pancreatitis or esophageal rupture.

options.label: E
options.explanation: For chylothorax; fluid not described as milky.

questions.explanation: In a lymphocytic exudate, especially from a TB-endemic setting, pleural ADA >40 U/L makes TB pleuritis highly likely; AFB smear and fluid culture have low sensitivity. Pleural biopsy (histology plus culture) has the highest yield when needed. Treatment is the same as pulmonary TB.

references.title: Tuberculous Pleural Effusion (Light, Turk Thorac J; PMC5783039)
references.supports: Easiest Dx: ADA >40 in lymphocytic effusion; Tx as pulmonary TB

references.title: Tuberculous pleural effusions: advances and controversies (J Thorac Dis 2015)
references.supports: Lymphocytic exudate + high ADA; biopsy/culture gold standard

questions.stem:
56F, BMI 48, w/ daytime sleepiness and morning headaches. Stable outpatient. No COPD or neuromuscular disease.

ABG (RA, awake): pH 7.37, PaCO2 54 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg
HCO3 31 mmol/L
PSG: AHI 52/h
questions.lead: Most appropriate initial Tx, alongside weight-loss counselling?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Doesn't treat hypoventilation; can worsen hypercapnia.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not recommended treatment for OHS.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Reserved for failure of PAP.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: first-line for stable OHS with severe OSA (AHI ≥30).

options.label: E
options.explanation: Respiratory stimulant without proven benefit.

questions.explanation: OHS = BMI ≥30, awake hypercapnia (PaCO2 ≥45) and sleep-disordered breathing, after excluding other causes. Stable ambulatory patients should receive PAP during sleep; with concomitant severe OSA (AHI ≥30), CPAP is first-line over NIV. Sustained weight loss of 25–30% (often bariatric surgery) can resolve OHS.

references.title: ATS guideline: Evaluation and Management of OHS (PMC6680300)
references.supports: PAP for stable OHS; CPAP first-line w/ severe OSA (AHI ≥30)

references.title: ATS OHS guideline summary (Guideline Central)
references.supports: Recs 2–3; weight loss 25–30%

questions.topic: Graves' hyperthyroidism in the first trimester
questions.stem:
30F, 8 wk pregnant, w/ palpitations, tremor and weight loss. Small diffuse goitre.

TSH <0.01 mIU/L
Free T4 48 pmol/L (high)
TRAb positive

options.label: A
options.explanation: First-trimester exposure linked to congenital anomalies.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Contraindicated in pregnancy.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Overt hyperthyroidism harms mother and fetus.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: preferred in the first trimester (less teratogenic than methimazole).

options.label: E
options.explanation: If needed, best done in the second trimester.

questions.explanation: For overt Graves' hyperthyroidism in the first trimester, PTU is preferred because methimazole is associated with embryopathy during organogenesis; consider switching to methimazole after the first trimester (PTU hepatotoxicity). Use the lowest dose keeping free T4 at or just above the upper reference limit. Repeat TRAb later in pregnancy.

references.title: ATA thyroid in pregnancy: Graves' management summary (Guideline Central)
references.supports: Diagnosed in 1st trimester: begin PTU; TRAb at 18–22 wk; surgery 2nd trimester

references.title: ATA vs Endocrine Society pregnancy thyroid guidelines (PMC3674680)
references.supports: PTU first trimester; consider switch to MMI after

source.book: ATA Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy Guideline 2017

questions.topic: Suspected male hypogonadism: confirming the Dx
questions.stem:
52M w/ 6 mo of low libido and fatigue. BMI 31. No meds. Single total testosterone drawn at 4 pm.

Total testosterone 7.8 nmol/L (low)
Hb 142 g/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: low T must be confirmed on a repeat early-morning fasting sample.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Off-label; not before diagnosis is confirmed.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Diagnosis not yet confirmed.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Only after confirmed low T with low/normal LH and FSH, plus other features.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not first-line; consider if primary hypogonadism suspected.

questions.explanation: Hypogonadism requires consistent symptoms plus unequivocally low testosterone on two fasting morning measurements; ~30% of initially low values are normal on repeat, and levels are lower in the afternoon and after eating. If confirmed, measure LH/FSH to separate primary from secondary causes; use free T when SHBG is altered (e.g., obesity).

references.title: Endocrine Society: Testosterone Therapy in Men With Hypogonadism (2018)
references.supports: Confirm by repeating fasting morning total T

references.title: Testosterone guideline abstract (PubMed 29562364)
references.supports: Fasting morning total T initial test; repeat; free T if SHBG altered

questions.stem:
66M w/ T2DM on metformin admitted for COPD exacerbation; started prednisone 50 mg each morning. Eating normally.

Capillary glucose: fasting 7.2, pre-lunch 13.8, pre-supper 17.5, bedtime 15.1 mmol/L
questions.lead: Best insulin strategy for this pattern?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Targets fasting glucose, which is near normal.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: NPH peak matches the afternoon/evening prednisone effect.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Leaves marked hyperglycemia untreated.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Reactive; doesn't prevent hyperglycemia.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not needed for a stable, eating ward patient.

questions.explanation: Once-daily morning prednisone raises glucose mainly from late morning to evening, with near-normal fasting values. Matching its ~12-h profile, intermediate-acting NPH given with the steroid dose (often ~0.1 U/kg per 10 mg prednisone, titrated daily) covers this pattern; taper insulin as the steroid is reduced.

references.title: Steroid-induced hyperglycemia: Diabetes Canada-based algorithm (AACI J table)
references.supports: Once-daily AM prednisone: AM NPH; FPG less affected

references.title: NPH and prednisone therapy (BC Diabetes)
references.supports: Give NPH with prednisone before breakfast; daily titration

source.book: Diabetes Canada; BC Diabetes NPH protocol

questions.topic: Suspected IBS with diarrhea: minimal testing
questions.stem:
26F w/ 8 mo of crampy abdominal pain relieved by defecation and loose stools 3–4/d. No weight loss, bleeding, nocturnal Sx, or family Hx of IBD or colon cancer. Exam normal.

CBC normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: Not recommended unless reproducible reactions.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not routine <45 y without alarm features.

options.label: C
options.text: Stool culture, O&P and C. difficile
options.explanation: Not routine unless Giardia risk.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: ACG positive diagnostic strategy with minimal targeted tests.

options.label: E
options.text: CT abdomen and pelvis w/ contrast
options.explanation: Not indicated without alarm features.

questions.explanation: Make a positive diagnosis of IBS from Rome IV symptoms with minimal testing rather than a diagnosis of exclusion. In IBS with diarrhea, check celiac serology (tTG-IgA w/ total IgA) and fecal calprotectin (or lactoferrin) plus CRP to exclude IBD. Avoid routine colonoscopy <45 y and routine stool cultures without alarm features.

references.title: ACG IBS guideline summary (Guideline Central)
references.supports: Celiac serology; no routine stool tests or colonoscopy <45 y; positive Dx strategy

references.title: ACG IBS guideline summary (NursingCenter 2021)
references.supports: Fecal calprotectin/lactoferrin + CRP to rule out IBD

questions.stem:
38F w/ 1 y of progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, and 4 kg weight loss.

EGD: retained saliva, puckered GE junction, no mass or stricture
Biopsies normal
questions.lead: Best test to confirm the Dx?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: gold standard; also defines subtype to guide Tx.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Only if malignant pseudoachalasia is suspected.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Assesses reflux, not motility.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Supportive; used if manometry unavailable.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Endoscopy alone can't diagnose achalasia.

questions.explanation: Achalasia: dysphagia to solids and liquids with regurgitation. EGD first excludes pseudoachalasia (tumour at the GEJ), but can't confirm the Dx. High-resolution manometry is the gold standard (impaired LES relaxation, absent peristalsis) and its subtype guides therapy; timed barium esophagram is complementary.

references.title: ACG Clinical Guidelines: Diagnosis and Management of Achalasia (Am J Gastroenterol 2020, PDF)
references.supports: HRM confirms Dx; EGD, barium complementary

references.title: ACG achalasia guidelines summary (Consultant360)
references.supports: HRM gold standard; EGD to exclude pseudoachalasia

questions.stem:
59M w/ alcohol-related cirrhosis and tense ascites causing dyspnea. Diagnostic tap negative for SBP. Therapeutic paracentesis removes 8 L.

Cr 92 µmol/L
Na 132 mmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Albumin is recommended once >5 L is removed.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: prevents post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction after >5 L.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Doesn't prevent circulatory dysfunction.

options.label: D
options.text: Albumin 1.5 g/kg now and 1 g/kg day 3
options.explanation: SBP regimen, not LVP.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Less effective than albumin at preventing circulatory dysfunction.

questions.explanation: After large-volume paracentesis >5 L, give albumin 6–8 g per litre removed (e.g., ~50–60 g for 8 L) to reduce post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction, AKI, hyponatremia and mortality. Smaller taps usually don't need it unless high risk (e.g., AKI).

references.title: AASLD 2021 ascites guidance excerpt (NICE consultation summary)
references.supports: Albumin at LVP >5 L; 6–8 g/L removed

references.title: Clinical Progress Note: IV albumin in cirrhosis (J Hosp Med 2021)
references.supports: Albumin after LVP ≥5 L, 6–8 g/L

questions.stem:
79F on apixaban 5 mg BID for AF, last dose 4 h ago, p/w hematemesis and melena.

BP 78/44, HR 124.
Hb 64 g/L
Cr 96 µmol/L
INR 1.3

Resuscitation and urgent endoscopy are arranged.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Reverses heparin, not apixaban.

options.label: B
options.explanation: No effect on apixaban.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Reverses dabigatran only.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Ineffective for factor Xa inhibitors; volume load.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: standard Canadian approach for life-threatening factor Xa inhibitor bleeding.

questions.explanation: For life-threatening bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban: stop the drug, resuscitate, control the source and give 4-factor PCC (typically 2000 U; 50 U/kg, max 3000 U) per Thrombosis Canada. Andexanet alfa is rarely used (thrombotic risk, limited availability). Vitamin K, plasma and protamine don't reverse factor Xa inhibitors.

references.title: Thrombosis Canada: DOACs, management of bleeding
references.supports: PCC 2000 U (50 U/kg, max 3000) for life-threatening Xa-inhibitor bleeding

references.title: Prothrombin Complex Concentrates (McMaster Textbook of IM)
references.supports: PCC for life-threatening Xa-inhibitor bleeding; max 3000 IU

source.book: Thrombosis Canada / McMaster Textbook of IM

issues: Andexanet statement is outdated: FDA safety communication 18 Dec 2025 on thromboembolic events; AstraZeneca ended US sales 22 Dec 2025; ANNEXA-I showed increased thrombotic events incl. ischemic stroke. Presenting it as a routine 'specific alternative' is no longer appropriate.
PCC dose: Thrombosis Canada gives 50 U/kg (max 3000), typical initial dose 2000 U; draft's '25-50 U/kg' is not what the Canadian guide states.
Thieme ref (Canadian cohort) returned a bot-check page; McMaster textbook only gives max 3000 IU. Thrombosis Canada guide is a better primary Canadian source.
Overlaps bank im-261030-17 (dabigatran reversal) only as distractor; distinct teaching point.

questions.stem:
32F, 24 wk pregnant, w/ pleuritic pain and dyspnea. Hemodynamically stable.

CTPA: segmental PE, no RV strain
Weight 78 kg
Plt 210 ×10⁹/L
Cr 54 µmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Only for life-threatening hemodynamic instability.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Teratogenic and causes fetal bleeding; avoid in pregnancy.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: ASH strongly recommends LMWH over UFH; doesn't cross placenta.

options.label: D
options.explanation: DOACs cross the placenta; avoid in pregnancy.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Only if anticoagulation is contraindicated.

questions.explanation: LMWH (weight-based, therapeutic) is the anticoagulant of choice for VTE in pregnancy: it doesn't cross the placenta and needs no routine anti-Xa monitoring. Warfarin and DOACs are avoided. Continue ≥6 wk postpartum and ≥3 mo total; plan delivery with timed interruption. Warfarin or LMWH is fine while breastfeeding.

references.title: ASH 2018 VTE in pregnancy guideline (PMC6258928)
references.supports: LMWH over UFH; no routine anti-Xa monitoring

references.title: Acute VTE in pregnancy (CanadiEM Blood & Clots)
references.supports: Warfarin and DOACs contraindicated in pregnancy

issues: Accurate: CanadiEM (Thrombosis Canada authors) - LMWH anticoagulant of choice; >=3 mo total and >=6 wk postpartum; warfarin and LMWH safe in breastfeeding; DOACs not used. ASH PMC page returned CAPTCHA.
Option homogeneity: lead asks 'Most appropriate anticoagulant?' but 'Systemic alteplase' and 'IVC filter' are not anticoagulants.
Main accessible ref is a FOAMed site (CanadiEM); acceptable as it summarizes ASH, but the ASH guideline should be the primary.

questions.stem:
48F w/ 5d of mild calf discomfort after a long flight. Fully mobile; no cancer, prior VTE or pregnancy.

Whole-leg US: short thrombus in one soleal (muscular) calf vein; popliteal and proximal veins clear

options.label: A
options.explanation: Doesn't change management here.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Extension must be excluded with repeat imaging.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Provoked, low-risk distal clot; no indefinite Tx.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Preferred only w/ severe Sx or extension risk factors.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: CHEST suggests surveillance for isolated distal DVT w/o severe Sx or extension risk.

questions.explanation: For acute isolated distal (calf) DVT without severe symptoms or risk factors for extension (e.g., cancer, prior VTE, inpatient, extensive or near-proximal thrombus), CHEST 2021 suggests serial US for 2 wk over anticoagulation; anticoagulate if it extends (strongly if into proximal veins). Severe symptoms or extension risk favour anticoagulation for 3 mo.

references.title: CHEST 2021 Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease (PDF)
references.supports: No anticoagulation if thrombus doesn't extend

issues: Single best answer is compromised: CHEST 2021 lists a positive D-dimer (particularly markedly elevated) as a factor favouring anticoagulation over serial imaging; stem includes 'D-dimer mildly elevated'. Thrombus in an axial (posterior tibial) vein also makes 'Apixaban for 3 mo' defensible; CHEST lists 'confined to the muscular veins of the calf' as favouring surveillance.
Guideline Central reference is a login page; CHEST PDF is fine.

questions.stem:
74F admitted w/ pyelonephritis; blood cultures grow E. coli (ceftriaxone-susceptible). On ceftriaxone, afebrile by day 2; source controlled (no obstruction on US). Switched to PO on day 4.

WBC normalized

options.label: A
options.explanation: Used for endovascular or bone infection.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Too short; no trial support below 7 d for bacteremia.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: noninferior to 14 d for non-S. aureus bacteremia w/ clinical improvement.

options.label: D
options.explanation: For complicated infection (e.g., endocarditis, osteomyelitis).

options.label: E
options.explanation: No added benefit over 7 d; more Abx exposure.

questions.explanation: For uncomplicated non–S. aureus bacteremia (mostly gram-negative, often urinary) in a patient improving with source control, 7 d of active therapy is noninferior to 14 d (BALANCE 2025 and earlier RCTs). Extend for undrained foci, endovascular or bone/device infection. S. aureus and candidemia need longer courses.

references.title: Trial supports shorter antibiotic treatment for bloodstream infections (CIDRAP)
references.supports: BALANCE: 7 d noninferior to 14 d; 71% gram-negative

references.title: BALANCE: 7 vs 14 days for bloodstream infection (NEJM Journal Watch)
references.supports: 7 d noninferior to 14 d

issues: Accurate: BALANCE (NEJM) - 7 d noninferior to 14 d for bloodstream infection; excluded S. aureus and severe immunosuppression.
Option 'Until repeat blood cultures negative x2' is not a duration and is heterogeneous with the other options (7 d, 14 d, 4 wk, 6 wk IV).
PulmCCM reference is paywalled; CIDRAP is news. Prefer the trial publication or NEJM Journal Watch.

questions.stem: 35M bitten on the dorsal hand by a neighbour's vaccinated dog 6 h ago. Two puncture wounds over the MCP joint, mild swelling, no signs of infection. Tetanus up to date. No allergies.
questions.lead: Most appropriate antibiotic management after irrigation?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Hand bites are high risk and warrant preemptive Tx.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Misses Pasteurella.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: preemptive Tx for hand bites; covers Pasteurella, anaerobes, staph/strep.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Poor Pasteurella activity.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Alternative agent; duration too long for prophylaxis.

questions.explanation: IDSA recommends 3–5 d of preemptive antibiotics for dog or cat bites in high-risk situations: hand or face wounds, moderate–severe injury, possible joint/bone penetration, edema, immunocompromise, asplenia or advanced liver disease. Amoxicillin-clavulanate covers Pasteurella, anaerobes and staph/strep. Don't close hand wounds primarily; assess rabies risk.

references.title: IDSA SSTI guideline: dog/cat bites (Guideline Central)
references.supports: Preemptive 3–5 d for high-risk bites; amoxicillin-clavulanate

references.title: Case studies: dog bite to the hand (Pharmacy Times, IDSA 2014)
references.supports: Criteria incl. hand injuries; amox-clav 875/125 BID

questions.stem:
67M w/ T2DM and 6 wk of worsening low back pain. Afebrile, hemodynamically stable, normal neuro exam.

CRP 96 mg/L, ESR 88 mm/h
Blood cultures ×2: no growth at 48 h
MRI: L3–L4 discitis-osteomyelitis, no epidural abscess

options.label: A
options.explanation: No neurological compromise or abscess.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Inadequate empiric therapy and obscures Dx.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: obtain a microbiologic Dx first when stable and neurologically intact.

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat MRI in 4 wk, no Abx
options.explanation: Delays diagnosis.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Empiric Abx before biopsy lowers yield; reserved for sepsis or neuro deficit.

questions.explanation: In native vertebral osteomyelitis, empiric antibiotics should be withheld in stable, neurologically intact patients until a microbiologic Dx is made, since biopsy yield falls after Abx. If blood cultures don't identify S. aureus, S. lugdunensis or Brucella, do image-guided aspiration/biopsy. Start empiric Tx immediately for sepsis, instability or neuro compromise. Treat ~6 wk.

references.title: 2015 IDSA native vertebral osteomyelitis guideline: executive summary (CID)
references.supports: Withhold empiric Abx unless septic/neuro compromise; biopsy

references.title: 2015 IDSA NVO guideline full text (PDF)
references.supports: Rec 14 biopsy if no blood culture Dx; Rec 17 empiric Abx if neuro compromise

questions.stem:
60M w/ COPD and alcohol use disorder p/w vomiting and drowsiness.

ABG: pH 7.12, PaCO2 44 mmHg
HCO3 14 mmol/L
Na 138 mmol/L
Cl 100 mmol/L
Lactate 9.8 mmol/L
questions.lead: Best description of the acid-base status?

options.label: A
options.text: Anion gap metabolic acidosis w/ respiratory acidosis
options.explanation: Correct: expected PaCO2 = 1.5×14 + 8 = 29 ± 2; measured 44 is too high.

options.label: C
options.explanation: HCO3 would rise, not fall.

options.label: D
options.text: Anion gap metabolic acidosis w/ respiratory alkalosis
options.explanation: PaCO2 would be below the expected range.

options.label: E
options.text: Anion gap metabolic acidosis w/ appropriate compensation
options.explanation: Compensation would bring PaCO2 to ~27–31 mmHg.

questions.explanation: Winter's formula predicts compensation for metabolic acidosis: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ± 2 (here 27–31 mmHg). A PaCO2 above the range means a concurrent respiratory acidosis (e.g., COPD, sedation, fatigue) and signals impending ventilatory failure. AG here is 24 (lactic acidosis).

references.title: Winter's Formula (Merck Manual calculator)
references.supports: Expected PCO2 = 1.5×HCO3 + 8 ± 2; mismatch = mixed disorder

references.title: Metabolic acidosis (WikEM)
references.supports: Winter's formula; pCO2 > expected = concurrent respiratory acidosis

issues: Content and arithmetic correct (expected PaCO2 29 +/- 2; AG 24; pH consistent with HCO3/PaCO2).
Both references are FOAMed/educational blogs (Respiratory Therapy Zone, WikEM) used as main sources. Merck Manual calculator is a better mainstream source.

questions.stem:
54M w/ alcohol use disorder admitted after 2 wk of minimal intake; started on enteral feeds at full goal on day 1. On day 3 he is weak and confused.

PO4 0.28 mmol/L (day 1: 0.86)
K 2.9 mmol/L
Mg 0.52 mmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Prolonged starvation worsens malnutrition.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Insulin drives PO4 and K into cells, worsening deficits.

options.label: C
options.text: Continue full feeds and replace electrolytes
options.explanation: Calories should be reduced until electrolytes stabilize.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Ca isn't low; doesn't correct PO4, K or Mg and may precipitate with PO4.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: treat electrolytes, slow refeeding, give thiamine.

questions.explanation: Refeeding syndrome: after prolonged poor intake, carbohydrate triggers an insulin surge that shifts PO4, K and Mg into cells and consumes thiamine, typically within 5 d. In high-risk patients start at 10–20 kcal/kg/d and advance slowly. If electrolytes fall sharply, replace them, reduce calories ~50%, and give thiamine.

references.title: ASPEN Consensus Recommendations for Refeeding Syndrome (Nutr Clin Pract 2020)
references.supports: Risk, 10–20 kcal/kg start, cut calories 50% if electrolytes fall, thiamine

references.title: Refeeding syndrome (EMCrit IBCC)
references.supports: Hypophosphatemia, hypoK, hypoMg; thiamine; avoid calcium; insulin worsens

issues: Answer correct: ASPEN 2020 consensus - RS within 5 d; start 10-20 kcal/kg; reduce calories by 50% if electrolytes fall precipitously; thiamine 100 mg before feeding.

Option 'IV calcium gluconate 2 g' explanation ('Calcium can worsen hypophosphatemia') is not a standard or referenced mechanism; EMCrit only advises avoiding calcium if possible during PO4 repletion (precipitation).
Both refs are FOAMed (WikEM, EMCrit IBCC) despite the WikEM title claiming ASPEN; the ASPEN consensus PDF is available.

questions.topic: Anemia in CKD: iron before ESA
questions.stem:
72F w/ CKD G4 (eGFR 22), not on dialysis, w/ fatigue. No GI Sx; colonoscopy 2 y ago normal.

Hb 92 g/L, MCV 82 fL
Ferritin 62 µg/L
TSAT 14%
B12, folate normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: KDIGO prefers ESA over HIF-PHI, and only after iron repletion.

options.label: B
options.explanation: ESA only after iron deficiency and other causes corrected.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not needed at Hb 92 in a stable patient.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Anemia is explained by CKD and iron deficiency.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: correct iron deficiency first; may raise Hb without ESA.

questions.explanation: In anemia of CKD, first correct reversible causes, especially iron deficiency; iron alone may raise Hb and lowers later ESA needs. KDIGO 2026 suggests iron in non-dialysis CKD when ferritin <100 µg/L with TSAT <40% (or ferritin 100–300 with TSAT <25%); oral or IV is acceptable. Consider an ESA only once iron-replete, individualized to symptoms and transfusion risk.

references.title: KDIGO 2026 anemia in CKD guideline spotlight (Guideline Central)
references.supports: Non-dialysis CKD: iron if ferritin <100 and TSAT <40%, or 100–300 and TSAT <25%

references.title: New KDIGO anemia guideline (Epocrates 2026)
references.supports: Address iron deficiency before anemia drugs; ESA over HIF-PHI

issues: Iron thresholds correct per KDIGO 2026 (non-dialysis: ferritin <100 and TSAT <40%, or ferritin 100-300 and TSAT <25%; oral or IV); ESA preferred over HIF-PHI first-line.
Last sentence inaccurate for non-dialysis CKD: KDIGO 2026 gives no fixed Hb threshold for ESA start in ND-CKD (the 90-100 g/L threshold applies to dialysis); decision is individualized.
Explanation 57 words is fine. Epocrates reference failed to load (server error).

questions.stem:
48M of Korean descent w/ 3 gout flares this year and CKD G3a (eGFR 52). Plan to start urate-lowering Tx.

Urate 560 µmol/L
questions.lead: Most appropriate step before starting allopurinol?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: ACR recommends testing in Southeast Asian (e.g., Korean, Han Chinese, Thai) and African American patients.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Relevant to azathioprine, not allopurinol.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Predicts abacavir hypersensitivity.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Relevant to pegloticase/rasburicase.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Doesn't change the choice of first-line ULT.

questions.explanation: HLA-B*58:01 strongly predicts allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS); risk rises further with CKD. ACR 2020 conditionally recommends testing before allopurinol in patients of Southeast Asian (Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) or African American descent, and against routine testing in others. If positive, use an alternative such as febuxostat.

references.title: HLA-B and allopurinol (Medical Genetics Summaries, NCBI)
references.supports: ACR: test before allopurinol in SE Asian and African American patients

references.title: ACR 2020 gout guideline release (Newswise)
references.supports: Conditional rec for HLA-B*5801 testing in high-prevalence groups

questions.stem:
62F w/ new GCA starting prednisone 50 mg daily, planned taper over ≥12 mo. No prior fracture.

DXA: femoral neck T-score −2.1
FRAX (GC-adjusted): 10-y major fracture 23%
Cr, Ca, 25-OH vitamin D normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: Insufficient for high fracture risk.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: high fracture risk on long-term GC warrants pharmacologic Tx.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not recommended for GIOP.

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat DXA in 2 y before deciding
options.explanation: Bone loss is fastest in the first months.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Risk starts at ≥2.5 mg/d for >3 mo; start now.

questions.explanation: Anyone expected to take prednisone ≥2.5 mg/d for >3 mo needs early fracture-risk assessment (FRAX adjusted for dose, BMD), calcium, vitamin D and lifestyle measures. For adults ≥40 at moderate or high risk, start osteoporosis therapy: oral bisphosphonates are strongly recommended (cheap, effective); denosumab or an anabolic agent are alternatives, favoured at very high risk.

references.title: ACR 2022 GIOP guideline summary (Guideline Central)
references.supports: Prednisone ≥2.5 mg >3 mo; oral BP for high risk ≥40; Tx for medium/high risk

references.title: ACR 2022 GIOP guideline (RheumNow)
references.supports: Calcium/vit D for all; options by risk

issues: Keyed answer is best among the options (no denosumab/anabolic option offered). ACR 2022: applies to prednisone >=2.5 mg/d >3 mo; oral bisphosphonates strongly recommended over no Tx for high risk (FRAX MOF >=20%).

Explanation overstates 'oral bisphosphonate is the usual first choice': per RheumNow summary, ACR 2022 conditionally prefers denosumab or PTH/PTHrP over bisphosphonates in some high-risk adults >=40 and anabolics for very high risk; the 2017 ACR version is the one that explicitly preferred oral BP. Prednisone 50 mg may also place her near very-high-risk territory.
Option 'Defer until prednisone <7.5 mg' explanation fine.

questions.stem:
71M on hydralazine for 2 y for resistant HTN (with isosorbide) p/w 6 wk of arthralgias, myalgias, fever and pleuritic pain. No rash, nephritis or neuro Sx.

ANA 1:1280 homogeneous
Anti-histone positive
Anti-dsDNA negative, C3/C4 normal
UA normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: Normal UA; nephritis is rare in drug-induced lupus.

options.label: B
options.explanation: No major organ involvement.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Unneeded without severe organ disease.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Culprit drug must be stopped.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: drug-induced lupus usually resolves within weeks of withdrawal.

questions.explanation: Drug-induced lupus (classically hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline, anti-TNF) causes arthralgia, myalgia, fever and serositis, with ANA and anti-histone antibodies; dsDNA, low complement and major organ disease are uncommon. Treatment is stopping the drug; symptoms resolve over weeks. NSAIDs or a short steroid course help symptoms.

references.title: Drug-Induced Lupus (University of Calgary teaching notes 2024)
references.supports: Anti-histone in 95%; dsDNA/low complement rare; stop drug; NSAIDs

references.title: Hydralazine-induced lupus with pneumonitis (PMC5591929)
references.supports: Anti-histone >95%; improvement after withdrawal

questions.topic: Prior contrast reaction: next contrast CT
questions.stem: 58F needs contrast-enhanced CT abdomen for suspected abscess. 2 y ago she had generalized urticaria (no hypotension or bronchospasm) after iohexol; resolved w/ cetirizine. No other allergies.
questions.lead: Per current Canadian guidance, best strategy?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Unnecessary; reactions are agent-specific.

options.label: B
options.text: Skin-test all agents before any CT
options.explanation: Not required for a prior mild–moderate reaction.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Inadequate imaging for abscess.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a different iodinated contrast agent
options.explanation: Correct: switching agents is the single best protective measure.

options.label: E
options.text: Same agent after prednisone 13, 7 and 1 h before
options.explanation: Steroid premedication isn't supported for low-osmolar agents.

questions.explanation: CAR/CSACI 2025: risk applies only to the same contrast class, and for a prior hypersensitivity reaction to an iodinated agent, switching to a chemically different agent is the single best protective measure. Steroid premedication for low-osmolar agents isn't supported by good evidence.

references.title: CAR/CSACI Practice Guidance for Contrast Media Hypersensitivity (Can Assoc Radiol J 2025)
references.supports: Canadian guidance on pretreatment strategies

references.title: Stop using steroids to pretreat contrast allergy: CAR/CSACI summary (First10EM)
references.supports: Switch agent single best measure; steroids not supported for LOCM

issues: Answer correct: CAR/CSACI 2025 Rec 2 (risk only with same contrast class), Rec 3 (switching to a chemically different agent is the single best protective measure), Rec 5 (steroid premedication not supported).
'Shellfish allergy is not a risk factor' is not stated in the CAR/CSACI guidance (only in a reader comment on First10EM); unsupported by the cited references and adds length.
First10EM is a FOAMed blog but used only as secondary to the primary guidance - acceptable.

questions.stem: 84M w/ advanced dementia, now incapable of consenting to a feeding tube. No guardian or power of attorney for personal care. Lives w/ his common-law partner of 15 y; his adult daughter, who visits weekly, disagrees with the partner's decision.
questions.lead: Under Ontario's Health Care Consent Act, who is the SDM?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Physicians aren't SDMs under the HCCA.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: spouse or partner ranks above children.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Only the highest-ranking available, capable, willing person decides.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Children rank below a spouse or partner.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Last resort when no one else qualifies.

questions.explanation: Ontario HCCA ranks SDMs: guardian, attorney for personal care, Consent and Capacity Board representative, spouse or partner, child or parent, parent w/ right of access, sibling, any other relative, then the Public Guardian and Trustee. The highest-ranking person who is capable, available and willing decides, guided by the patient's known prior capable wishes, else best interests.

references.title: Substitute Decision-Maker (UHN Advance Care Planning)
references.supports: Ontario SDM hierarchy

references.title: Health Care Consent Act, 1996 (Ontario e-Laws)
references.supports: s.20 SDM ranking

issues: Content correct (spouse/partner ranks above child; highest-ranking capable, available, willing SDM decides).

Reference 1 (HQO quality statement) now 302-redirects to a generic Ontario Health page - dead link. Reference 2 points to e-Laws '/v2', a historical version of the HCCA, not the current consolidation.

Yield caveat: Ontario-specific statute recall is lower-yield for a national Royal College exam; the transferable principles (SDM hierarchy, prior capable wishes then best interests) are what matter. Acceptable for an Ontario-based learner.

questions.stem:
61M w/ metastatic melanoma on pembrolizumab. 6 wk ago transient thyrotoxicosis (painless, resolved). Now mild fatigue; managing daily activities.

TSH 38 mIU/L
Free T4 7 pmol/L (low)
AM cortisol 420 nmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Not needed for a replaceable endocrinopathy.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: replace hormone; ICI can usually continue for thyroid irAEs.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Overt symptomatic hypothyroidism needs treatment.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Thyrotoxic phase was destructive and has passed; now hypothyroid.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Steroids don't help immune thyroiditis.

questions.explanation: ICI thyroiditis is often a transient painless thyrotoxic phase followed by permanent hypothyroidism. Treat hypothyroidism with levothyroxine; corticosteroids aren't helpful, and the ICI can usually continue (hold only temporarily for significant symptoms). Check cortisol first to exclude hypophysitis/adrenal insufficiency before starting thyroid hormone.

references.title: Immune-Related Thyroiditis with ICIs (Thyroid 2018; PMC6157359)
references.supports: Hypothyroidism after thyroiditis; remained on levothyroxine and ICI

references.title: Anti-PD-1 thyroiditis management guidance (Ann Transl Med; PMC4971373)
references.supports: Continue anti-PD-1 while treating thyroid disorder; hydrocortisone before LT4 if AI

questions.stem:
24M, 1 wk after a viral URTI, p/w pleuritic chest pain. Hemodynamically stable.

ECG: diffuse ST elevation
hs-troponin T 410 ng/L (rising)
CRP 64 mg/L
TTE: LVEF 50%, mild inferolateral hypokinesis
Coronary angiography: normal coronaries
questions.lead: Best next test to confirm the Dx?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Rarely changes management; doesn't confirm myocarditis.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: tissue characterization (edema, LGE) confirms myocarditis noninvasively.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Contraindicated with active myocardial inflammation.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Coronaries already shown normal.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Reserved for unstable, fulminant or unexplained cases.

questions.explanation: Chest pain with rising troponin and unobstructed coronaries in a young adult after a viral illness suggests acute myocarditis. Cardiac MRI (2018 Lake Louise criteria: T2-based edema plus T1-based injury such as LGE) is the key noninvasive confirmatory test; endomyocardial biopsy is reserved for unstable, fulminant or atypical cases. Avoid strenuous exercise for 3–6 mo.

references.title: ACC 2024 ECDP on myocarditis: key points (ACC)
references.supports: CMR valuable for Dx; EMB not routine; avoid strenuous activity 3–6 mo

references.title: ACC myocarditis 2024 guidelines spotlight (Guideline Central)
references.supports: Stable patient: CMR and, when necessary, EMB

issues: Accurate per ACC 2024 ECDP: CMR for diagnosis, EMB for selected cases, avoid strenuous exercise 3–6 mo. Lake Louise criteria are not in the cited pages but are standard. No overlap with the bank.

questions.topic: Stable chest pain: first-line anatomic test
questions.stem:
56F w/ 2 mo of exertional chest tightness relieved by rest. HTN, smoker. Able to exercise. No prior CAD.

Resting ECG normal
Cr 70 µmol/L
hs-troponin normal ×2

options.label: A
options.explanation: Doesn't assess stenosis or noncalcified plaque.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Lower diagnostic accuracy; no longer preferred first-line.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Reserved for high probability or high-risk features.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Typical angina with risk factors warrants testing.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: first-line for low–intermediate pretest probability of obstructive CAD.

questions.explanation: For suspected chronic coronary syndrome with low to moderate pretest likelihood of obstructive CAD, ESC 2024 recommends CCTA first-line to diagnose CAD and guide prevention (AHA/ACC 2021 accept CCTA or stress testing); functional imaging is preferred at higher probability. Exercise ECG alone is less accurate. Invasive angiography is for high probability or refractory symptoms.

references.title: Comments on the 2024 ESC chronic coronary syndromes guidelines (Rev Esp Cardiol)
references.supports: CCTA recommended for low–moderate (>5–50%) pretest likelihood (IA)

references.title: 2021 AHA/ACC Chest Pain Guideline: ten points to remember (ACC)
references.supports: US guidance accepts CCTA or stress testing for intermediate-risk stable chest pain

issues: ESC 2024 supports CCTA (IA) for low–moderate (>5–50%) pretest likelihood. However, the 2021 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline does not rank CCTA above functional testing (either is acceptable), so 'ESC/ACC guidance' and 'ACC/AHA 2021' overstate the evidence.
Second reference is a small systematic review in a low-impact journal (WJC); it adds little.

questions.stem:
33F w/ chronic HTN on ramipril 10 mg daily has a positive pregnancy test at 7 wk. No proteinuria.

BP 146/94
Cr 62 µmol/L

options.label: A
options.text: Stop ramipril; no Tx unless BP ≥160/110
options.explanation: Tight control (DBP ~85) is now preferred.

options.label: B
options.explanation: ACEi should be stopped as soon as pregnancy is known.

options.label: C
options.explanation: ARBs are also contraindicated in pregnancy.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: ACEi fetotoxic; labetalol (or nifedipine, methyldopa) first-line.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not a preferred agent in pregnancy.

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal renal toxicity, oligohydramnios) and should be switched as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. First-line oral agents are labetalol, nifedipine (long-acting) or methyldopa. Canadian and most guidelines treat BP ≥140/90 and target diastolic ~85 (CHIPS). Start ASA 81–162 mg nightly before 16 wk.

references.title: SOGC Guideline No. 426: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy (JOGC 2022)
references.supports: Avoid RAS blockers in pregnancy; first-line agents; ASA for preeclampsia prevention

references.title: Preferred antihypertensives in pregnancy (JACC 2021, PMC8061780)
references.supports: First-line labetalol, nifedipine ER, methyldopa; ACEi/ARB contraindicated

issues: Content is correct: stop ACEi/ARB, use labetalol/nifedipine/methyldopa, treat ≥140/90 with DBP target 85 (SOGC 2022, Hypertension Canada, CHIPS).
Primary reference is a Research Square preprint (Feb 2026, not peer-reviewed); the second (PMC table) returns a CAPTCHA. Neither is a primary guideline.
Nifedipine ER is an equally valid first-line choice and isn't offered, so labetalol is uncontested. Acceptable.

questions.stem:
64M w/ prior MI on atorvastatin 80 mg c/o symmetric thigh aches for 6 wk that limit his walking. Strength normal. No dark urine.

CK 180 U/L (normal <200)
TSH normal
LDL-C 1.5 mmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Normal CK and strength; not indicated.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Symptoms warrant reassessment rather than ignoring.

options.label: C
options.text: Pause, then rechallenge at lower dose
options.explanation: Correct: dechallenge–rechallenge; lower-dose statin beats no statin.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Premature 'intolerance' label forfeits proven secondary-prevention benefit.

options.label: E
options.explanation: No convincing benefit for statin myalgia.

questions.explanation: Statin muscle symptoms with normal CK are common and often not statin-caused (nocebo). Use a dechallenge–rechallenge approach: stop briefly until symptoms resolve, then restart at a lower dose, a different statin, or intermittent dosing; add ezetimibe if needed. Stop and investigate if CK >4× ULN, weakness or rhabdomyolysis. Avoid labelling intolerance too quickly in high-risk patients.

references.title: NHS England statin intolerance pathway (2022)
references.supports: Muscle symptoms without CK rise; dechallenge, rechallenge lower dose/alternative statin

issues: The stem doesn't say the symptoms are intolerable. Per the NHS AAC pathway, tolerable myalgia with CK <4× ULN can continue the statin, which makes 'Continue atorvastatin 80 mg unchanged' defensible.
GPnotebook is a tertiary reference site (weak). The NHS pathway is adequate, and a Canadian source would be better.

questions.stem:
66F w/ HTN and dyslipidemia, no known CAD, stroke or PAD. On ramipril and rosuvastatin. Nonsmoker. Asks whether to start daily ASA 81 mg.

10-y CV risk: 14%

options.label: A
options.explanation: Net benefit not shown for primary prevention at this age.

options.label: B
options.explanation: PPI doesn't create an indication for ASA.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: in primary prevention ≥60 y, bleeding risk offsets benefit.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Higher dose adds bleeding without benefit.

options.label: E
options.explanation: No primary-prevention indication.

questions.explanation: Without established ASCVD, routine ASA isn't recommended; USPSTF 2022 advises against starting ASA for primary prevention at ≥60 y (bleeding risk offsets the small benefit), and ACC/AHA advise against it >70 y or with raised bleeding risk. Focus on BP, lipids and smoking. ASA remains indicated for secondary prevention.

references.title: USPSTF aspirin for CVD prevention: clinician summary (2022)
references.supports: Age ≥60: do not initiate ASA for primary prevention

references.title: USPSTF recommends against initiating aspirin ≥60 y (AAFP POEM 2022)
references.supports: D recommendation ≥60; shared decision 40–59 if risk ≥10%

issues: Accurate (USPSTF 2022 grade D ≥60 y). Canadian guidance also doesn't support routine primary-prevention ASA. No duplication.

questions.stem:
28F w/ asthma, using only salbutamol PRN, treated in the ED for an exacerbation. After salbutamol, ipratropium and prednisone 50 mg, she is comfortable.

SpO2 97% RA
PEF 78% predicted (initially 45%)

options.label: A
options.text: Prednisone 14 d taper, no inhaler change
options.explanation: Controller therapy is the key gap here.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: GINA discharge bundle.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Less effective than ICS-containing therapy.

options.label: D
options.explanation: No role without bacterial infection.

options.label: E
options.explanation: salbutamol-only Tx is unsafe; ICS needed after an exacerbation.

questions.explanation: After an ED visit for asthma, GINA recommends starting (or stepping up) regular ICS-containing therapy, ideally budesonide-formoterol MART, plus a 5–7 d oral corticosteroid course (prednisone 40–50 mg) for adults. Check technique and adherence, give a written action plan, and arrange follow-up within 2–7 d. Never discharge on salbutamol alone.

references.title: GINA Summary Guide 2024
references.supports: Post-ED discharge: start/step up ICS-containing therapy, 5–7 d OCS, follow-up within 2–7 d

issues: Content matches GINA: ICS-containing maintenance (ICS-formoterol MART preferred), OCS for 5–7 d, follow-up within 2–7 d.
Reference 1 is a university library proxy (bestpractice-bmj-com.bibliotheek.ehb.be); reference 2 (PMC table) returns a CAPTCHA.
Partial overlap with bank im-261030-11 and im-261031-37 (ICS-formoterol, never SABA alone), but the post-ED discharge angle is distinct.

questions.stem:
68M, 50 pack-years, w/ progressive exertional dyspnea.

Post-BD FEV1/FVC 0.52
FEV1 48% predicted, no significant BD response
TLC 128% predicted
RV 165% predicted
DLCO 38% predicted
Hb 148 g/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: obstruction w/ hyperinflation and low DLCO.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Obstruction w/ normal or near-normal DLCO.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Restrictive (low TLC) w/ low DLCO.

options.label: D
options.explanation: DLCO normal or high; often significant BD response.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Isolated low DLCO w/ normal spirometry.

questions.explanation: Interpret PFTs stepwise: FEV1/FVC for obstruction, TLC for restriction/hyperinflation, then DLCO. Obstruction with hyperinflation (high TLC, RV) and low DLCO indicates alveolar–capillary loss, i.e., emphysema. Asthma and chronic bronchitis usually have normal (asthma sometimes high) DLCO; low DLCO with restriction suggests ILD.

references.title: Pulmonary function tests: quick talk (Society of Hospital Medicine)
references.supports: Abnormal DLCO with obstruction suggests emphysema rather than asthma

references.title: Pulmonary function tests (Vanderbilt IM book)
references.supports: Low DLCO + obstruction: emphysema; normal DLCO + obstruction: asthma

issues: Accurate and appropriate level.

Overlaps bank im-261030-39 (stepwise PFT interpretation, restriction with low DLCO). The last explanation sentence ('isolated low DLCO suggests pulmonary vascular disease or anemia') is nearly verbatim from that item.
The VUMC handbook is an institutional teaching page (acceptable but weak).

questions.topic: CAP: when to order urinary antigens
questions.stem:
52M admitted to the ward w/ CAP in January (influenza circulating locally). No recent travel or known Legionella outbreak. Started on ceftriaxone + azithromycin.

T 38.4, HR 98, RR 22, BP 128/76, SpO2 93% on 2 L.
CURB-65: 1
Not meeting severe CAP criteria
questions.lead: Which additional test is recommended routinely?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Shouldn't be used to withhold Abx for confirmed CAP.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Only severe CAP or MRSA/Pseudomonas risk factors.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: test for influenza in all CAP when it's circulating.

options.label: D
options.explanation: ATS/IDSA: only in severe CAP.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Only severe CAP, outbreak, or travel exposure.

questions.explanation: ATS/IDSA 2019: in nonsevere inpatient CAP, routine blood and sputum cultures and pneumococcal/Legionella urinary antigens aren't recommended. Reserve urinary antigens for severe CAP (and Legionella testing for outbreaks or travel). When influenza is circulating, test all CAP patients with a molecular assay, since a positive result changes management.

references.title: CAP: updated ATS/IDSA recommendations (AFP 2020)
references.supports: No routine cultures or urinary antigens in nonsevere CAP; influenza testing when circulating

references.title: Understanding the new pneumonia guideline (ACEP 2019)
references.supports: Against urinary antigens unless severe or outbreak; test influenza

issues: The key (influenza PCR) is correct only 'when influenza is circulating', but the stem doesn't say so, so the keyed answer isn't strictly supported.

The 2025 ATS CAP update (ATS-only) addresses antibiotics, steroids and duration. Search results don't show it changing the 2019 testing recommendations, though this wasn't confirmed against the full text.

questions.topic: Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: oxygen strategy
questions.stem:
61F w/ multilobar pneumonia, alert, no COPD. Despite non-rebreather mask:

RR 32, SpO2 88%, HR 112, BP 118/70.
ABG: pH 7.46, PaCO2 32 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg
CXR: bilateral consolidation

options.label: A
options.explanation: Premature; noninvasive support first.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Lower FiO2 than current; inadequate.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: ERS suggests HFNC over conventional O2 and NIV in hypoxemic ARF.

options.label: D
options.explanation: HFNC preferred for hypoxemic, non-hypercapnic failure.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not yet required: alert, protecting airway; monitor closely.

questions.explanation: In acute hypoxemic (non-hypercapnic) respiratory failure, ERS 2022 suggests HFNC over conventional oxygen and over NIV; it delivers high FiO2 with some PEEP and dead-space washout and is well tolerated. For hypercapnic COPD exacerbations, trial NIV first. Reassess within 1–2 h and avoid delaying intubation if failing.

references.title: ERS clinical practice guidelines: HFNC in acute respiratory failure (ERJ 2022)
references.supports: HFNC over COT and over NIV in hypoxaemic ARF; NIV first in hypercapnic COPD

references.title: ERS HFNC guideline abstract (PubMed 34649974)
references.supports: Eight conditional recommendations

issues: Consistent with ERS 2022 HFNC guideline (HFNC over COT and over NIV in hypoxaemic ARF). Both ERS links failed to load (site error), but search results confirm the guideline. No duplication; complements bank im-261031-09 (NIV in hypercapnic AECOPD).

questions.stem:
82F on digoxin for AF, recently started on clarithromycin; 3 d of nausea, confusion and yellow-tinged vision. eGFR 28.

HR 38, irregular; BP 84/50
K 6.1 mmol/L
Digoxin 4.2 nmol/L (high)
ECG: slow AF, scooped ST depression

options.label: A
options.explanation: Digoxin's large Vd makes dialysis ineffective.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Temporizes K but leaves toxicity untreated.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Doesn't reverse toxicity; Fab preferred.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: life-threatening bradyarrhythmia, hypotension, hyperkalemia.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not first-line for digoxin-related hyperkalemia; Fab is definitive.

questions.explanation: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments are indicated for known or suspected digoxin toxicity with life-threatening arrhythmia, hemodynamic instability, cardiac arrest, or K ≥5 mmol/L after acute ingestion. They work within ~30–60 min. Toxicity is often precipitated by CKD or interacting drugs (macrolides, amiodarone, verapamil). Monitor K (may drop) and watch for rebound in CKD.

references.title: Management of digoxin toxicity (Aust Prescr 2016, PMC4816869)
references.supports: Fab for life-threatening arrhythmia, arrest, K >5.0

references.title: Quebec antidote guide: digoxin-specific antibodies (CIUSSS Capitale-Nationale)
references.supports: Indications for digoxin Fab

source.book: Digoxin Fab product monograph; Aust Prescr review

issues: Key is correct.

The explanation lists 'K >5 mmol/L' as a general Fab indication. The Quebec antidote guide lists K ≥5 only for acute ingestion; in chronic toxicity, hyperkalemia often reflects renal failure. Here the bradyarrhythmia and hypotension carry the indication.
Reference 2 is the 2009 DIGIBIND monograph (a discontinued product). Replace it with a current Canadian antidote source.

questions.topic: New T2DM well above target: initial therapy
questions.stem:
52M w/ newly Dx T2DM. Asymptomatic, no weight loss. No ASCVD, CKD or HF. eGFR 88.

HbA1c 9.1%
Fasting glucose 11.2 mmol/L
No ketones

options.label: A
options.explanation: Metformin remains first-line.

options.label: B
options.explanation: For symptomatic hyperglycemia or decompensation.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Too slow; target should be reached in 3–6 mo.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Inadequate when HbA1c is ≥1.5% above target.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: HbA1c ≥1.5% above target → consider dual therapy.

questions.explanation: Diabetes Canada: start lifestyle measures and metformin at diagnosis; if HbA1c is ≥1.5% above target, consider starting a second agent concurrently. Start insulin immediately for symptomatic hyperglycemia or metabolic decompensation. With ASCVD, CKD or HF, add an agent with cardiorenal benefit (SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA). Aim to reach target within 3–6 mo.

references.title: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 13: Pharmacologic glycemic management of T2DM
references.supports: Metformin at diagnosis; add second agent if HbA1c ≥1.5% above target

issues: Accurate per Diabetes Canada Ch. 13: metformin first-line; consider 2 agents if A1C ≥1.5% above target; insulin if symptomatic/decompensated; target in 3–6 mo.
Reference 1 URL (2024 Quick Reference Guide PDF) now redirects to the general guidelines page, so the link is dead.

questions.stem:
70F w/ osteoporosis treated w/ denosumab 60 mg q6mo for 5 y. Now wishes to stop. No fractures on Tx. Last dose 5 mo ago.

DXA: femoral neck T-score −2.0 (was −2.8)
eGFR 72

options.label: A
options.explanation: Rapid rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: transition to a bisphosphonate prevents rebound bone loss.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Doesn't prevent rebound resorption.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Delays/permits rebound; not recommended.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Weaker antiresorptive; not shown to prevent rebound.

questions.explanation: Denosumab's effect wears off ~6 mo after a dose, causing rebound bone turnover, rapid BMD loss and multiple vertebral fractures. It shouldn't be stopped without follow-on therapy: give a bisphosphonate, usually zoledronic acid 6–8 mo after the last injection (or oral alendronate), ideally with specialist input after ≥5 doses; some need a repeat infusion. Unlike bisphosphonates, denosumab has no drug holiday.

references.title: Denosumab discontinuation and multiple vertebral fractures (Cleve Clin J Med 2020)
references.supports: Rebound-associated vertebral fractures after cessation

references.title: Osteoporosis Canada position statement: BTMs after denosumab discontinuation
references.supports: Bisphosphonate transition after stopping denosumab

issues: Teaching point is correct and high-yield. It complements bank im-261030-181 (bisphosphonate holiday) without duplicating it.

Reference 1 is an MDedge news blog (weak). Osteoporosis Canada (2024) advises specialist input after ≥5 doses. The Endocrine Society suggests zoledronic acid ~8 mo after the last dose and ECTS ~6 mo, so '6 mo' is too precise.
Options 'Stop; no further therapy' and 'Drug holiday with DXA in 2 y' are essentially the same action.

questions.stem:
48M s/p transsphenoidal resection of a nonfunctioning macroadenoma, on hydrocortisone and levothyroxine 75 µg. Persistent fatigue.

TSH 0.08 mIU/L
Free T4 9 pmol/L (low-normal 9–23)
Adherent to hydrocortisone 15 mg/d

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: in central hypothyroidism, titrate to free T4, not TSH.

options.label: B
options.text: Recheck TSH in 6 wk, no change
options.explanation: TSH can't guide therapy here.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not first step; optimize T4 dose.

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce dose because TSH is low
options.explanation: TSH is unreliable with pituitary disease.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Free T4 is at the bottom of range with symptoms.

questions.explanation: In central (secondary) hypothyroidism TSH is low or inappropriately normal and can't guide replacement; dosing by TSH leads to under-treatment. Titrate levothyroxine to a free T4 in the mid–upper reference range, rechecking 2–3 wk after changes (sooner than the usual 6–8 wk TSH interval). Always replace cortisol before thyroid hormone if adrenal insufficiency coexists.

references.title: MKSAP: monitoring levothyroxine in central hypothyroidism (ACP IM Matters 2024)
references.supports: Free T4 test of choice; mid–upper half; check 2–3 wk after change

references.title: Central hypothyroidism: diagnosis and monitoring (Can Fam Physician, PMC3114669)
references.supports: TSH can't monitor therapy; free T4 upper half

issues: Accurate (free T4 mid–upper range; recheck 2–3 wk).
'AM cortisol on Tx adequate' is clinically meaningless: AM cortisol isn't used to monitor hydrocortisone replacement.

questions.topic: Acute lower GI bleed, hemodynamically stable
questions.stem:
76M w/ diverticulosis p/w 3 episodes of maroon stool. Now no further bleeding. Not on anticoagulants.

HR 88, BP 132/76 (shock index <1)
Hb 104 g/L (baseline 130)
Urea normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: No outcome benefit over nonurgent inpatient scope.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Only after positive CTA in unstable bleeding.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Restrictive threshold of 70 applies.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: urgent (<24 h) colonoscopy doesn't improve outcomes.

options.label: E
options.text: CT angiography of the abdomen now
options.explanation: For hemodynamically significant ongoing bleeding.

questions.explanation: ACG 2023: risk-stratify lower GI bleeding (e.g., Oakland score). Stable patients needing admission should have nonurgent inpatient colonoscopy after bowel prep, since urgent colonoscopy within 24 h hasn't improved rebleeding or mortality. CT angiography first for hemodynamically significant ongoing bleeding. Use a restrictive Hb threshold of 70 g/L (80 with CAD); upper source if unstable with high urea.

references.title: Management of acute LGIB: ACG guideline summary (AFP 2024)
references.supports: Colonoscopy standard for stable; CTA for unstable; delayed as effective as <24 h

issues: Accurate per ACG 2023 (nonurgent inpatient colonoscopy; CTA for hemodynamically significant bleeding; Hb threshold 70, 80 with CVD).
Reference 2 is the emDocs FOAMed blog; AFP is sufficient.

questions.stem:
24F w/ ileal Crohn's Dx 2 mo ago: 6 loose stools/d, abdominal pain, weight loss 5 kg. Improved on prednisone but flares on taper below 20 mg. Currently on mesalamine 4 g/d.

CRP 38 mg/L
Calprotectin 820 µg/g

options.label: A
options.explanation: Antibiotics aren't maintenance therapy for luminal CD.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Avoid chronic steroids; use steroid-sparing therapy.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not effective for maintenance.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Mesalamine is ineffective in Crohn's.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: advanced therapy for moderate–severe, steroid-dependent CD.

questions.explanation: ACG 2025 recommends against oral mesalamine for induction or maintenance in Crohn's disease. Moderate–severe or steroid-dependent disease should start advanced therapy early (anti-TNF such as infliximab or adalimumab, or ustekinumab, vedolizumab, risankizumab, upadacitinib), rather than step-up. Steroids are for short-term induction only (taper ≤3 mo). Screen for TB and HBV first.

references.title: Updated 2025 ACG Crohn's guideline (EBGI)
references.supports: Against step-up; against mesalamine; anti-TNF etc.

references.title: ACG Crohn's disease guideline highlights 2025
references.supports: Against mesalamine; early advanced therapy

issues: Accurate per ACG 2025 (against mesalamine and budesonide maintenance; early advanced therapy; steroids <3 mo).
Reference 1 is a university library proxy (jamanetwork-com.libproxy.ajou.ac.kr).

questions.stem:
56M w/ alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites. Cr rose from 90 to 240 µmol/L over 4 d. Diuretics stopped and albumin 1 g/kg/d given for 2 d without improvement. No shock, nephrotoxins or proteinuria; normal renal US.

Na 128 mmol/L
Urine Na <10 mmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: first-line vasoconstrictor therapy for HRS-AKI.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Lowers renal perfusion; contraindicated.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Volume already optimized; worsens ascites.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Worsens renal perfusion.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Needs a vasoconstrictor once HRS-AKI is diagnosed.

questions.explanation: HRS-AKI is diagnosed when AKI in cirrhosis with ascites persists after diuretic withdrawal and 2 d of albumin (1 g/kg/d), without shock, nephrotoxins or structural kidney disease. AASLD/EASL recommend terlipressin plus albumin first-line; norepinephrine (ICU) or midodrine-octreotide are alternatives. Watch for volume overload and hypoxemia. Refer for liver transplant assessment.

references.title: Terlipressin in hepatorenal syndrome (Cleve Clin J Med 2023)
references.supports: AASLD 2021/EASL: terlipressin + albumin first-line; HRS criteria

references.title: HRS-AKI management (PMC10038893)
references.supports: Albumin 1 g/kg ×2 d; vasoconstrictors with albumin; caution pulmonary edema

issues: Accurate per AASLD 2021/EASL (terlipressin + albumin first-line; HRS-AKI criteria).

Canadian access to terlipressin may be limited; I couldn't confirm Health Canada status. The explanation already names norepinephrine and midodrine-octreotide as alternatives, which covers this. Consider adding '(availability in Canada is limited)'. No duplication.

questions.stem:
54F w/ fatigue and pruritus. No alcohol or new meds.

ALP 380 U/L (×3 ULN), GGT high
ALT 62 U/L, bilirubin normal
US: normal bile ducts, no mass
AMA positive (1:320)

options.label: A
options.explanation: Not effective for PBC.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Ducts normal on US; PSC unlikely with AMA positive.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: raised ALP + AMA establishes PBC; biopsy not needed.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Only if AMA-negative or overlap suspected.

options.label: E
options.text: Repeat LFTs in 6 mo, no Tx
options.explanation: UDCA improves outcomes; start now.
