questions.explanation: PBC is diagnosed with chronic cholestatic ALP elevation plus AMA >1:40 (or PBC-specific ANA); biopsy is reserved for AMA-negative disease or suspected overlap with autoimmune hepatitis. All patients should start lifelong UDCA 13–15 mg/kg/d; assess response at 12 mo and add a second-line PPAR agonist (elafibranor, seladelpar) or fibrate if inadequate. Screen bone density.

references.title: BSG/UK-PBC guideline (Gut 2018)
references.supports: UDCA 13–15 mg/kg/d first-line; AMA sufficient without biopsy

references.title: Intercept withdraws obeticholic acid (Ocaliva) from US market (HCPLive)
references.supports: Obeticholic acid withdrawn; second-line options

issues: Diagnosis and UDCA dosing are accurate (BSG 2018).
Outdated: obeticholic acid was withdrawn from the US market in Sept 2025 at FDA request (liver injury). Second-line therapy is now PPAR agonists (elafibranor, seladelpar) or fibrates.
Reference 1 is a university library proxy (jamanetwork-com.libproxy.ajou.ac.kr).

questions.stem: 71M w/ AF (CHADS-65 positive) on apixaban 5 mg BID scheduled for elective total hip replacement (high bleeding risk). CrCl 74 mL/min. No prior stroke.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Routine coagulation testing not needed.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Unsafe for high-bleed-risk surgery.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Low-bleed-risk interval only.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: PAUSE protocol for high-bleed-risk surgery.

options.label: E
options.text: Hold 5 d pre-op w/ LMWH bridging
options.explanation: Bridging adds bleeding; DOAC half-life short.

questions.explanation: PAUSE showed a standardized approach is safe: omit apixaban or rivaroxaban 1 d before low-bleed-risk and 2 d before high-bleed-risk procedures (longer for dabigatran with CrCl <50), resume 1 d after low-risk and 2–3 d after high-risk surgery, with no heparin bridging and no preoperative coagulation testing.

references.title: PAUSE cohort study (JAMA Intern Med 2019, PMC6686768)
references.supports: Omit 1 d low-risk, 2 d high-risk; no bridging; low bleeding/stroke

references.title: Standardized approach to periop DOACs (The Hospitalist)
references.supports: High risk: hold 2 d, resume 2–3 d after

issues: Accurate per PAUSE/ACCP 2022 (hold 2 d before high-bleed-risk, no bridging, no testing). Distinct from bank im-261030-170 (warfarin).
Minor: if neuraxial anesthesia is planned, many centres hold apixaban 3 d (ASRA). No 3-d option is offered, so the key stands.

questions.stem:
67M, asymptomatic, routine CBC. No lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.

WBC 18.6 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes 13.9 ×10⁹/L
Hb 138 g/L, Plt 205 ×10⁹/L
Smear: small mature lymphocytes, smudge cells

options.label: A
options.explanation: Not required for CLL Dx.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Lymphocytosis >5 ×10⁹/L warrants evaluation now.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not needed in asymptomatic early disease.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: confirms clonal CD5+/CD23+ B cells of CLL.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Persistent mature lymphocytosis w/ smudge cells suggests CLL.

questions.explanation: CLL requires ≥5 ×10⁹/L clonal B lymphocytes; peripheral blood flow cytometry (CD19/CD5/CD23, light-chain restriction) is sufficient for Dx. Bone marrow biopsy and CT aren't needed at diagnosis in asymptomatic patients. Most early-stage patients are managed by watch-and-wait; treat only active disease (cytopenias, bulky or progressive nodes/spleen, B symptoms).

references.title: Diagnosis and treatment of CLL: a review (JAMA 2023)
references.supports: Flow cytometry necessary and adequate; no BM or imaging if asymptomatic; observation

references.title: Lymphocytosis and CLL in primary care (Clin Med, PMC9135088)
references.supports: ≥5 ×10⁹/L monoclonal B cells confirmed by flow; watch and wait

issues: Accurate per JAMA 2023 CLL review (flow cytometry sufficient; no marrow or CT if asymptomatic). No duplication.
The reference URL (binasss.sa.cr) is a Costa Rican library mirror of the JAMA article. Prefer the JAMA/PubMed citation (Shadman, JAMA 2023;329:918–932).

questions.stem:
63F found to have an M-protein during workup of a raised total protein. Asymptomatic.

IgG kappa M-protein 8 g/L
Free light chain ratio normal
Hb 132 g/L, Ca 2.32 mmol/L, Cr 70 µmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: No treatment for MGUS.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Small lifelong risk of progression warrants monitoring.

options.label: C
options.text: SPEP at 6 mo, then q2–3 y
options.explanation: Correct: IMWG plan for low-risk MGUS.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Not needed for low-risk MGUS.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Excessive for low-risk disease.

questions.explanation: Low-risk MGUS (M-protein <15 g/L, IgG type, normal FLC ratio) has ~5% risk of progression at 20 y. IMWG suggests repeat SPEP at 6 mo, then every 2–3 y or sooner with symptoms (bone pain, anemia, renal or calcium changes). Intermediate/high-risk MGUS: 6 mo then annually; consider marrow if features suggest myeloma.

references.title: IMWG MGUS/SMM consensus risk factors (IMF)
references.supports: Low-risk MGUS definition; monitoring

references.title: IMWG MGUS monitoring (Birmingham research portal)
references.supports: SPEP at 6 mo then every 2–3 y if stable

issues: Accurate per IMWG (low-risk: SPEP at 6 mo then q2–3 y).
The stem includes 'Skeletal imaging: no lytic lesions'. Imaging isn't indicated in low-risk MGUS and models unnecessary testing.
The IMWG 2010 citation is old but still the standard.

questions.stem:
26M w/ 3 d of dysuria and purulent urethral discharge. No allergies.

Urine NAAT: N. gonorrhoeae positive, C. trachomatis negative
HIV and syphilis serology pending
questions.lead: Most appropriate Tx, per current Canadian guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM + azithromycin 1 g PO
options.explanation: Older regimen, replaced in Dec 2024.

options.label: B
options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 d alone
options.explanation: Treats chlamydia; inadequate for gonorrhea.

options.label: C
options.explanation: High fluoroquinolone resistance.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Not recommended as monotherapy; resistance.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: PHAC 2024 preferred monotherapy.

questions.explanation: PHAC's Dec 2024 interim guidance: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose is the preferred treatment for all uncomplicated gonococcal infections (urethral, cervical, rectal, pharyngeal), replacing ceftriaxone 250 mg plus azithromycin. Add chlamydia treatment (doxycycline) only if chlamydia hasn't been excluded. Notify and treat partners; test of cure at all positive sites.

references.title: PHAC/NAC-STBBI interim guidance: uncomplicated gonococcal infections (2024)
references.supports: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose monotherapy preferred

references.title: Ontario OCMOH memo on gonorrhea treatment (Jan 2025)
references.supports: Ceftriaxone 500 mg; treat chlamydia if not ruled out

issues: Key is correct (PHAC Dec 2024; page updated June 2026).
Explanation says 'test of cure as indicated', but PHAC recommends a test of cure for ALL positive gonorrhea sites (NAAT 3–4 wk after Tx).
Typo: '3d' should be '3 d'.

questions.stem:
34F w/ 3 d of crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody diarrhea after a petting zoo visit. Minimal fever. Tolerating fluids.

Hb 128 g/L, Plt 210 ×10⁹/L
Cr 68 µmol/L
Stool: Shiga toxin 2 detected

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: Abx may raise HUS risk in STEC O157/Stx2.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Avoid antibiotics with Shiga toxin 2.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Antibiotics are avoided in STEC (HUS risk).

options.label: D
options.explanation: Antimotility agents avoided in bloody diarrhea/STEC.

options.label: E
options.explanation: For C. difficile, not STEC.

questions.explanation: IDSA 2017: avoid antibiotics in infection with STEC O157, Shiga toxin 2 or STEC of unknown genotype, as they may increase hemolytic uremic syndrome risk; also avoid antimotility drugs in bloody diarrhea. Give supportive care with early IV fluids if needed, and monitor CBC, platelets and Cr for HUS over the following week.

references.title: Infectious diarrhea: IDSA updates guidelines (AFP 2018)
references.supports: Avoid antimicrobials w/ STEC O157, Stx2, or unknown genotype

questions.stem:
58M who emigrated from Vietnam 20 y ago is newly Dx w/ GCA; high-dose prednisone is needed today. No GI Sx.

Eosinophils 0.6 ×10⁹/L
Strongyloides serology sent; result pending (1–2 wk)

options.label: A
options.text: No action; remote exposure 20 y ago
options.explanation: Infection persists for decades via autoinfection.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: CATMAT recommends empiric Tx if steroids can't wait.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Risks vision loss in GCA; don't delay.

options.label: D
options.explanation: For hyperinfection, not prophylaxis.

options.label: E
options.text: Stool O&P ×1; treat only if positive
options.explanation: Single stool test is insensitive.

questions.explanation: Strongyloides can persist for decades through autoinfection; corticosteroids can trigger hyperinfection with gram-negative sepsis and high mortality. Canadian (CATMAT) guidance: screen those from endemic regions with serology before immunosuppression, and give empiric ivermectin (200 µg/kg ×2 doses) if steroids must start before results return.

references.title: Strongyloides hyperinfection after steroids (CMAJ 2022)
references.supports: CATMAT: screen at-risk; empiric ivermectin if immunosuppression must start first

references.title: Strongyloidiasis in immigrants and refugees in Canada (CMAJ 2015, PMC4674411)
references.supports: Screening recommended for immigrants from endemic regions

issues: Accurate per CATMAT via CMAJ (screen at-risk patients; empiric ivermectin if immunosuppression can't wait). CATMAT dose is 200 µg/kg/d ×2 doses. No duplication.

questions.stem:
62M w/ 3 wk of fatigue, epistaxis and arthralgias.

Cr 386 µmol/L (normal 3 mo ago)
UA: 3+ blood, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, 2+ protein
Renal US: normal-sized kidneys, no hydronephrosis

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: RPGN is an emergency; serology and early biopsy.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Inappropriate in rapidly rising Cr; misses Dx.

options.label: C
options.text: IV fluids and recheck Cr in 1 wk
options.explanation: Delays Dx; this isn't prerenal AKI.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Weeks of delay risk irreversible kidney loss.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Delays the key diagnostic steps.

questions.explanation: Rapidly rising Cr with active (nephritic) sediment suggests rapidly progressive GN, a medical emergency. Send ANCA (MPO/PR3), anti-GBM, complement (C3/C4), ANA/anti-dsDNA and others urgently, involve nephrology same day, and arrange early kidney biopsy. Empiric pulse steroids may start pending results when suspicion is high.

references.title: Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (Merck Manual Professional 2025)
references.supports: Serology: anti-GBM, ANCA, complement; early biopsy essential

references.title: RPGN (McMaster Textbook of IM, ebm.one)
references.supports: Tests incl. anti-GBM, ANCA, ANA, dsDNA; biopsy usually required

issues: Accurate. Merck Manual and the McMaster Textbook (ebm.one) are acceptable tertiary sources. Complements bank im-261031-28 (GPA induction) without duplicating it.

questions.stem:
45F on lithium for 12 y w/ bipolar disorder c/o polyuria (5 L/d) and thirst. Lithium level therapeutic.

Na 146 mmol/L
Serum osm 298 mOsm/kg
Urine osm 140 mOsm/kg
After desmopressin: urine osm 160 mOsm/kg
Glucose normal, Ca normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: Serum Na/osm would be low-normal, not high.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: dilute urine w/ minimal response to desmopressin on lithium.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Urine osm would rise >50% after desmopressin.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Causes hyponatremia with concentrated urine.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Urine osm >300; glucose and urea normal here.

questions.explanation: Lithium accumulates in collecting duct cells and reduces aquaporin-2, causing nephrogenic DI in up to ~20% on long-term therapy: hypotonic polyuria with high-normal Na and little rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin (central DI rises >50%). Management: adequate water access, review lithium with psychiatry; amiloride (blocks lithium entry) is first-line if lithium must continue.

references.title: Lithium-induced NDI: renal effects of amiloride (CJASN 2008, PMC2518801)
references.supports: Up to 20% develop AVP-resistant polyuria; amiloride improves concentration

references.title: Lithium-induced partial NDI (Cureus, PMC7255560)
references.supports: Water deprivation/desmopressin; amiloride first-line

issues: Accurate. Both PMC references are behind CAPTCHA, so I couldn't verify them, but the content is standard.
Optional: mention the 2022 renaming to 'AVP resistance' (nephrogenic DI) and 'AVP deficiency' (central DI).

questions.topic: AKI in an older man: exclude obstruction
questions.stem:
81M admitted w/ pneumonia; on day 3 Cr rose from 98 to 196 µmol/L and urine output fell. Started diphenhydramine for sleep and oxybutynin for urgency on admission. Lower abdominal discomfort.

BP 134/78
UA: bland

options.label: A
options.explanation: Not indicated before excluding obstruction.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Contrast and delay; bladder scan first.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Doesn't address possible retention; volume risk.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Poor test for interstitial nephritis.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: quickly identifies urinary retention (post-renal AKI).

questions.explanation: Every AKI needs obstruction excluded. In an older man with new anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, oxybutynin), and suprapubic discomfort, urinary retention is likely: check a bladder scan/PVR first, and catheterize if large. Renal US is next if hydronephrosis is suspected without retention. Stop anticholinergics (Beers list).

references.title: Urinary retention in adults: evaluation and initial management (AFP 2018)
references.supports: Anticholinergic drugs cause retention; PVR by bladder scan; catheterize

issues: Teaching point is sound.
Both references are FOAMed (EM Cases, EMCrit). Replace with a peer-reviewed review.
Mild overlap with bank im-261030-57 (diphenhydramine → urinary retention in an older man with BPH), though the angle here is distinct (AKI workup).

questions.stem:
27M w/ 1 wk of a swollen right knee and left ankle and heel pain, 3 wk after urethritis. Red eyes last week.

Knee aspirate: WBC 18 ×10⁹/L, no crystals, Gram stain and culture negative
Urine NAAT: C. trachomatis positive

options.label: A
options.explanation: Not first-line; NSAIDs preferred.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Culture negative; picture fits reactive arthritis.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Only if chronic or refractory.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: NSAIDs first-line; treat the active infection.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Sterile inflammatory effusion; not septic.

questions.explanation: Reactive arthritis is a sterile asymmetric oligoarthritis with enthesitis 1–4 wk after GU (Chlamydia) or GI infection, sometimes with conjunctivitis. NSAIDs are first-line; intra-articular steroids help. Treat active chlamydia and partners, though antibiotics don't clearly change the arthritis. Most resolve within 6 mo; use sulfasalazine if chronic (>6 mo).

references.title: Treatment of reactive arthritis: a practical guide (BioDrugs, PubMed 18034510)
references.supports: NSAIDs; treat Chlamydia; sulfasalazine for >6 mo

references.title: A review of reactive arthritis (Rheumatology Network)
references.supports: NSAIDs first-line; csDMARDs for chronic/refractory

issues: Key is correct (NSAIDs first-line; treat chlamydia).
The explanation's 'Most resolve in 6–12 mo' conflicts with sources (typically 3–5 mo; >6 mo = chronic).
rheum-live is a news site. PubMed 18034510 ('Treatment of reactive arthritis: a practical guide') is acceptable but returned a CAPTCHA.

questions.topic: SLE w/ proteinuria: when to biopsy
questions.stem:
29F w/ SLE (on hydroxychloroquine) p/w new leg edema.

UPCR 140 mg/mmol (~1.4 g/d)
UA: 2+ blood, dysmorphic RBCs
Cr 84 µmol/L (baseline 70)
C3, C4 low; anti-dsDNA high

options.label: A
options.explanation: Histology guides class-specific Tx.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Doesn't address possible proliferative nephritis.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Adjunct, not substitute for Dx and induction.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Delay risks irreversible damage.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: proteinuria ≥0.5 g/d in SLE warrants biopsy to class LN.

questions.explanation: In SLE, persistent proteinuria ≥0.5 g/d (UPCR ≥50 mg/mmol), especially with active sediment or rising Cr, should prompt kidney biopsy (KDIGO 2024, ACR 2024) to confirm lupus nephritis, define ISN/RPS class, and guide induction (e.g., glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide, ± belimumab or voclosporin). Steroids may start while awaiting biopsy.

references.title: ACR 2024 lupus nephritis guideline (RheumNow)
references.supports: Biopsy for proteinuria >0.5 g/g or unexplained impaired kidney function

references.title: Kidney biopsy in lupus nephritis (The Rheumatologist 2024)
references.supports: KDIGO: biopsy if proteinuria >0.5 g/day or declining GFR

issues: Accurate (ACR and KDIGO: biopsy if proteinuria >0.5 g/d or unexplained eGFR decline). Distinct from bank im-261030-146 (HCQ for all).
References are news sites (RheumNow, The Rheumatologist). Acceptable, but the KDIGO 2024 LN guideline would be stronger.

questions.stem: 47M asks about colon cancer screening. Father was Dx w/ colon cancer at age 68; no other relatives affected. No Sx. Never screened.
questions.lead: Per Ontario ColonCancerCheck (2026), most appropriate screening?

options.label: A
options.explanation: For one FDR <60 or ≥2 FDRs.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: one FDR Dx at ≥60 = average risk; FIT from 45.

options.label: C
options.text: Colonoscopy at 58 (10 y before father's age)
options.explanation: Applies only to increased-risk family history.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Not a program screening test.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Ontario lowered average-risk start age to 45 in 2026.

questions.explanation: Since July 2026, Ontario screens average-risk people with FIT every 2 y from age 45. One first-degree relative Dx at ≥60 is now treated as average risk (FIT, not colonoscopy). Increased risk (one FDR Dx <60, or ≥2 FDRs at any age) gets colonoscopy from 40, or 10 y before the youngest relative's Dx, repeated every 5 y.

references.title: Colon cancer testing and prevention (Ontario.ca, 2026)
references.supports: From July 2026: age 45 average risk; 40 increased risk

references.title: Colon cancer screening eligibility is changing (Ontario Health)
references.supports: One FDR ≥60 → FIT; FDR <60 or ≥2 → colonoscopy at 40 or 10 y earlier

issues: Verified: Ontario changes effective July 1, 2026 (FIT q2y from 45; one FDR ≥60 = average risk; increased risk → colonoscopy q5y from 40 or 10 y before).
This is provincial-program detail, which is moderately high-yield for an Ontario resident.
Bank im-261030-98 (CTFPHC, age 50) isn't a duplicate, but its explanation should note that Ontario now starts at 45, to avoid apparent conflict.

questions.topic: Subclinical hyperthyroidism in an older adult
questions.stem:
72F w/ osteoporosis (on no therapy) and palpitations. Not on thyroid hormone.

TSH <0.01 mIU/L on 2 occasions 3 mo apart
Free T4 and T3 normal
Uptake scan: toxic multinodular goitre
ECG: sinus rhythm

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: TSH <0.1 at ≥65 y with osteoporosis warrants treatment.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Symptom control only; doesn't correct hyperthyroidism.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Toxic nodular goitre rarely remits; antithyroid drugs need long-term use.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Worsens thyrotoxicosis.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Persistent TSH <0.1 at ≥65 raises AF and fracture risk.

questions.explanation: Subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH, normal free T4/T3) should be confirmed on repeat testing. ATA recommends treating when TSH is persistently <0.1 in adults ≥65, or with heart disease, osteoporosis or hyperthyroid symptoms, because of higher risk of AF, HF and fractures. Toxic nodular goitre is usually treated with radioactive iodine (or surgery); antithyroid drugs are an option.

references.title: Subclinical hyperthyroidism: when to consider treatment (AFP 2017)
references.supports: Treat TSH <0.1 in ≥65 or with heart disease/osteoporosis

issues: Key is correct (ATA 2016: treat persistent TSH <0.1 at ≥65 y; RAI preferred for toxic nodular goitre).
Reference 2 (Guideline Central ATA page) shows only a title and metadata.
Options 'Treat only if free T4 rises above normal' and 'Observe; repeat TSH yearly' are the same action.

questions.stem:
34M p/w chest pain 1 h after using cocaine. Agitated and diaphoretic.

BP 172/98, HR 118, SpO2 98% on room air
ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST elevation
hs-troponin pending
ASA given

options.label: A
options.explanation: Not first-line; benzodiazepines address the sympathomimetic toxicity.

options.label: B
options.explanation: No STEMI; lysis adds bleeding risk without benefit.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Avoid acutely: unopposed alpha stimulation may worsen coronary vasospasm.

options.label: D
options.explanation: No STEMI or high-risk features; most cocaine chest pain isn't MI.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: benzodiazepines treat agitation, tachycardia and hypertension in cocaine toxicity.

questions.explanation: Cocaine-associated chest pain is managed like possible ACS (ASA, nitroglycerin), plus IV benzodiazepines as first-line for agitation, tachycardia and hypertension. The AHA scientific statement advises avoiding beta-blockers in the acute setting because of unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction, though later observational data question this. Only a small minority have MI; low-risk patients can be observed with serial ECGs and troponins.

references.title: AHA guidelines on cocaine-associated chest pain (BU AOD Health summary)
references.supports: IV benzodiazepines; manage as possible ACS with ASA

references.title: Cocaine-associated chest pain (UCSF Hospital Handbook)
references.supports: Benzodiazepines first-line; ~6% have MI; beta-blocker debate

source.book: AHA Scientific Statement: Cocaine-Associated Chest Pain 2008

issues: Accuracy fine: IV benzodiazepines first-line, beta-blockers avoided acutely per AHA 2008; UCSF handbook confirms benzodiazepines first-line, ~6% MI and notes the beta-blocker controversy.
Reference 1 (professional.heart.org commentary) failed to load (site client error).
Single best answer clear; high-yield; stem and options well formed.

questions.stem:
58M w/ 2 episodes of exertional chest pain in 2 d, now pain-free. Smoker, HTN.

BP 138/84, HR 72
ECG (pain-free): biphasic T waves V2–V3, no ST elevation, preserved R waves, no Q waves
hs-troponin: mildly elevated

options.label: A
options.explanation: Contraindicated; may precipitate a large anterior MI.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Doesn't meet STEMI criteria; lysis not indicated.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: Wellens pattern signals critical proximal left anterior descending stenosis.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Unsafe; this is high-risk unstable disease, not low risk.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Most untreated patients progress to anterior MI within days.

questions.explanation: Biphasic (type A) or deeply inverted (type B) T waves in V2–V3 recorded while pain-free, with preserved R waves and no Q waves, is Wellens pattern, a marker of critical proximal left anterior descending (LAD) stenosis. Many untreated patients develop extensive anterior MI within a week. Manage as high-risk ACS with urgent angiography and revascularization; stress testing is contraindicated.

references.title: Wellens' syndrome: a case report and review (PMC4612484)
references.supports: Urgent angiography; avoid stress testing; 75% progress to anterior MI within 1 wk

references.title: Wellens' syndrome case report (BMJ Case Rep, PMC3618597)
references.supports: Bypass stress testing; emergency angiography

issues: Verified: Wellens type A biphasic / type B deep inversion in V2–V3; ~75% untreated progress to anterior MI within 1 wk; avoid stress testing; urgent angiography (PMC4612484, PMC3618597 case report).
Diagnosis not named in stem; options homogeneous; high-yield ECG pattern.

questions.stem:
48F born in Ethiopia w/ new AF. h/o rheumatic fever in childhood. No prior stroke.

BP 118/72, HR 104 irregular
Cr 64 µmol/L
TTE: rheumatic mitral stenosis, valve area 1.2 cm², enlarged left atrium

options.label: A
options.explanation: DOACs not recommended here; rivaroxaban was inferior to warfarin in INVICTUS.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not first-line; oral anticoagulation is indicated.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Antiplatelets don't adequately prevent stroke in AF.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Significant mitral stenosis needs anticoagulation regardless of score.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: warfarin is the anticoagulant for AF with rheumatic mitral stenosis.

questions.explanation: AF with moderate or severe (especially rheumatic) mitral stenosis carries a high thromboembolic risk and warrants warfarin (INR 2–3) regardless of CHA2DS2-VASc. These patients were excluded from pivotal DOAC trials, and in INVICTUS rivaroxaban led to more adverse events than vitamin K antagonist therapy. For AF with other native valve disease (e.g., mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis), DOACs are preferred over warfarin.

references.title: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline: valvular heart disease table (PMC11104284)
references.supports: Warfarin over DOACs for rheumatic or moderate+ MS; DOACs for other VHD

references.title: Anticoagulation for rheumatic mitral stenosis: INVICTUS in perspective (Curr Opin Cardiol 2023)
references.supports: VKA remains standard of care for rheumatic MS with AF

issues: Content correct: VKA (INR 2–3) for AF with moderate–severe/rheumatic MS; INVICTUS favoured VKA over rivaroxaban (Verma & Latter 2023 review, Epistemonikos). ACC/AHA performance measures exclude DOACs in moderate/severe MS.
Reference 1 (PMC11104284 table T62, likely 2023 ACC/AHA AF guideline) could not be loaded: reCAPTCHA interstitial; returned by search for the 2023 AF guideline so likely valid.
Partial thematic overlap with bank im-261030-01 (AF stroke prevention, CCS algorithm) but distinct teaching point (valvular AF → warfarin). Trial acronym only in explanation, acceptable.

questions.stem: 70M at an annual visit. Ex-smoker (40 pack-years). HTN on amlodipine. No abdominal or back pain. No pulsatile abdominal mass on exam.
questions.lead: Per CTFPHC, most appropriate AAA screening?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Screening is one-time; surveillance only if an AAA is found.

options.label: B
options.text: No screening if no pulsatile mass
options.explanation: Palpation is insensitive; normal exam doesn't exclude AAA.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Radiation and contrast; ultrasound is the screening test.

options.label: D
options.text: Screen only with a family history
options.explanation: Recommended for all men 65–80, not just those with family history.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: recommended for men 65–80.

questions.explanation: The Canadian Task Force (2017) recommends one-time ultrasound screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm in men aged 65–80 (weak recommendation), and recommends against screening men over 80 or women. Screening reduces AAA-related death, rupture and emergency repair. Smoking is a key risk factor, but no separate recommendation is made for smokers. Abdominal palpation is unreliable.

references.title: CTFPHC AAA screening: clinician summary
references.supports: One-time US for men 65–80; not >80 or women

references.title: Recommendations on screening for AAA in primary care (CMAJ 2017, PMC5595553)
references.supports: Guideline and evidence

issues: Verified against CTFPHC clinician summary: one-time US for men 65–80 (weak, moderate-quality), not >80 (weak), not women (strong); no separate smoker recommendation. Still current CTFPHC guidance.
Reference 2 (PMC5595553, CMAJ 2017 guideline) not verifiable: PMC pages repeatedly returned a reCAPTCHA interstitial to the fetcher (not dead links); content could not be verified directly.
No duplication (bank has lung and CRC screening, not AAA).

questions.stem:
62M p/w 1 h of chest pain. Lungs clear, JVP elevated.

BP 82/50, HR 54
ECG: ST elevation II, III, aVF (III > II); ST elevation in V4R
Cath lab activated
questions.lead: Most appropriate immediate measure for the hypotension?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Worsens bradycardia and hypotension.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: the infarcted RV is preload-dependent.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Venodilation lowers preload; avoid in RV infarction.

options.label: D
options.explanation: High JVP reflects RV failure, not overload; worsens hypotension.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Preload reduction can cause profound hypotension.

questions.explanation: Inferior STEMI with hypotension, clear lungs and raised JVP suggests RV infarction, confirmed by ST elevation in V4R (record right-sided leads in all inferior STEMIs). The ischemic RV is preload-dependent: give cautious fluid boluses, avoid nitrates, diuretics and opioids, and maintain heart rate and atrioventricular synchrony. If hypotension persists after fluids, add vasopressor/inotropic support (norepinephrine, or dobutamine for low output); prompt reperfusion is the cornerstone.

references.title: The challenges in the management of RV infarction (Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care 2013, PMC3821821)
references.supports: Early revascularization; fluids to maintain preload; HR and AV synchrony

references.title: RV infarction—a tale of two ventricles: key points (ACC 2024)
references.supports: Bradycardia/hypotension red flags; right-sided ECG

issues: Keyed answer correct and high-yield. ACC 'Ten points' (JACC 2024 RV MI seminar) confirms right-sided ECG in all inferior MI, optimize RV preload, avoid IV nitroglycerin and beta-blockers.
Explanation's 'Use inotropes (e.g., dobutamine) if fluids fail' differs from the cited ACC summary, which names norepinephrine and dopamine as initial agents if vasopressor support is needed.
Reference 1 (PMC3821821) not verifiable: PMC pages repeatedly returned a reCAPTCHA interstitial to the fetcher (not dead links); content could not be verified directly.

questions.stem:
67F w/ acute PE on CTPA. No bleeding Hx.

BP 118/74 (stable over 2 h), HR 108, SpO2 93% on 2 L
CTPA: RV/LV ratio 1.3
hs-troponin elevated
Simplified PESI: 1

options.label: A
options.explanation: Not low risk: RV dysfunction and raised troponin.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Filters only if anticoagulation is contraindicated.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: intermediate-high risk; reperfusion only if she deteriorates.

options.label: D
options.explanation: For high-risk PE when lysis fails or is contraindicated.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not routine: more major and intracranial bleeding, no mortality benefit.

questions.explanation: Normotensive PE with RV dysfunction on imaging and raised troponin is intermediate-high risk (ESC). Anticoagulate and monitor closely rather than giving routine systemic thrombolysis: in PEITHO, tenecteplase reduced decompensation but increased major and intracranial bleeding. Rescue reperfusion is for hemodynamic deterioration. The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline gives lysis or catheter-based therapy in this group only a weak recommendation.

references.title: The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline for the management of acute PE (Endovascular Today)
references.supports: 2026 categories; weak (2B) recommendation for advanced therapy

references.title: HI-PEITHO and reperfusion strategies in PE (ACC 2026)
references.supports: PEITHO bleeding; anticoagulation remains standard

source.book: ESC Acute PE Guideline 2019; AHA/ACC PE Guideline 2026

issues: Keyed answer still correct, but explanation is outdated: the 2026 AHA/ACC PE guideline introduced a new A–E classification (normotensive with RV dysfunction + troponin ≈ category C3) and gives systemic lysis, catheter-directed lysis and thrombectomy only a 2B ('unclear benefit') recommendation; LMWH preferred over UFH (Class 1).

'Catheter-directed approaches are being studied' is out of date: HI-PEITHO (ACC, Sept 2026) showed catheter-directed fibrinolysis reduced early deterioration (4% vs 10.3%) in a selected population, though anticoagulation alone remains standard.
Reference 1 (PMC9197594) not verifiable: PMC pages repeatedly returned a reCAPTCHA interstitial to the fetcher (not dead links); content could not be verified directly.
Option C text is less specific than others; naming the anticoagulant makes it homogeneous.

questions.stem:
38F w/ asthma for 10 y, now uncontrolled despite high-dose budesonide-formoterol. Expectorates brown mucus plugs.

Eosinophils 1.2 ×10⁹/L
Total IgE 2400 IU/mL
CT chest: central bronchiectasis, mucoid impaction

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: fungal sensitization is a mandatory diagnostic criterion.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not needed; Dx is serologic plus imaging.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Used for invasive aspergillosis, not the allergic form.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Aspergillus isolation is supportive but nonspecific.

options.label: E
options.explanation: For eosinophilic granulomatosis w/ polyangiitis; doesn't explain central bronchiectasis and mucus plugs.

questions.explanation: Poorly controlled asthma with eosinophilia, very high total IgE, central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction suggests allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Revised ISHAM criteria (2024) require fungal sensitization (A. fumigatus–specific IgE or skin test) plus total IgE ≥500 IU/mL, and two of: fungal-specific IgG, blood eosinophilia, or suggestive imaging. Acute disease is treated with prednisone or itraconazole.

references.title: Revised ISHAM-ABPA working group guidelines (Eur Respir J 2024)
references.supports: Mandatory sensitization + IgE ≥500 + two of IgG, eosinophilia, imaging

references.title: Updated definition of ABPA (Agarwal, Aspergillus.org.uk)
references.supports: Af-IgE ≥0.35 kUA/L; thresholds

issues: Verified: revised ISHAM-AWG 2024 criteria require fungal sensitization (Af-IgE ≥0.35 kUA/L) plus total IgE ≥500 IU/mL and 2 of IgG, eosinophils ≥500/µL, imaging; acute ABPA treated with prednisolone or itraconazole monotherapy.
Moderately niche but a classic exam topic; no duplicates in bank.
Reference 2 is a presentation PDF on a charity site that notes the criteria were 'still in peer review'; acceptable alongside the JKU repository record of the published ERJ guideline.

questions.topic: Chronic cough on an ACE inhibitor
questions.stem:
62F c/o dry cough for 3 mo. Started ramipril 5 mo ago for HTN. Nonsmoker. No heartburn, postnasal drip or wheeze.

CXR normal
Spirometry normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: stopping the ACEi is the only effective Tx; ARBs rarely cause cough.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Symptomatic only; doesn't remove the cause.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Normal CXR and an obvious drug cause; not needed now.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Treat GERD only if cough persists after stopping the ACEi.

options.label: E
options.explanation: No features of asthma or eosinophilic bronchitis.

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitor cough is bradykinin-mediated and can begin weeks to months after starting the drug. The only effective treatment is stopping the ACEi, substituting another renin-angiotensin blocker such as an ARB; cough usually resolves within 1–4 wk, occasionally up to 3 mo, and resolution confirms the Dx. Evaluate for asthma, GERD or upper airway cough only if cough persists.

references.title: ACE inhibitor-related cough with ramipril: observational study (PMC3560643)
references.supports: Stop ACEi, substitute RAS inhibitor; resolution 1–4 wk, up to 3 mo

references.title: Recognising and managing ACE inhibitor–induced cough (J Manag Pharm Pract 2026)
references.supports: Stopping ACEi; resolution 1–4 wk; switch to ARB

issues: Correct and high-yield. PMC3560643 supports 'only effective therapy is cessation', resolution 1–4 wk; JMPF 2026 article supports up to 3 mo and ARB switch.

Insulin follows fluid resuscitation; JBDS starts low-dose insulin (0.05 units/kg/h) once glucose stops falling on fluids, or earlier with significant ketonemia. Avoid rapid falls in osmolality.

questions.explanation: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction is first managed supportively: nasogastric/rectal decompression, correct electrolytes, stop opioids and anticholinergics, mobilize. Aim for proteinuria <0.5 g/d, ideally <0.3 g/d. Disease-specific therapy (e.g., targeted-release budesonide, sparsentan) is for persistent proteinuria ≥0.5 g/d.

questions.stem:
29F w/ fatigue after a viral illness. No rash, arthritis, Raynaud, oral ulcers or sicca. Exam normal.

CBC, Cr, UA normal
TSH normal
ANA positive 1:80, speckled (ordered at a walk-in clinic)

options.label: A
options.text: Anti-dsDNA and extractable nuclear antigen panel
options.explanation: Low pretest probability; more false positives.

options.label: B
options.explanation: No autoimmune disease to treat.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Serial ANA titres don't guide care.

options.label: D
options.explanation: No features of systemic autoimmune disease.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: low-titre ANA is common in healthy people.

questions.explanation: A low-titre ANA is found in up to ~20% of healthy people, more often in women, older adults and after infections. Without specific features of SLE or another systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease, it has very low predictive value, and further serology invites false positives and mislabelling. The CRA's Choosing Wisely list advises against ANA as a screening test. Re-evaluate if new features appear.

references.title: CRA Choosing Wisely: nine tests and treatments to question in rheumatology (2025)
references.supports: Don't screen with ANA; positive in up to 20% healthy

references.title: ANA testing appropriateness (CMAJ Open 2020)

High-yield; options homogeneous.

questions.topic: RA not at target on conventional therapy
questions.stem:
45F w/ seropositive RA on SC methotrexate 25 mg weekly, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine for 6 mo, well tolerated. Still 7 swollen joints.

CRP 32 mg/L
CDAI 28 (high)
TB screen, HBV and HCV serology negative

options.label: A
options.text: Continue current Tx; reassess in 6 mo
options.explanation: Treat-to-target requires change when target isn't met.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Steroids are for short-term bridging only.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Exceeds usual maximum; more toxicity.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Adding another conventional agent is unlikely to reach target.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: not at target by 6 mo; add a biologic (or JAK inhibitor).

questions.explanation: Treat-to-target: aim for remission or low disease activity, changing therapy if there's <50% improvement by 3 mo or the target isn't reached by 6 mo. After an inadequate response to methotrexate-based conventional therapy, add a biologic such as a TNF inhibitor, usually with methotrexate (EULAR 2025); JAK inhibitors are an alternative after weighing cardiovascular, cancer and VTE risk. Avoid long-term glucocorticoids.

references.title: EULAR RA management with DMARDs: 2025 update timeline (Guideline Central)
references.supports: Treat-to-target; add biologic after conventional therapy fails

references.title: CRA position: criteria for access to targeted agents for RA (2026)
references.supports: Inadequate response to methotrexate before targeted agents

issues: Reference 1 is the EULAR 2019 update; EULAR 2025 update (published 2026) is current and no longer stratifies by poor prognostic factors: if target not achieved with csDMARD strategy, add a bDMARD; JAKi may be considered after weighing risk factors.
Explanation 'especially with poor prognostic factors' is outdated per EULAR 2025.
CRA 2026 access criteria verified: MTX 20–25 mg/wk for ≥12 wk, combination csDMARD with MTX anchor; leflunomide not mandatory.
Distinct from bank im-261030-108 (RA initial DMARD).

questions.stem:
32F w/ 4 episodes of CAP and recurrent sinusitis over 2 y, each responding to Abx. Nonsmoker. No meningitis, abscesses or fungal infections. HIV negative.

CBC normal
CT chest: mild bronchiectasis

options.label: A
options.explanation: Complement defects cause Neisseria infections.

options.label: B
options.text: Serum IgG, IgA and IgM levels
options.explanation: Correct: screens for antibody deficiency such as CVID.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Screens for chronic granulomatous disease (abscesses, fungi).

options.label: D
options.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is unlikely to present first at this age without other features.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Cellular defects cause viral/opportunistic infections; not first.

questions.explanation: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria in an adult suggest a primary antibody deficiency, most often common variable immunodeficiency. Start with quantitative IgG, IgA and IgM (CVID: low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM), then test specific vaccine responses (e.g., tetanus, pneumococcal). Confirmed CVID is treated with immunoglobulin replacement; bronchiectasis is a common complication.

references.title: Common variable immunodeficiency (Merck Manual Professional, Canada)
references.supports: Low IgG and IgA/IgM, poor vaccine response; IgG replacement

references.title: Investigating recurrent respiratory infections: antibody deficiency (BMJ, MDC Berlin repository)
references.supports: Measure serum IgG, IgA, IgM first

issues: Verified: CVID requires low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM and impaired vaccine response; IgG replacement (Merck Manual). BMJ 2009 Rational Testing: measure IgG, IgA, IgM first.
Option D explanation is longer than the others; minor.

questions.stem:
68F on lithium for bipolar disorder, recently started on ramipril. 4 d of vomiting, coarse tremor and drowsiness.

GCS 12
Lithium 3.4 mmol/L
Cr 240 µmol/L (baseline 90)
Na 134 mmol/L
questions.lead: Most appropriate Tx in addition to stopping lithium and ramipril?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: decreased consciousness meets EXTRIP criteria.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Worsens volume and sodium loss; reduces lithium clearance.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Doesn't bind lithium.

options.label: D
options.text: IV fluids alone; recheck level in 12 h
options.explanation: Neurotoxicity plus impaired clearance warrants dialysis.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Only for acute ingestion of sustained-release tablets.

questions.explanation: Chronic lithium toxicity is often precipitated by AKI, ACEi/ARBs, thiazides or NSAIDs. EXTRIP recommends extracorporeal removal (hemodialysis preferred) for decreased consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmias, or lithium >4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidney function; it's suggested for confusion, lithium >5.0, or expected time to <1.0 mmol/L >36 h. Expect rebound and recheck levels after dialysis.

references.title: Extracorporeal treatment for lithium poisoning: EXTRIP recommendations (CJASN 2015, PMC4422246)
references.supports: Indications for ECTR; HD preferred

references.title: Haemodialysis for lithium poisoning: translating EXTRIP (PMC7163377)
references.supports: Table of EXTRIP criteria

issues: Verified EXTRIP criteria (Buckley 2020, PMC7163377): recommended for decreased consciousness, seizures, life-threatening dysrhythmia, or Li >4.0 with impaired kidney function; suggested for confusion, Li >5.0, or expected time to <1.0 mmol/L >36 h.
PMC4422246 (EXTRIP 2015) returned by search but not loadable (reCAPTCHA).
Distinct from bank im-261101-55 (lithium nephrogenic DI).

questions.stem: 80M w/ Alzheimer dementia, MoCA 14/30. Now needs reminders to bathe and dress, can't manage his medications or finances, and gets lost in familiar areas. Still drives daily in Toronto; family is worried.

options.label: A

options.explanation: May help, but doesn't replace the mandatory report.

options.label: B

options.explanation: The duty arises from the medical condition, not a crash.

options.label: C

options.explanation: Advice alone doesn't meet the legal duty to report.

options.label: D
options.text: Report to the Ministry of Transportation
options.explanation: Correct: mandatory report for impairment limiting daily function.

options.label: E
options.text: Refer for an on-road test before reporting
options.explanation: Reporting is mandatory now; the Ministry decides on testing.

questions.explanation: Ontario's Highway Traffic Act requires physicians to report patients ≥16 with a prescribed condition, including cognitive impairment affecting attention, judgment, memory or visuospatial perception that substantially limits activities of daily living. Moderate dementia like this also contraindicates driving. A diagnosis alone or mild age-related change doesn't trigger a mandatory report; discretionary reporting is allowed. The Ministry, not the physician, decides on the licence.

issues: Verified (OMA 2018): mandatory report for cognitive impairment affecting attention, judgment, memory, visuospatial perception etc. that substantially limits ADLs; discretionary reporting otherwise. MTO fact sheet: Ministry decides licence action.
Canada/Ontario-specific and high-yield for the Royal College exam.

options.label: D

options.label: E

questions.explanation: Since October 2024, the Ontario Breast Screening Program lets average-risk people aged 40–49 self-refer for screening mammography after a conversation about benefits and harms; most who choose screening should have mammography every 2 y, continuing every 2 y from 50–74. Annual MRI plus mammography is reserved for high-risk people, such as gene variant carriers or those with prior chest radiation.

questions.stem:
82F w/ newly Dx nonvalvular AF, h/o HTN. Starting anticoagulation. No interacting drugs.

Weight 64 kg
Cr 118 µmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: only 1 of 3 reduction criteria (age ≥80) is met.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Needs ≥2 of: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, Cr ≥133 µmol/L.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Apixaban is dosed twice daily in AF.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Not an approved AF dose; underdoses stroke prevention.

options.label: E
options.text: 10 mg BID ×7 d, then 5 mg BID
options.explanation: Acute VTE treatment regimen, not AF.

questions.explanation: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg BID in AF only when ≥2 of 3 criteria are present: age ≥80 y, weight ≤60 kg, or Cr ≥133 µmol/L. Age alone isn't enough, so she gets 5 mg BID. The 10 mg BID loading dose is for acute VTE, not AF.

references.title: Apixaban 2.5 mg film-coated tablets – SmPC (emc)
references.supports: AF dose reduction: ≥2 of age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, Cr ≥133 µmol/L

questions.stem:
58M p/w 1 h of crushing chest pain and diaphoresis.

BP 128/76, HR 88, SpO2 97% RA.
ECG: horizontal ST depression 2 mm V1–V3, upright T waves, R/S >1 in V2. No ST elevation in other leads.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Pattern is ischemic posterior MI, not PE.

options.label: B
options.text: IV metoprolol; repeat ECG in 6 h
options.explanation: Delays reperfusion; not the priority.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: posterior STEMI equivalent; obtain V7–V9 but don't delay reperfusion.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Contraindicated in ongoing acute MI.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Treats it as NSTEMI and delays reperfusion of an occluded artery.

questions.explanation: Horizontal ST depression maximal in V1–V3 with upright T waves and a dominant R in V2 is the mirror image of posterior ST elevation: a STEMI equivalent. Posterior leads (V7–V9) showing ≥0.5 mm elevation confirm it, but if the 12-lead criteria are met, treat as STEMI even if posterior leads are unrevealing.

references.title: The reperfusion guidelines finally catch up (ACEP Now)
references.supports: Posterior MI criteria; STEMI equivalent; treat even if V7–V9 negative

references.title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction (StatPearls)
references.supports: ST depression V1–V3 prompts posterior leads; prompt recognition guides reperfusion

issues: Accurate; ACEP Now confirms the posterior criteria and treating as STEMI even if V7-V9 lack >=0.5 mm elevation.
StatPearls reference could not be fetched (site blocks robots); acepnow alone supports the key points. Consider replacing StatPearls with a guideline/ECG review that loads.
No bank duplicate (bank has Wellens and STEMI-at-non-PCI-centre, different teaching points).

questions.stem:
79M w/ HFpEF, bilateral carpal tunnel release, lumbar spinal stenosis.

ECG: low QRS voltage
TTE: LV wall 17 mm, apical-sparing longitudinal strain
NT-proBNP 2,400 ng/L
questions.lead: Along with Tc-99m bone scintigraphy, most important initial test?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: must exclude a monoclonal protein (AL) before scintigraphy can diagnose ATTR.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Done after ATTR is confirmed, to separate variant from wild-type.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Supports amyloid but can't type AL vs ATTR.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Not needed if scan grade 2–3 and no monoclonal protein.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Doesn't address the infiltrative phenotype.

questions.explanation: Grade 2–3 cardiac uptake on bone scintigraphy diagnoses ATTR cardiomyopathy without biopsy only when AL amyloid has been excluded with serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation. Bone tracers can also light up in AL, and AL is a hematologic emergency, so the monoclonal screen is mandatory. If it's abnormal, refer for tissue diagnosis.

references.title: Diagnosing transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis by Tc-99m PYP (JACC Imaging, PMC)
references.supports: PYP diagnostic only if AL excluded by FLC, SPEP/UPEP with immunofixation

references.title: Noninvasive diagnosis of ATTR cardiomyopathy (Gillmore et al. summary)
references.supports: If FLC or immunofixation abnormal, refer for further evaluation

issues: Accurate: grade 2-3 uptake diagnoses ATTR-CM only when FLC plus serum/urine immunofixation are negative; abnormal results need referral/tissue diagnosis.
Cueing: correct option A (52 chars) is ~2.5x longer than the other options.
Lead 'Along with Tc-99m bone scintigraphy' tells the reader the Dx is amyloid; acceptable since the teaching point is the AL screen, but the vignette is already classic.

questions.stem:
71F w/ T2DM p/w rest chest pain 6 h ago, now pain-free.

BP 142/80, HR 84. Lungs clear.
ECG: dynamic ST depression V4–V6
hs-troponin rising (diagnostic of NSTEMI)
GRACE score 152
questions.lead: Most appropriate timing of coronary angiography?

options.label: A
options.text: Only if a stress test is positive
options.explanation: Selective strategy is for low-risk patients.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: confirmed NSTEMI, dynamic ST changes and GRACE >140 are high-risk.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Too late given her high-risk features.

options.label: D
options.explanation: For very-high-risk features, e.g. instability or refractory pain.

options.label: E
options.text: Elective, after 6 wk of medical therapy
options.explanation: Not appropriate for NSTEMI.

questions.explanation: In NSTE-ACS, an early invasive strategy (angiography within 24 h) is advised for high-risk patients: confirmed NSTEMI, dynamic ST/T changes, transient ST elevation, or GRACE >140 (ESC 2023, class IIa). Immediate (<2 h) angiography is reserved for very-high-risk features such as hemodynamic instability or refractory angina.

references.title: Critical appraisal of the 2023 ESC ACS guidelines (J Clin Med, PMC)
references.supports: Early invasive <24 h for NSTEMI, dynamic ST change, transient STE, GRACE >140 (IIa)

references.title: Indications for an early invasive strategy in NSTE-ACS (Neth Heart J, PMC)
references.supports: Immediate invasive for very-high-risk (instability, refractory angina)

issues: Accurate: ESC 2023 early invasive <24 h (IIa, downgraded from I in 2020) for NSTEMI, dynamic ST/T, transient STE, GRACE >140; immediate for very-high-risk features.
High-yield and appropriate level. No bank duplicate (bank NSTEMI items cover lipids, DAPT, AF+PCI).

questions.stem: 54M w/ confirmed HTN (home BP avg 148/92) despite 3 mo of lifestyle changes. No DM, CKD or CVD. Not at high risk of symptomatic hypotension.
questions.lead: Per Hypertension Canada 2025, preferred initial pharmacotherapy?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: low-dose 2-drug combination, ideally one pill (e.g. irbesartan–HCTZ).

options.label: B
options.explanation: Beta-blockers aren't among the 3 first-line classes.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Full-dose monotherapy isn't the preferred start.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Monotherapy now reserved for those at risk of symptomatic hypotension.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Triple therapy is the step after 2-drug therapy fails.

questions.explanation: Hypertension Canada's 2025 primary care guideline recommends starting most patients on low-dose combination therapy, ideally a single pill, using 2 of 3 classes: ACEi/ARB, long-acting dihydropyridine CCB, thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic. Irbesartan–HCTZ was chosen as the preferred initial pill. If BP stays above target, step to full-dose, then 3-drug therapy, then add spironolactone.

references.title: Hypertension Canada 2025 guideline: implementation
references.supports: SPC preferred; irbesartan–HCTZ preferred initial combination

references.title: Overview of Hypertension Canada's new primary care guideline (FMF 2025)

questions.stem:
34F w/ intermittent wheeze and nocturnal cough. Spirometry before and 15 min after salbutamol.

Pre-bronchodilator FEV1 1.50 L
questions.lead: Which post-bronchodilator FEV1 meets the GINA adult reversibility criterion?

options.label: A
options.explanation: +8%, +120 mL: below both thresholds.

options.label: B
options.explanation: +5%: no significant response.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: +220 mL and +14.7% (>200 mL and >12%).

options.label: D
options.explanation: +10%, +150 mL: below both thresholds.

options.label: E
options.explanation: +12.7% but only +190 mL: fails the volume criterion.

questions.explanation: GINA defines significant bronchodilator reversibility in adults as an FEV1 rise of >12% AND >200 mL from baseline. Both are needed: small lungs can hit 12% with <200 mL. A negative test doesn't exclude asthma; repeat when symptomatic, or use bronchoprovocation or PEF variability. (ERS/ATS 2021 interpretation uses >10% of predicted, but GINA keeps 12%/200 mL.)

references.title: ATS 2025: GINA vs ATS/ERS bronchodilator responsiveness thresholds (CiplaMed)
references.supports: ATS/ERS >10% predicted vs GINA >12% and >200 mL

issues: Accurate: GINA adult criterion is FEV1 rise >12% AND >200 mL; arithmetic for every option checks out (C = +220 mL/14.7%).
Options not homogeneous: A alone adds 'with FEV1/FVC 0.62', which is extra information and a red herring of a different type.
PMC12442436 reference returned a captcha; the ERS/ATS 2021 contrast was confirmed instead via a search result (Cipla ATS 2025 abstract summary: ATS/ERS >10%, GINA >12% and >200 mL).

questions.topic: Suspected PE in pregnancy with DVT signs
questions.stem:
29F G1 at 30 wk p/w 2 d of dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. L calf swollen and tender.

Pre-BD FEV1/FVC 0.67
