references.title: What's new in the 2025 GOLD report (PMC)
references.supports: Flow responders to >0.7 post-BD need monitoring

issues: Replacement for a rejected duplicate; second review: keep

Accurate. The GOLD PDF supports both points: post-BD FEV1/FVC <0.7 confirms COPD, and a pre-BD ratio >=0.7 usually excludes it. Halpin & Singh 2025 (PMC12097743) supports the flow-responder statement: these patients have a high prevalence of later COPD and need careful prospective monitoring. GOLD 2 = FEV1 50-79% is standard GOLD grading; the cited sources don't contain it.
Single best answer is clear. Post-BD 0.73 with FEV1 82% isn't COPD, isn't PRISm and doesn't suggest restriction. No other option can be defended.

questions.stem:
72F found drowsy at home; stopped levothyroxine months ago.

T 34.1 °C, HR 46, BP 84/50, RR 10.
Na 124 mmol/L
Glucose 4.1 mmol/L
TSH 68 mIU/L; free T4 undetectable

options.label: A
options.explanation: Treats Na, not the cause; Na 124 w/o seizures.

options.label: B
options.text: IV hydrocortisone, then IV levothyroxine load
options.explanation: Correct: stress steroids first, then IV T4 (gut absorption unreliable).

options.label: C
options.explanation: Delays essential thyroid hormone replacement.

options.label: D
options.explanation: May precipitate adrenal crisis if adrenal insufficiency coexists.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Oral absorption is unreliable in myxedema coma; too slow.

questions.explanation: Myxedema coma needs ICU care with IV thyroid hormone, because gut absorption is impaired, plus empirical stress-dose IV glucocorticoid given before levothyroxine. Restoring metabolic rate raises cortisol clearance and can unmask adrenal insufficiency. Give a large IV T4 load, then daily IV doses; add IV T3 if no improvement.

references.title: Myxedema and coma (severe hypothyroidism), Endotext
references.supports: IV route; stress hydrocortisone; T3 if no improvement

references.title: UCSF Hospital Handbook: hypothyroidism and myxedema coma
references.supports: IV T4 load; stress steroids before T4 until adrenal insufficiency excluded

issues: Accurate: IV T4 load (Endotext 300-500 ug, UCSF 200-400 ug), stress hydrocortisone, steroids given before T4 until AI excluded (UCSF handbook); T3 if no improvement.
The guidelinecentral ATA pocket card URL loads no content, so the 'ATA: glucocorticoid preceding levothyroxine' claim is not verifiable from it; UCSF Hospital Handbook supports the sequence.
Lead asks for 'initial endocrine therapy' but option A (3% saline) is not endocrine therapy - heterogeneous option.

questions.stem:
61M w/ sudden severe headache, vomiting and new bitemporal field loss.

BP 92/58, HR 112.
Na 129 mmol/L
CT head: hemorrhagic sellar mass; no SAH.
Bloods drawn for cortisol, TSH, free T4, prolactin.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Hyponatremia here likely reflects cortisol deficiency; restriction worsens shock.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Thyroid hormone before steroids can precipitate adrenal crisis.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not initial therapy in apoplexy; ACTH deficiency is the threat.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Stabilize with steroids first; surgery decided after.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: empirical steroids are potentially lifesaving; give after drawing bloods.

questions.explanation: Pituitary apoplexy with hemodynamic instability, reduced consciousness or visual compromise needs empirical IV hydrocortisone (100–200 mg bolus, then infusion or q6h dosing) after drawing baseline bloods (Society for Endocrinology). MRI confirms the Dx. Surgery is considered after stabilization for severe or persistent visual deficits or falling consciousness.

references.title: SfE emergency guidance: pituitary apoplexy in adults (Endocr Connect)
references.supports: Steroid indications/doses; MRI; surgery indications

issues: Accurate: Society for Endocrinology guidance - empirical hydrocortisone 100-200 mg IV bolus for instability, reduced consciousness or visual compromise; MRI to confirm; surgery for severe/persistent visual deficit or falling consciousness after stabilization.
Minor cue: correct option E is the only one with a dose. Acceptable.
Not neurology content (endocrine emergency). No bank duplicate (bank adrenal crisis item is a different scenario). Shares the 'steroids before thyroid hormone' distractor with Q11 - acceptable.

questions.stem:
66F w/ Hashimoto hypothyroidism, stable on levothyroxine 100 µg; TSH 1.8 last y. 3 mo ago started calcium carbonate and ferrous sulfate; takes all pills together at breakfast. Now fatigued.

TSH 9.4 mIU/L
Free T4 low-normal

options.label: A
options.text: Space Ca/Fe from LT4; recheck TSH
options.explanation: Correct: fix the interaction before changing the dose.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Treats the number but leaves the absorption problem.

options.label: C
options.explanation: No indication; same interaction issue.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Unnecessary; spacing doses is enough.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Diagnosis already known; doesn't explain the change.

questions.explanation: Calcium carbonate and iron chelate levothyroxine in the gut and raise TSH. Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach and separate it from calcium, iron, antacids, sucralfate and binders by at least 4 h (some advise longer for calcium). Always screen adherence and interfering products before raising the dose.

references.title: Benvenga S. L-T4 therapy in the presence of pharmacological interferents (Front Endocrinol 2020)
references.supports: Ca/Fe reduce LT4 absorption; spacing intervals

issues: Accurate: Ca/Fe bind levothyroxine; separate ~4 h (ATA calls 4 h 'traditional'; Benvenga 2020 suggests >=6 h for calcium, >=4 h for iron); screen adherence/interferents before raising dose.
Cueing: correct option A (54 chars) is far longer than others.
Weak sources: drugs.com is a consumer site and the MDedge URL is a QA/staging cache domain (mdedge-cache.qa01) - not a stable citation.

questions.stem:
44M ate steak 3 h ago; now can't swallow saliva, drooling, retrosternal discomfort. h/o intermittent solid-food dysphagia.

Vitals normal. Breathing comfortably. No crepitus.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Contraindicated: aspiration risk, impairs endoscopic view.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: complete obstruction needs emergent therapeutic endoscopy.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Medical therapy shouldn't delay endoscopy.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Timing for incomplete obstruction only.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not needed for uncomplicated nonbony bolus.

questions.explanation: Inability to swallow saliva means complete esophageal obstruction: ESGE recommends emergent therapeutic EGD, preferably within 2 h and at the latest within 6 h. Skip imaging for an uncomplicated nonbony bolus, and don't let glucagon delay endoscopy. Gently push the bolus into the stomach, and biopsy to look for an underlying cause such as eosinophilic esophagitis.

references.title: ESGE guideline: removal of foreign bodies in the upper GI tract in adults
references.supports: Emergent EGD <2–6 h; no radiology; medical Rx shouldn't delay; biopsy

issues: Accurate: ESGE - emergent EGD for complete obstruction, preferably <2 h, at latest <6 h; no radiology for uncomplicated nonbony bolus; medical therapy shouldn't delay; push gently; biopsy.
Cueing: correct option B carries a parenthetical '(ideally <2 h, max 6 h)' that no other option has, and contrasts directly with D ('within 24 h').
ESGE doesn't name glucagon specifically (says medical treatment shouldn't delay EGD) - explanation wording 'don't let glucagon delay' is a fair paraphrase.

questions.stem:
38M born in Vietnam, routine screening. Asymptomatic.

HBsAg positive (×2, 6 mo apart)
HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive
HBV DNA 900 IU/mL
ALT 22 U/L (ULN 35)
Elastography: no significant fibrosis

options.label: A
options.explanation: Noninvasive fibrosis testing already reassuring.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not indicated; poor benefit–risk here.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not indicated in the inactive phase without cirrhosis.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Not indicated; no treatment threshold met.

options.label: E
options.text: Monitor ALT and HBV DNA; no antiviral
options.explanation: Correct: inactive phase (DNA <2,000, normal ALT, no cirrhosis).

questions.explanation: HBeAg-negative, normal ALT, HBV DNA <2,000 IU/mL and no cirrhosis is the inactive phase: monitor, don't treat. AASLD advises ALT and HBV DNA every 3 mo for the first year, then every 6–12 mo, with yearly HBsAg. The 2025 AASLD/IDSA update still recommends no treatment for HBeAg-negative patients with DNA <2,000.

references.title: Monitoring persons with chronic HBV (Hepatitis B Online, U Washington)
references.supports: Monitoring schedule for untreated HBeAg-negative

references.title: Highlights from the 2025 AASLD/IDSA HBV guideline (Gastroenterol Hepatol)
references.supports: No treatment if HBeAg-negative with DNA <2,000

issues: Accurate and current: 2025 AASLD/IDSA still recommends no treatment for HBeAg-negative with HBV DNA <2,000 IU/mL; monitoring ALT/DNA q3mo in year 1 then less often.
Minor: UW source gives ALT q6mo after year 1; explanation's '6-12 mo' is close enough.
Mild cue: correct option E is longest. No bank duplicate (bank has serology interpretation and rituximab prophylaxis).

questions.stem:
34F w/ iron deficiency anemia from heavy menses (gyne managing). Started ferrous sulfate 300 mg TID; stopped after 1 wk due to nausea.

Hb 104 g/L
Ferritin 6 µg/L

options.label: A
options.text: Ferrous sulfate once on alternate days
options.explanation: Correct: higher fractional absorption, possibly fewer GI effects.

options.label: B
options.explanation: More doses raise hepcidin and side effects.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Split dosing raises hepcidin without better absorption.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Calcium impairs iron absorption.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Food lowers absorption; TID dosing already failed.

questions.explanation: An oral iron dose raises hepcidin for about 24 h, cutting absorption of the next day's dose. Single doses on alternate days increased fractional absorption by 40–50% in women with iron deficiency anemia, with a trend to fewer GI effects. Split dosing raises hepcidin further. Consider IV iron if oral iron fails or isn't tolerated.

references.title: Iron absorption greater with alternate vs consecutive day dosing in IDA women (Haematologica 2020)
references.supports: FIA 40–50% higher; hepcidin dynamics

references.title: Alternate-day iron better absorbed (ACP Internist on Lancet Haematol 2017)
references.supports: Split dosing raises hepcidin and reduces absorption

issues: Accurate: alternate-day single doses raised fractional absorption ~40-50% (Haematologica/Stoffel); GI side-effect reduction was only a non-significant trend (explanation correctly says 'trend'). Split dosing raises hepcidin.
Correct option slightly longer than others; acceptable. No bank duplicate.

questions.topic: Fever and rigors during RBC transfusion
questions.stem:
68F w/ GI bleed receiving 2nd unit RBC for Hb 68 g/L. 20 min in: rigors, T 39.3 °C (baseline 36.8).

BP 112/64 (baseline 118/70), HR 108, SpO2 96% RA. No urticaria or dyspnea.

options.label: A
options.text: Continue the unit; vitals q15 min
options.explanation: Continuing risks a hemolytic or septic reaction.

options.label: B
options.explanation: For TACO; no dyspnea or hypoxemia here.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Resuming is only for low-risk fever (38–38.9 °C, no other Sx).

options.label: D
options.text: Stop; do not restart; DAT, cultures, IV Abx
options.explanation: Correct: ≥39 °C or rigors may be sepsis or hemolysis, not just FNHTR.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Treats allergic reactions; doesn't address sepsis or hemolysis.

questions.explanation: Fever ≥39 °C or rigors during transfusion could be FNHTR, bacterial contamination or acute hemolysis. Per the TTISS-ON acute reaction chart (Canadian Blood Services): don't restart the transfusion; return the unit for clerical check and culture; send group and screen, DAT, patient blood cultures and a hemolysis workup; start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Low-risk fever (38–38.9 °C, no other Sx) may get an antipyretic and resumption.

references.title: TTISS-ON acute transfusion reaction chart v4.0 (Canadian Blood Services)
references.supports: High-risk fever: do not restart; DAT, cultures, IV Abx; low-risk: antipyretic, may resume

issues: Replacement for a rejected duplicate; second review: revise

Accurate. The chart's high-risk fever criteria are >=39 C, fever with other Sx, or rigors. Actions: do not restart, return the unit for clerical check and culture, G&S + DAT, patient blood cultures, urinalysis, hemolysis work-up, and broad-spectrum IV Abx without waiting for cultures. Low risk is 38-38.9 C with no other Sx: antipyretic, and the transfusion may resume. The McMaster Textbook agrees: stop and investigate if >=39 C or fever with Sx.

Source attribution: the chart is the TTISS-ON Acute Transfusion Reaction Chart, Version 4.0 (Oct 2020), hosted on Canadian Blood Services' profedu site. 'Canadian Blood Services chart' is slightly loose. It is still current.

questions.stem:
31M w/ HIV started dapsone 1 wk ago (sulfa allergy). Now dark urine and fatigue.

Hb 82 g/L (was 138)
Reticulocytes 9%
LDH 780 U/L; haptoglobin undetectable
DAT negative
Smear: bite and blister cells
G6PD activity: normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: Reticulocytes have high G6PD activity, masking deficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: Stop dapsone; repeat G6PD assay in 2–3 mo
options.explanation: Correct: assay can be falsely normal during acute hemolysis.

options.label: C
options.explanation: DAT negative; smear points to oxidant injury.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Acute drug-triggered episode; bite cells, not spherocytes.

options.label: E
options.explanation: No thrombocytopenia or schistocytes described.

questions.explanation: Acute DAT-negative hemolysis with bite/blister cells after an oxidant drug suggests G6PD deficiency. During or soon after hemolysis the assay may be falsely normal because the oldest, most deficient cells have lysed and reticulocytes are G6PD-rich. Stop the trigger, give supportive care, and repeat the assay weeks to months later.

references.title: G6PD deficiency (Merck Manual Professional)
references.supports: Smear findings; false-negative assay; supportive Rx

references.title: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase test (ARUP Consult)
references.supports: Repeat ≥2–3 mo after hemolytic episode

issues: Accurate: assay can be falsely normal during/after hemolysis because deficient old cells are destroyed and reticulocytes are G6PD-rich; Merck says repeat after several weeks, ARUP >=2-3 mo.
Teaching aside worth adding (optional): G6PD should be checked before starting dapsone.
No bank duplicate.

questions.stem:
27M requests HIV PrEP. Condomless anal sex w/ new partner 12 d ago; since then fever, sore throat, myalgia and rash.

4th-gen HIV Ag/Ab: negative
Cr 80 µmol/L
HBsAg negative

options.label: A
options.explanation: PEP must start within 72 h of exposure.

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat Ag/Ab in 3 mo, then start PrEP
options.explanation: Leaves possible acute HIV undiagnosed and him unprotected.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Risks HIV resistance if acute infection is present.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Same resistance concern; acute HIV not excluded.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: rule out acute HIV before starting 2-drug PrEP.

questions.explanation: Symptoms of acute HIV after a recent exposure mean he may be in the window period of the Ag/Ab test. TDF/FTC alone is an incomplete regimen and can select resistance in undiagnosed HIV, so assess urgently with HIV RNA before PrEP. Baseline Cr and HBV status are also required (TDF/FTC is active against HBV).

references.title: Canadian guideline on HIV PrEP and nPEP: pharmacist summary (Can Pharm J)
references.supports: Window period; acute HIV symptoms need urgent testing; HIV RNA

references.title: National HIV PrEP Curriculum: baseline evaluation (U Washington)
references.supports: HIV RNA if acute HIV suspected; baseline Cr, HBV

issues: Accurate: with acute HIV symptoms after recent exposure, do HIV RNA and delay PrEP until results; PEP only within 72 h; TDF/FTC alone risks resistance; baseline Cr and HBV needed.
Broken reference: the Strides prescribing-information URL returns a 404 page.
No bank duplicate (bank PEP item is occupational timing).

questions.stem:
39M w/ new HIV Dx (CD4 45 ×10^6/L) p/w 3 wk of dry cough and dyspnea. Bilateral interstitial infiltrates; BAL PCR positive for Pneumocystis. Starting TMP-SMX.

ABG on RA: PaO2 62 mmHg

options.label: A
options.explanation: Pulse dosing isn't the studied regimen.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Misses a proven mortality benefit in hypoxemic HIV-associated PJP.

options.label: C
options.explanation: No role as standard add-on therapy.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: PaO2 <70 mmHg; start within 72 h of TMP-SMX.

options.label: E
options.explanation: TMP-SMX remains first line; more toxic.

questions.explanation: In HIV-associated PJP, give adjunctive corticosteroids when PaO2 <70 mmHg, A–a gradient ≥35 mmHg, or SpO2 <92% on room air, ideally within 72 h of starting anti-Pneumocystis therapy. Usual regimen: prednisone 40 mg BID ×5 d, 40 mg daily ×5 d, then 20 mg daily ×11 d. Evidence in HIV-negative patients is weaker.

references.title: When should I give corticosteroids to my patient with PJP? (Cleve Clin J Med 2024)
references.supports: Criteria, timing, 21-d regimen, HIV-negative data

issues: Accurate: steroids if PaO2 <70, A-a >=35 or SpO2 <92%, within 72 h; 21-d prednisone regimen; weaker evidence in HIV-negative.
Cueing: correct option D is longer and more specific than most options.
No bank duplicate (bank has PJP prophylaxis only).

questions.stem:
81F on post-op day 6 after hip fracture repair; Foley still in. Afebrile, no urinary or flank Sx.

WBC 7.8 ×10^9/L
Urine culture: Candida albicans >10^5 CFU/mL
Not neutropenic; no urologic procedure planned.

options.label: A
options.explanation: For symptomatic cystitis, not asymptomatic candiduria.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not recommended for asymptomatic candiduria.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace catheter and give fluconazole ×7 d
options.explanation: Antifungal unnecessary; remove catheter if feasible.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Poor urinary levels; no indication.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: asymptomatic candiduria usually clears once the catheter is out.

questions.explanation: Most asymptomatic candiduria is colonization and clears once the catheter is removed or antibiotics stopped. Antifungals aren't indicated unless high risk: neutropenia or an upcoming urologic procedure. Fluconazole is for symptomatic Candida cystitis or pyelonephritis.

references.title: Candiduria (Interna, McMaster textbook)
references.supports: No Rx for most; resolves with catheter removal

references.title: Candiduria (McMaster Textbook of Internal Medicine, empendium)
references.supports: Treatment of symptomatic and high-risk candiduria

issues: Accurate: asymptomatic candiduria usually needs no antifungal and often resolves with catheter removal; treat only if neutropenic or before urologic procedures (McMaster Textbook). Fluconazole 200 mg x14 d is the symptomatic cystitis regimen.
The guidelinecentral IDSA URL loads no guideline content, so the explicit 'IDSA recommends' claim isn't verified from a cited source.
Teaching point parallels bank im-261030-46 (asymptomatic bacteriuria) but different organism and decision - acceptable.

questions.stem:
62F w/ essential thrombocythemia, routine labs. Asymptomatic. No RAAS inhibitors.

K 6.4 mmol/L (serum, no hemolysis reported)
Plt 1,150 ×10^9/L
Cr 70 µmol/L
ECG: normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: Treating pseudohyperkalemia can cause true hypokalemia.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Risks hypoglycemia and hypokalemia if K is truly normal.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: platelets release K when the serum sample clots.

options.label: D
options.explanation: No ECG changes; likely spurious result.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Premature before confirming true hyperkalemia.

questions.explanation: With marked thrombocytosis (or leukocytosis), platelets release potassium as blood clots in a serum tube, falsely raising serum K. Suspect it when K is high with normal kidney function, no symptoms and a normal ECG. Measure plasma K in a lithium-heparin tube: serum exceeding plasma by >0.4 mmol/L confirms pseudohyperkalemia. Treating it can cause iatrogenic hypokalemia.

references.title: Pseudohyperkalaemia unmasking thrombocytosis (Pulse)
references.supports: Mechanism; paired serum/plasma; >0.4 mmol/L

references.title: Pseudohyperkalemia in thrombocytosis (Electrolyte Blood Press, PMC)
references.supports: Platelet K release during clotting raises serum K in vitro

issues: Accurate: platelets release K during clotting; paired lithium-heparin plasma; serum - plasma >0.4 mmol/L supports pseudohyperkalemia.
PMC4535006 returned a captcha; mechanism verified by Pulse article. Pulse is a UK GP trade magazine - acceptable but a peer-reviewed review would be stronger.
No bank duplicate (bank pseudothrombocytopenia is a different spurious lab).

questions.stem:
69M on pantoprazole for 4 mo. Routine labs show rising Cr. No NSAIDs, contrast or new Abx. Euvolemic.

Cr 168 µmol/L (baseline 82)
UA: WBC 15–20/hpf, WBC casts, no RBC casts, protein 1+
Urine culture negative
US: normal kidneys, no hydronephrosis

options.label: A
options.explanation: Poor sensitivity and specificity; won't change management.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Euvolemic; picture isn't prerenal.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Usually reserved for no improvement after stopping the drug.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop pantoprazole; recheck Cr in ~1 wk
options.explanation: Correct: drug withdrawal is the mainstay of AIN Tx.

options.label: E
options.explanation: For atypical findings or failure to improve.

questions.explanation: Sterile pyuria with WBC casts and rising Cr on a PPI suggests drug-induced AIN. Stopping the culprit is the mainstay; with mild disease, close follow-up is enough. Glucocorticoids are generally reserved for patients who don't improve within days of stopping, and biopsy for atypical features or nonrecovery. Delayed withdrawal worsens recovery.

references.title: MKSAP Quiz: AIN after omeprazole (ACP Internist)
references.supports: Stop drug; steroids for nonresponders; biopsy if inconsistent

references.title: Drug-induced AIN: pathology, pathogenesis and treatment (Iran J Kidney Dis 2015)
references.supports: Steroids if no improvement 3–5 d after stopping

issues: Accurate: stopping the culprit is mainstay; steroids generally for nonresponders; biopsy if atypical or nonrecovery; urine eosinophils not useful.
Option C (early steroids) is defensible to some nephrologists (observational data favour steroids within ~7 d), but for mild AKI after a culprit is identified, D is the best answer.

PubMed 25599729 hit a captcha; search confirms it is Praga et al. 'Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis: pathology, pathogenesis, and treatment' - the specific '3-5 d' claim couldn't be read directly.

questions.stem:
45F w/ T1DM, 3 d of persistent vomiting.

Na 134, Cl 82, HCO3 14 mmol/L
Glucose 28 mmol/L
VBG: pH 7.30, PaCO2 29 mmHg
Albumin 40 g/L
questions.lead: Best description of her acid–base status?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Delta ratio >2 shows HCO3 higher than expected.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: AG 38, delta ratio 26/10 = 2.6 (>2).

options.label: C
options.explanation: PaCO2 isn't below the expected range.

options.label: D
options.explanation: That gives a delta ratio <0.8.

options.label: E
options.explanation: PaCO2 29 fits Winter's formula (27–31).

questions.explanation: AG = 134 − (82 + 14) = 38, so ΔAG = 26 while ΔHCO3 = 10: delta ratio 2.6. A ratio >2 means HCO3 fell less than expected, implying a coexisting metabolic alkalosis, here from vomiting. Winter's formula (1.5 × 14 + 8 = 29 ± 2) shows appropriate respiratory compensation. Pure DKA usually gives a ratio near 1.

references.title: Updated review of serum anion gap (MDCalc / Scholastica)
references.supports: Delta ratio formula and interpretation ranges

references.title: Tales of the anion gap, part III (HCPLive)
references.supports: DKA ratio ~1; >2 = concomitant metabolic alkalosis

issues: Accurate: AG 38, delta ratio 26/10 = 2.6 (>2 = concurrent metabolic alkalosis); Winter's 29 +/- 2 matches PaCO2 29; pH consistent by Henderson-Hasselbalch (~7.31).
Overlap with bank im-261101-22 (Winter's formula) is partial; delta-ratio point is new.

questions.stem:
76M w/ CKD (eGFR 28) and AF on apixaban. Currently taking clarithromycin-based H. pylori Tx. Acute flare of R knee, L ankle and L wrist.

Knee aspirate: MSU crystals, Gram stain negative.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Contraindicated w/ clarithromycin in renal impairment; fatal toxicity reported.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct: avoids NSAID and colchicine hazards; suits polyarticular flare.

options.label: C
options.explanation: CKD stage 4 plus anticoagulant: high renal and bleeding risk.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Doesn't treat the flare; too high a start in CKD.

options.label: E
options.explanation: For when first-line agents are contraindicated; prednisone isn't.

questions.explanation: ACR 2020 strongly recommends colchicine, NSAIDs or glucocorticoids (oral, intra-articular or IM) for flares, chosen by patient factors. Here NSAIDs are unsafe (CKD, anticoagulation) and colchicine is contraindicated with a strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitor such as clarithromycin in renal impairment. With several joints involved, oral prednisone is best.

references.title: 2020 ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout (abstract)
references.supports: Colchicine, NSAIDs or glucocorticoids strongly recommended for flares

references.title: Colchicine tablets prescribing information
references.supports: Contraindicated w/ P-gp or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors in renal impairment

issues: Accurate: ACR 2020 strongly recommends colchicine, NSAID or glucocorticoid for flares; colchicine contraindicated with strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors (clarithromycin) in renal impairment; NSAID unsafe with eGFR 28 and apixaban.
Cueing: correct option B (43 chars, includes dose and 'short taper') is about twice the length of A, C and E.
No bank duplicate (bank gout items cover ULT target, ULT start during flare, HLA-B*58:01).

questions.stem: 48F w/ new seropositive RA starting methotrexate 15 mg PO weekly. Baseline CBC, Cr, ALT and hepatitis serology normal.
questions.lead: Most appropriate addition to this regimen?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: reduces transaminase rise, GI effects and dropouts.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Doesn't prevent hepatotoxicity or cytopenias.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Rescue regimen for MTX overdose or toxicity, not routine use.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Not used to prevent MTX hepatotoxicity.

options.label: E
options.explanation: No role; doesn't counter MTX's antifolate effect.

questions.explanation: Prescribe folic acid with every low-dose MTX regimen. In a Cochrane review of RA trials, folate cut transaminase elevations (RR 0.23), GI adverse effects (RR 0.74) and MTX withdrawal (RR 0.39), with no loss of anti-arthritic effect. Folic and folinic acid work similarly; folic acid (commonly 5 mg weekly, not on MTX day) is cheaper.

references.title: Folic and folinic acid for reducing MTX side effects in RA: Cochrane review (J Rheumatol)
references.supports: RR 0.23 LFTs, 0.74 GI, 0.39 withdrawal; efficacy preserved

references.title: Using folic acid with methotrexate in RA (GPnotebook)
references.supports: 5 mg weekly on a different day to MTX

source.book: Cochrane: folate with MTX in RA

issues: Accurate: Cochrane - folate cuts transaminase rise (RR 0.23), GI effects (RR 0.74), withdrawal (RR 0.39) without loss of efficacy.
Low discrimination: distractors (ursodiol, B12, NAC) are implausible, so the item tests recognition only.
Options/lead rebuilt after second review

questions.stem:
64M on metoprolol develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension 10 min after IV cefazolin. Given IM epinephrine 0.5 mg ×3, 2 L NS; epinephrine infusion running.

BP 74/42, HR 58, SpO2 93% on O2.

options.label: A
options.explanation: No acute effect on hypotension.

options.label: B
options.explanation: For bronchospasm; won't fix hypotension.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: bypasses beta-blockade by activating adenylyl cyclase.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Treats itch/urticaria only, not shock.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Adjunct for skin symptoms; doesn't treat shock.

questions.explanation: Beta-blockers can blunt the response to epinephrine. For refractory anaphylaxis in a beta-blocked patient, add glucagon 1–5 mg IV over 5 min, then 5–15 µg/min, which raises cAMP independent of beta receptors. Give slowly and protect the airway, since it causes vomiting. Continue epinephrine and fluids; add vasopressors if still refractory.

references.title: Anaphylaxis (Merck Manual Professional)
references.supports: Glucagon dose for beta-blocked patients; vasopressors if refractory

issues: Accurate: glucagon 1-5 mg IV over 5 min then 5-15 ug/min for beta-blocked patients; rapid administration causes vomiting; vasopressors if refractory (Merck).
Broken reference: the NursingCenter pocket-card URL loads no content.
Correct option C is the longest and only one with an infusion; mild cue.

questions.stem:
58F becomes cyanotic and dyspneic 30 min after TEE w/ benzocaine throat spray.

SpO2 85% on 100% O2 via non-rebreather
ABG: PaO2 310 mmHg
Co-oximetry: MetHb 32%
No known G6PD deficiency; no serotonergic drugs

options.label: A
options.explanation: SpO2 is falsely low; PaO2 is high. Treat the cause.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Alternative only when methylene blue is contraindicated (G6PD).

options.label: C
options.text: Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min
options.explanation: Correct: symptomatic and MetHb >20%.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Reserved for refractory cases; not first line.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Reserved for failure of methylene blue.

questions.explanation: Cyanosis with SpO2 stuck near 85% despite 100% O2 and a high PaO2 (saturation gap) suggests methemoglobinemia; confirm with co-oximetry. Treat if symptomatic or MetHb >20%: methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min. Avoid it in G6PD deficiency (ineffective, hemolysis) and with serotonergic drugs (serotonin syndrome).

references.title: CPT Pearl: acquired methemoglobinemia (U Calgary)
references.supports: Clues, indications, dose, G6PD and serotonin cautions

references.title: Methemoglobinemia (OpenAnesthesia)
references.supports: SpO2 ~85%; benzocaine; vitamin C in G6PD; exchange transfusion

issues: Accurate: saturation gap, co-oximetry, methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV over 5 min if symptomatic or MetHb >20%; avoid in G6PD deficiency and with serotonergic drugs; vitamin C as G6PD alternative.
Error in option D explanation: hyperbaric O2 is listed (OpenAnesthesia) as a treatment for refractory methemoglobinemia, so 'for carbon monoxide, not methemoglobinemia' is wrong.
No bank duplicate.

questions.topic: Chronic insomnia in an older adult
questions.stem: 78F w/ 6 mo of trouble staying asleep ≥3 nights/wk, daytime fatigue. No depression, OSA Sx, pain or nocturia. No sedating meds. Sleep hygiene advice already tried.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Beers: avoid benzodiazepines in older adults.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Anticholinergic; not recommended in older adults.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Unclear efficacy; higher doses add side effects.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: first line, durable and without drug harms.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Beers: avoid Z-drugs (falls, fractures, delirium).

questions.explanation: CBT-I (stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy) is first line for chronic insomnia and works better long term than drugs. The 2023 Beers Criteria advise avoiding benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults because of delirium, falls, fractures and crashes for minimal sleep benefit. Avoid sedating antihistamines too.

references.title: Insomnia reference card (Alosa Health 2024)
references.supports: CBT-I best; avoid benzos, Z-drugs, diphenhydramine; trazodone unclear

references.title: Sleep disorders in older adults (UCLA, AGS recommendations)
references.supports: Beers 2023: avoid benzodiazepines and Z-drugs

issues: Accurate: CBT-I is initial treatment for chronic insomnia (ACP, strong); Beers 2023 avoid benzodiazepines and Z-drugs; avoid diphenhydramine; trazodone evidence weak.
Overlap: bank im-261030-57 (Beers: diphenhydramine) and im-261030-153 (BZRA deprescribing + CBT-I) share distractor content, but first-line therapy for new chronic insomnia is a distinct decision.
Not neurology content (geriatrics/sleep primary care).

questions.stem: 64M w/ metastatic prostate cancer to bone on morphine SR 60 mg PO q12h; baseline pain well controlled. Now episodic pain on walking.
questions.lead: Most appropriate PRN morphine IR dose (PO)?

options.label: A
options.explanation: ~33%: excess sedation/respiratory risk.

options.label: B
options.explanation: ~4%: below the usual proportional range.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct: 12.5% of the 120 mg/24 h dose (range 12–24 mg).

options.label: D
options.explanation: Equals a full q12h dose; unsafe as PRN.

options.label: E
options.explanation: ~2% of daily dose: likely ineffective.

questions.explanation: For breakthrough cancer pain, dose an immediate-release oral opioid (other than rapid-onset fentanyl) at 10–20% of the total 24-h around-the-clock dose. He takes 120 mg/d of morphine, so 12–24 mg; 15 mg fits. Tiny doses are a common cause of uncontrolled breakthrough pain; titrate to effect.

references.title: Breakthrough cancer pain: systematic review of pharmacologic management (CJON 2017)
references.supports: 10–20% of 24-h ATC dose

references.title: Short-acting opioids proportional to basal dose (ONS PEP)
references.supports: 10–20%; not for rapid-onset fentanyl

issues: Accurate: IR opioid at 10-20% of 24-h dose (ONS CJON systematic review); 120 mg/d -> 12-24 mg, 15 mg fits. ONS proportional-dosing page gives a wider 5-20% range - option B (5 mg, ~4%) still falls below it.
Minor overlap: bank im-261030-210 (opioid rotation) mentions breakthrough ~10% in its explanation only.

questions.stem:
64M p/w 2 h of palpitations. h/o MI 2019. Alert, no chest pain.

BP 118/72, HR 168, SpO2 96%
ECG: regular wide-complex tachycardia, QRS 150 ms, no clear P waves

options.label: A
options.explanation: Slow AV nodal agent; ineffective for VT.

options.label: B
options.explanation: AV nodal blocker; won't terminate VT and may worsen BP.

options.label: C
options.explanation: CCBs can cause collapse in VT; avoid in wide-complex tachycardia of unknown origin.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Presume VT; procainamide is a reasonable first-line drug for stable monomorphic VT.

options.label: E
options.explanation: For torsades (polymorphic VT), not regular monomorphic WCT.

questions.explanation: Treat a regular wide-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise, especially with prior MI. If stable: IV procainamide (amiodarone if procainamide unavailable or failed) or synchronized cardioversion, with pads on. Never give verapamil or diltiazem to a wide-complex tachycardia of unknown origin: if it's VT, it can precipitate collapse.

references.title: Procainamide vs Amiodarone: The Evidence Behind Treating Stable, Monomorphic VT (Cooper EM)
references.supports: Presume VT; procainamide reasonable first line; avoid CCBs in WCT

references.title: Treatment of Stable VT (RCEMLearning)
references.supports: Procainamide more effective than amiodarone; DC cardioversion reasonable first line

source.book: ACC/AHA/ESC VT guidance (via Cooper EM review)

questions.stem:
58M p/w 3 h of rest chest pain, now resolved. ECG: 1 mm ST depression V4–V6.

BP 142/86, HR 78
hs-troponin T 64 ng/L, rising

Given ASA 160 mg. Angiography planned within 24 h.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Same issue; load once anatomy known and PCI is chosen.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Pretreatment before anatomy is known adds bleeding and may delay CABG; load at PCI.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Prasugrel pretreatment increased bleeding without benefit; give only at PCI.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer until coronary anatomy is known
options.explanation: ESC 2023 Class III: no routine pretreatment when early (<24 h) angiography planned.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not routine; reserved for bailout or thrombotic complications at PCI.

questions.explanation: In NSTE-ACS with early invasive angiography (<24 h) planned and anatomy unknown, ESC 2023 recommends against routine P2Y12 pretreatment (Class III): load once anatomy is known and PCI is chosen. Pretreatment may be considered if angiography is expected to be delayed and bleeding risk is low. ACC/AHA 2025 similarly allows upstream clopidogrel or ticagrelor (IIb) only if angiography is expected >24 h.

references.title: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of ACS – summary (PCRonline)
references.supports: Routine P2Y12 pretreatment not recommended when anatomy unknown and early invasive planned

references.title: Pretreatment with antiplatelet agents in patients undergoing coronary revascularisation (EuroIntervention)
references.supports: ESC 2023 Class III; IIb if delayed invasive; ACC/AHA 2025 comparison

issues: Option A explanation 'Same issue; ...' refers to another option and breaks if options are shuffled; each option explanation must stand alone.
Explanation sentence 'Up to 1 in 5 may need CABG or have a non-ACS diagnosis' isn't supported by either reference (EuroIntervention review gives no proportion).

For Canadian context, CCS/CAIC 2023 antiplatelet focused update couldn't be verified on pretreatment (CCS news page doesn't state it); ACC/AHA 2025 gives IIb for upstream clopidogrel/ticagrelor only when angiography >24 h; consistent with key.

questions.stem:
71F s/p surgical bioprosthetic AVR 8 mo ago. New persistent AF. h/o HTN, T2DM.

BP 134/80, HR 88 irregular
Cr 82 µmol/L
TTE: normally functioning bioprosthesis, no mitral stenosis

options.label: A
options.explanation: Higher target is for some mechanical valves, not bioprostheses.

options.label: B
options.explanation: DOAC recommended for AF >3 mo after a bioprosthetic valve.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Reserved for patients who can't take oral anticoagulation.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Antiplatelet alone is inadequate for AF stroke prevention.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Inferior to oral anticoagulation, with similar bleeding.

questions.explanation: A bioprosthetic valve doesn't make AF 'valvular' in the warfarin-only sense: >3 mo after implantation, ESC and ACC/AHA guidelines recommend a DOAC for AF (aortic or mitral position). Warfarin is still required for mechanical valves and moderate–severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. Within the first 3 mo, a VKA is generally preferred.

references.title: Direct oral anticoagulants in surgical bioprosthetic valves (Rev Port Cardiol 2023)
references.supports: ACC/AHA DOAC 1A and ESC DOAC IIa >3 mo; VKA <3 mo

49M p/w 20 min of retrosternal pressure that began 5 h ago; now pain-free.

BP 128/78, HR 72
ECG: normal sinus rhythm, no ischemic changes
hs-cTnT (Elecsys) on arrival: <5 ng/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Older 0/3-h pathway; unnecessary with a very low value after 3 h.

options.label: B
options.explanation: No evidence of MI or high-risk features.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.explanation: Outdated serial strategy; delays disposition without added safety.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Single hs-cTnT <5 ng/L with onset >3 h earlier rules out NSTEMI.

questions.explanation: In the ESC 0/1-h algorithm for hs-cTnT, a single value <5 ng/L rules out NSTEMI if chest pain began >3 h before sampling and the ECG is non-ischemic. Early presenters need the 1-h value (rule-out: 0 h <12 ng/L and Δ1h <3 ng/L). Cut-offs are assay-specific. Ruling out MI doesn't exclude CAD: arrange risk-based follow-up.

references.title: Roche Accelerated AMI Algorithm brochure (ESC 0/1 h cut-offs for hs-cTnT)

questions.stem:
68M w/ HFrEF (EF 25%) admitted w/ 1 wk of orthopnea and 6 kg weight gain. On bisoprolol 10 mg, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone, dapagliflozin.

BP 124/76, HR 84, SpO2 92% RA
Warm extremities, JVP 10 cm
Cr 108 µmol/L, lactate 1.2 mmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Not an evidence-based HFrEF beta-blocker; no reason to switch.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Interruption lowers later beta-blocker use and worsens outcomes.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Warm, normotensive, no bradycardia: continuing is associated with lower mortality.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Dose reduction is for bradycardia or hypotension.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Withdrawal is associated with higher in-hospital and short-term mortality.

questions.explanation: In ADHF, continue the home beta-blocker unless the patient is in cardiogenic shock (stop) or has bradycardia or hypotension (reduce). Stopping it is associated with higher in-hospital and short-term mortality and lower beta-blocker use after discharge. This patient is warm and wet with normal BP: diurese and continue.

references.supports: Withdrawal associated with higher in-hospital and short-term mortality

questions.stem:
74F p/w 4 mo of progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough. On nitrofurantoin 100 mg nightly ×2 y for UTI prophylaxis. Nonsmoker.

SpO2 93% RA, fine bibasilar crackles
CT chest: bilateral lower-zone ground-glass and reticulation
PFTs: restrictive, low DLCO

options.label: A
options.explanation: Drug withdrawal is the key step; most chronic cases improve after stopping.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not needed when exposure, timing and imaging fit.

options.label: C
options.explanation: May exclude infection, but doesn't replace stopping the drug.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Steroids may be added in severe cases, but the drug must stop.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Antifibrotic for IPF; remove the culprit drug first.

questions.explanation: Long-term nitrofurantoin (months–years, often older women on UTI prophylaxis) can cause chronic ILD that usually improves once the drug is stopped. Stopping it is the main intervention; corticosteroids may be added for severe or non-resolving disease. Check the medication list before labeling ILD idiopathic.

references.title: Nitrofurantoin-Induced Pulmonary Toxicity: Mechanisms, Diagnosis, and Management (Toxics 2025)
references.supports: Discontinuation is the primary intervention; steroids may be added

references.title: Nitrofurantoin-induced interstitial lung disease: case report and review (PMC)

questions.stem:
66M w/ severe COPD seen at a routine clinic visit; no recent exacerbation.

ABG (RA):
pH 7.35
PaCO2 60 mmHg
HCO3 31 mmol/L
PaO2 58 mmHg

options.label: A
options.explanation: HCO3 isn't above the expected chronic range.

options.label: B
options.explanation: PaCO2 up 20 → expected HCO3 ≈30–32 with chronic compensation; 31 fits.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Acute HCO3 rise is only 1–2 per 10 mmHg (expect ~26).

options.label: D
options.explanation: HCO3 would be below the expected range.

options.label: E
options.explanation: pH would be lower and HCO3 below the chronic expectation.

questions.explanation: Expected HCO3 rise per 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2: acute 1–2 mmol/L (buffering), chronic 3–4 mmol/L (renal compensation over 3–5 d). Here PaCO2 is up 20, so chronic HCO3 ≈30–32; 31 fits a simple chronic respiratory acidosis. HCO3 above the range implies added metabolic alkalosis; below it, an acute component or metabolic acidosis.

references.title: Primary Changes and Compensations in Simple Acid-Base Disorders (Merck Manual Professional)
references.supports: Acute 1–2, chronic 3–4 mEq/L HCO3 per 10 mmHg PaCO2

questions.stem: 52F, nonsmoker, treated as outpatient w/ amoxicillin for RLL CAP. Afebrile and asymptomatic by day 5. Clinic visit at 3 wk: no cough, normal chest exam. Not eligible for lung cancer screening.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.explanation: Radiographic clearing lags recovery; low yield.

options.label: C
options.explanation: ATS/IDSA: don't routinely image if symptoms resolved within 5–7 d.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Not indicated in a recovered, low-risk patient.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Traditional practice, now not recommended routinely.

questions.explanation: ATS/IDSA 2019 recommends against routine follow-up chest imaging in adults whose CAP symptoms resolved within 5–7 d: radiographic resolution lags clinical recovery and the yield for cancer is low. Image if symptoms persist or recur, and offer lung cancer screening to eligible patients.

references.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia: ATS/IDSA guidelines update (emDOCs)
references.supports: Rec 16: no routine follow-up imaging if symptoms resolve in 5–7 d

questions.stem:
24F w/ mild asthma, Sx <2×/mo, no exacerbations. Uses as-needed budesonide-formoterol only. Started running; gets cough and wheeze 10 min after hard runs.

Spirometry: normal, FEV1 95% predicted
questions.lead: Most appropriate advice for exercise Sx?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Use the same anti-inflammatory reliever pre-exercise; no separate SABA.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Exercise is encouraged; EIB is preventable.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Less effective; neuropsychiatric warning; not preferred.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Overtreatment for mild, well-controlled asthma.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Those using ICS-formoterol as reliever should use it, not a separate SABA.

questions.explanation: In mild asthma on as-needed ICS-formoterol, take the same inhaler before exercise instead of a separate SABA; as-needed budesonide-formoterol reduced EIB about as much as daily ICS. Frequent EIB suggests poor control and calls for review of overall treatment. Warming up also reduces EIB.

questions.stem:
61M w/ newly Dx non-Hodgkin lymphoma p/w progressive dyspnea. Large L pleural effusion. Thoracentesis: milky, odorless fluid that stays turbid after centrifugation.

Pleural protein 38 g/L, LDH 140 U/L
Pleural triglycerides 3.1 mmol/L
Pleural cholesterol 2.4 mmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: High cholesterol (>5.18 mmol/L), low TG, chronic effusions, cholesterol crystals.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Supernatant clears after centrifugation; purulent, low pH/glucose.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Pleural Hct >50% of blood Hct; bloody, not milky.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Lymphocytic exudate with high ADA; not milky.

options.label: E
options.explanation: TG >1.24 mmol/L with cholesterol <5.18 mmol/L is diagnostic.

questions.explanation: Pleural TG >1.24 mmol/L (110 mg/dL) with cholesterol <5.18 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) is diagnostic of chylothorax; borderline TG needs lipoprotein electrophoresis for chylomicrons. Lymphoma is the most common malignant cause of non-traumatic chylothorax. Pseudochylothorax is the reverse: high cholesterol, low TG, in long-standing effusions. Appearance alone is unreliable.

references.title: Non-traumatic chylothorax: diagnostic and therapeutic strategies (Breathe 2022)
references.supports: TG >1.24 and cholesterol <5.18 diagnostic; lymphoma most common malignant cause

references.title: Non-traumatic chylothorax (Breathe 2022, PMC full text)
references.supports: Causes: lymphoma is most common malignant cause

questions.stem: 79F w/ T2DM on gliclazide, eGFR 28, brought in confused. Glucose 1.8 mmol/L; improves w/ D50W. Over the next 4 h, two more episodes <3.0 mmol/L despite D10W infusion.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Suppresses insulin release; cuts recurrent hypoglycemia and dextrose needs.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Hyperglycemic surges drive more insulin secretion: rebound cycle.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Less effective than octreotide; causes hypotension.

options.label: D
options.explanation: No role without adrenal insufficiency.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Brief effect; can further stimulate insulin release.

questions.explanation: Sulfonylurea hypoglycemia recurs because dextrose stimulates more insulin release from sulfonylurea-primed β-cells. Octreotide (e.g., 50 µg SC q6–8h) suppresses insulin secretion, cutting recurrent episodes and dextrose needs; give it with dextrose and observe closely, often >24 h in CKD, where sulfonylurea effects last longer.

references.title: Octreotide: an antidote for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia (Ann Emerg Med 2000)
references.supports: Octreotide reduced recurrent hypoglycemia and dextrose use

references.title: Octreotide's role in sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia (J Med Toxicol 2010)
references.supports: Evidence supports octreotide with supplemental dextrose

questions.topic: Transition off IV insulin after DKA
questions.stem:
26M w/ T1DM admitted w/ DKA, on IV insulin infusion. Now alert, eating breakfast.

Glucose 9.8 mmol/L
HCO3 20 mmol/L, anion gap 10
pH 7.34

options.label: A
options.text: SC basal insulin now; stop IV in 1–2 h
options.explanation: Overlap prevents a gap in insulin coverage.

options.label: B
options.explanation: DKA has resolved; prolonging IV insulin risks hypoglycemia.

options.label: C
options.text: Stop IV now; mealtime insulin only
options.explanation: Without basal insulin, ketosis recurs between meals.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop IV now; correction insulin only
options.explanation: T1DM always needs basal insulin; DKA can recur.

options.label: E
options.text: Stop IV now; basal insulin at bedtime
options.explanation: IV insulin lasts minutes: gap → rebound hyperglycemia and ketosis.

questions.explanation: Once DKA has resolved and the patient can eat, start SC insulin (basal ± prandial) and continue the IV infusion for 1–2 h. IV insulin has a half-life of minutes, so stopping it before SC insulin acts causes rebound hyperglycemia and recurrent DKA. People with T1DM always need basal insulin.

references.title: Hyperglycemic crises in adults: a look at the 2024 consensus report (Cleve Clin J Med 2025)
references.supports: Start basal insulin at least 1–2 h before stopping IV insulin

references.title: Overlap of basal insulin when transitioning from IV insulin (InpharmD)
references.supports: ADA: continue IV insulin 1–2 h after SC insulin

questions.stem:
31F w/ schizophrenia, stable on risperidone ×8 mo, p/w 4 mo of amenorrhea and galactorrhea that began after starting it.

β-hCG negative
Prolactin 78 µg/L (ref <25)
TSH 1.8 mU/L
Cr 64 µmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Dopamine agonist may worsen psychosis; not first step.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Exclude drug cause first; MRI if prolactin doesn't fall or onset doesn't fit.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Drug cause likely; switch to a prolactin-sparing agent, then recheck.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Suggested for asymptomatic hyperprolactinemia; she is symptomatic.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Don't stop an antipsychotic without the prescribing psychiatrist.

questions.explanation: Drugs are a common cause of hyperprolactinemia, especially antipsychotics such as risperidone, usually with prolactin 25–100 µg/L. Exclude drugs, pregnancy, hypothyroidism and kidney failure before ordering a pituitary MRI. When symptoms began with the drug, switch (with psychiatry) to a prolactin-sparing agent and recheck prolactin. Order MRI if prolactin doesn't fall or onset didn't coincide with the drug.

references.title: Experts issue guidance for diagnosing, treating hyperprolactinemia (Healio; Endocrine Society 2011)
references.supports: Exclude medication before MRI; stop/substitute and recheck

references.title: New Endocrine Society guidelines for hyperprolactinemia (Nat Rev Endocrinol 2011)
references.supports: Don't stop antipsychotic without its prescriber; drug-induced is first-line differential

questions.stem:
63M p/w 3 mo of epigastric burning pain. No dysphagia, weight loss, GIB or vomiting. No NSAIDs. Not on a PPI.

Vitals normal, exam unremarkable
Hb 146 g/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: For <60 y who are H. pylori negative or still symptomatic.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Doesn't assess mucosal disease or upper GI cancer.

options.label: C
options.explanation: ACG/CAG: dyspepsia at age ≥60 → EGD to exclude neoplasia.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Initial strategy for patients <60 y.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Less sensitive than EGD; no biopsy.

questions.explanation: ACG/CAG 2017: patients ≥60 with dyspepsia should have an EGD to exclude upper GI cancer. Under 60, use noninvasive H. pylori test-and-treat, then a PPI trial; alarm features alone don't mandate endoscopy under 60 but can be considered case by case (e.g., family history, origin from a high-risk country).

references.title: ACG and CAG Clinical Guideline: Management of Dyspepsia (2017)
references.supports: ≥60 y: endoscopy; <60 y: H. pylori test-and-treat then PPI

questions.stem:
22M noticed yellow sclerae after 2 d of fasting during a viral illness. Otherwise well; no meds.

Total bilirubin 46 µmol/L (ref <20)
Conjugated bilirubin 4 µmol/L
ALT 22 U/L, ALP 70 U/L
Hb 150 g/L, reticulocytes normal
LDH, haptoglobin normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: Rarely needed; the lab pattern suffices.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Hepatitis raises conjugated bilirubin and transaminases.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not indicated in Gilbert syndrome.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassure; no imaging or further workup
options.explanation: Isolated unconjugated rise, normal enzymes, no hemolysis: Gilbert.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Unconjugated rise with normal enzymes isn't biliary obstruction.

questions.explanation: Mild, isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (usually <3× ULN, >70% unconjugated) with normal liver enzymes and no hemolysis, worse with fasting or illness, is Gilbert syndrome. It's benign: reassure, and skip imaging, biopsy and genetic testing. Repeat bilirubin once to confirm stability; re-evaluate (consider hemolysis) if it rises or the pattern doesn't fit.

references.title: Abnormal Liver Chemistry – Evaluation and Interpretation (BC Guidelines)
references.supports: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia commonly Gilbert; benign

references.title: Gilbert's disease: diagnosis (GPnotebook)
references.supports: <3× ULN, >70% unconjugated, normal LFTs; biopsy not indicated

source.book: BC Guidelines: Abnormal Liver Chemistry; GPnotebook

issues: Both references are weak: WikEM (wiki) and GPnotebook (UK reference site). Need a peer-reviewed or guideline source.
GPnotebook advises repeating bilirubin in 1–3 mo to confirm stability, so 'no further testing' in option D is slightly overstated.
Low difficulty: the fasting trigger plus isolated unconjugated rise makes this a giveaway; acceptable as a 'don't over-investigate' item but low yield.

questions.stem: 38F w/ refractory ITP booked for elective laparoscopic splenectomy in 4 wk. No vaccines since childhood.
questions.lead: Best timing for pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccines?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Too late for an optimal response.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Timing used after emergency splenectomy, not planned surgery.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Leaves her unprotected during the highest-risk period.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Gives the best antibody response before asplenia.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Response is better ≥2 wk postop; elective cases vaccinate before.

questions.explanation: For elective splenectomy, give pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccines ≥2 wk before surgery. After emergency splenectomy, vaccinate ≥2 wk postop (or before discharge if follow-up is uncertain). Add yearly influenza vaccine and teach her to seek urgent care for fever.

questions.stem:
45M p/w 6 wk of a painless 3 cm L supraclavicular node, night sweats and 5 kg weight loss.

CBC normal, LDH 410 U/L
CT: bulky mediastinal and retroperitoneal nodes

options.label: A
options.explanation: Preserves architecture for subtyping; preferred for accessible nodes.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Staging test; doesn't establish primary nodal Dx.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Staging after histologic Dx, not a diagnostic test.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Cells only, no architecture; inadequate for primary Dx.

questions.explanation: Lymphoma diagnosis and WHO subtyping need nodal architecture plus immunophenotyping, so excision of an accessible node is preferred. FNA isn't adequate for primary diagnosis; large-gauge core biopsy is for deep nodes and may still need excision if non-diagnostic. PET-CT and marrow biopsy are staging tests.

questions.stem:
81F admitted w/ acute PE, hemodynamically stable. AKI on CKD. Weight 52 kg.

Cr 248 µmol/L (CrCl ~15 mL/min)
Plt 210 ×10⁹/L
INR 1.1

options.label: A
options.explanation: Avoid with CrCl <30, especially in unstable AKI.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Renally cleared; contraindicated with CrCl <30.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not renally cleared, short-acting, reversible: preferred at CrCl <30.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Accumulates when CrCl <30 → bleeding.

options.label: E
options.explanation: About 80% renally cleared; contraindicated with CrCl <30.

questions.explanation: With CrCl <30 mL/min, LMWHs (especially enoxaparin) accumulate and raise bleeding risk. IV UFH is preferred for therapeutic anticoagulation because it isn't renally cleared, is short-acting, can be fully reversed and is titrated to aPTT/anti-Xa, which matters with fluctuating AKI.

questions.stem:
24M p/w 5 d of dysuria and scant urethral discharge. One new female partner. No allergies.

Urine NAAT: C. trachomatis positive, N. gonorrhoeae negative

options.label: A
options.explanation: Gonorrhea Tx; no reliable chlamydia activity.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Alternative only in pregnancy.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Preferred regimen; higher cure rates than azithromycin, especially rectal.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Gonorrhea alternative; no chlamydia activity.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not recommended for chlamydia.

questions.explanation: Doxycycline 100 mg BID ×7 d is preferred for chlamydia (CDC 2021), with higher cure rates than single-dose azithromycin, especially rectal. PHAC lists doxycycline or azithromycin 1 g once, favouring azithromycin if adherence is a concern or in pregnancy. Treat partners, abstain for 7 d after treatment, and rescreen at 3 mo.

references.title: Chlamydia and LGV guide: Treatment and follow-up (PHAC)
references.supports: Canadian regimens: doxycycline or azithromycin

references.title: 2021 CDC guidelines on sexually transmitted infections (J Fam Pract)
references.supports: Doxycycline first line; abstain 7 d; retest 3 mo

source.book: CDC STI Guidelines 2021; PHAC Chlamydia Guide

issues: Not single best answer for a Canadian exam: the PHAC Chlamydia and LGV guide (last modified 2022-04-28) lists doxycycline 100 mg BID ×7 d OR azithromycin 1 g once as equally preferred for uncomplicated urogenital infection; CMAJ 2023 table says the same. Option D is therefore defensible, and its explanation ('Now an alternative') is wrong for Canada. Doxycycline is preferred by CDC 2021 and Sinai Health (rectal cure rates).
Minor overlap: bank im-261101-51 (gonorrhea) mentions doxycycline for chlamydia co-treatment.

questions.stem: 58M p/w deep puncture wound to the sole from a rusty garden nail 6 h ago. Wound irrigated. Unsure whether he was ever vaccinated against tetanus.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Passive protection only; active immunization also needed.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Unknown/<3 doses + tetanus-prone wound → vaccine and TIG.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Enough for a clean minor wound, or a tetanus-prone wound after ≥3 doses if ≥5 y since last dose.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Antibiotics don't prevent tetanus; TIG is needed.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Tetanus-prone wound with unknown history needs prophylaxis.

questions.explanation: For a tetanus-prone wound (soil, puncture, devitalized tissue) with unknown or <3 prior doses, give a tetanus-containing vaccine plus TIG 250 units IM at a separate site, then complete the primary series. Clean minor wounds need vaccine only. With ≥3 prior doses, TIG isn't needed; boost if >5 y (dirty wound) or >10 y (clean).

references.title: Tetanus Post-exposure Prophylaxis in Injury/Wound Management (Alberta Immunization Policy)
references.supports: TIG for tetanus-prone wound with <3 or unknown doses, plus vaccine

references.title: Summary Guide to Tetanus Prophylaxis in Routine Wound Management (Minnesota Dept of Health)
references.supports: TIG 250 U IM; separate site from vaccine

issues: Option C explanation 'or a dirty one after ≥3 doses' is incomplete: with ≥3 doses and a tetanus-prone wound, a booster is needed only if ≥5 y since the last dose (Alberta policy).
Alberta policy doesn't give the TIG dose; Minnesota DOH supports 250 U IM at a separate site.
Key is correct; no overlap in bank (dog-bite item only states tetanus up to date).

questions.topic: CoNS in 1 of 2 blood culture sets
questions.stem: 67M admitted w/ CAP, improving on ceftriaxone; afebrile by day 3. No central line or prosthetic material. Of 2 admission blood culture sets, 1 aerobic bottle grows coagulase-negative staphylococci at 40 h.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Endocarditis workup is for true bacteremia (e.g., S. aureus).

options.label: B
options.text: Treat as contaminant; no new Abx
options.explanation: 1 of 2 sets, no devices, no compatible syndrome: contamination.

options.label: C
options.explanation: No role; organism is likely a skin contaminant.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Treating a likely contaminant adds toxicity and cost.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Repeat only if doubt; don't start vancomycin empirically.

questions.explanation: CoNS are the most common blood culture contaminants. Growth in only 1 of ≥2 sets, in a patient without indwelling devices, prosthetic material or a compatible syndrome, is presumed contamination: don't treat. Suspect true infection with ≥2 positive sets from separate sites, a central line or prosthetic material.

references.title: Determining the clinical significance of CoNS isolated from blood cultures (Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol)
references.supports: Single positive CoNS culture usually a contaminant without clinical evidence of infection

issues: Sources: memorial.org PDF now redirects to an unrelated homepage (dead); WikEM is a wiki. No reliable working source remains. Content is correct and the teaching point isn't in the bank.
WikEM table lists S. aureus contamination at 25%, which contradicts its own 'never a contaminant' line; avoid citing it for that point.

questions.stem:
78F p/w 2 wk of fatigue. HCTZ 25 mg started 6 wk ago for HTN. Euvolemic; alert and oriented.

Na 122 mmol/L, K 3.1 mmol/L
Urine Na 58 mmol/L, urine osm 380 mOsm/kg
TSH and AM cortisol normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: Same class; chlorthalidone carries at least as much risk.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Ongoing thiazide sustains the diluting defect.

options.label: C
options.explanation: For severe symptoms (seizure, obtundation); she's mildly symptomatic with chronic hyponatremia.

options.label: D
options.explanation: The thiazide must be stopped; vaptans aren't first line.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Cornerstone: stop thiazide, replete cations, restrict free water.

questions.explanation: Thiazide-associated hyponatremia (often older women, often within weeks of starting) is treated by stopping the thiazide, repleting K and Na, and restricting fluids, while avoiding overly rapid correction. Hypertonic saline is for severe symptoms. Recurrence on rechallenge is common, so choose a non-thiazide antihypertensive.

references.title: Thiazide-Associated Hyponatremia: Clinical Manifestations and Pathophysiology (AJKD 2020)
references.supports: Cornerstone: stop thiazide, cation repletion, fluid restriction

references.title: Thiazide-induced hyponatremia (Best Pract Res Clin Endocrinol Metab 2025)
references.supports: Acute severe: hypertonic saline; chronic: stop thiazide, restrict fluid, replete solute

references.title: Diuretics and electrolyte abnormalities (AHRQ PSNet)
references.supports: Hyponatremia reproducible on thiazide rechallenge

issues: Single best answer: stem symptom 'nausea' places her in the European guideline's 'moderately severe' category, where a single 3% saline infusion can be considered, making option C arguable. Remove nausea to make the case clearly mild.
Refs support stop thiazide, cation repletion, fluid restriction; hypertonic saline for acute/severe. Recurrence on rechallenge isn't in the listed refs but is supported by AHRQ PSNet.
Distinct from bank hyponatremia items (correction limit, SIADH, severe symptomatic).

questions.stem:
72M w/ HTN and CKD G3a on ramipril 10 mg and HCTZ 25 mg. Started ibuprofen 400 mg TID 10 d ago for knee OA. Now fatigue and low urine output.

Cr 212 µmol/L (baseline 118)
K 5.6 mmol/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: COX-2 inhibitors carry the same renal risk.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Worsens volume depletion; not indicated.

options.label: C
options.text: Stop ibuprofen; hold ramipril and HCTZ
options.explanation: All three impair renal perfusion; hold until recovery.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Clear hemodynamic precipitant; biopsy not needed.

options.label: E
options.explanation: ACEi and diuretic also impair autoregulation; K is high.

questions.explanation: NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic (the 'triple whammy') reduces glomerular perfusion three ways: afferent vasoconstriction, loss of efferent tone, and volume depletion. Risk is highest in the first 30 d of the combination. Stop the NSAID and hold the ACEi and diuretic until kidney function recovers; use acetaminophen or topical agents for pain.

references.title: Combining diuretics, antihypertensives and NSAIDs may pose risk of kidney injury (ACP IM Matters; BMJ 2013 Lapi)
references.supports: Triple therapy ↑ AKI, highest in first 30 d

references.title: NSAIDs and Acute Kidney Injury (Medsafe Prescriber Update)
references.supports: Mechanisms; stop NSAID if AKI

questions.stem: 56F w/ T2DM ×4 y. BP 128/78. Annual screening: eGFR 84, random urine ACR 4.8 mg/mmol. No UTI, fever, menses or recent heavy exercise.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Not part of albuminuria screening.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Albuminuria must be persistent: ≥2 of 3 samples over 3 mo.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Single ACR is insufficient; confirm persistence first.

options.label: D
options.explanation: An abnormal result needs confirmation within 3 mo.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Random ACR is the test of choice.

questions.explanation: Screen for CKD in diabetes yearly with eGFR plus random urine ACR (T2DM from diagnosis; T1DM after 5 y). An ACR ≥2.0 mg/mmol must be persistent, i.e., ≥2 of 3 samples abnormal over 3 mo, before diagnosing CKD, since exercise, UTI, fever and menses cause transient rises. Once confirmed, kidney-protective therapy is indicated.

references.title: Chronic Kidney Disease in Diabetes (Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 29)
references.supports: ACR test of choice; ≥2 of 3 samples over 3 mo

references.title: Updated CKD in diabetes guideline released (Diabetes Canada 2025)
references.supports: Annual eGFR + ACR; T1DM after 5 y, T2DM at Dx

questions.stem:
34F w/ unprovoked L femoral DVT 6 wk ago, on rivaroxaban. Tests sent at Dx:

Anticardiolipin IgG 62 GPL (ref <20)
Anti-β2-glycoprotein I IgG positive
Lupus anticoagulant not done

options.label: A
options.explanation: DOACs cause false-positive LA results.

options.label: B
options.explanation: A single positive set can be transient; confirm first.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Too soon; transient aPL may persist for weeks.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Doesn't address APS; low yield.

options.label: E
options.text: Repeat aPL tests ≥12 wk after first
options.explanation: Persistence on 2 occasions ≥12 wk apart is required.

questions.explanation: aPL can be transiently positive with infection, drugs or acute thrombosis, so classification requires persistence: LA, aCL or anti-β2GPI positive on ≥2 occasions ≥12 wk apart. Confirm before labeling APS, because it changes anticoagulant choice (warfarin, especially if triple-positive) and duration. DOACs interfere with LA testing.

questions.stem:
52M seen for a work physical. No h/o gout, kidney stones or tophi. BMI 31; HTN on amlodipine.

Uric acid 560 µmol/L
Cr 90 µmol/L, eGFR 85

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.explanation: ACR 2020 conditionally recommends against urate-lowering therapy for asymptomatic hyperuricemia: most people never develop gout, and ULT hasn't been shown to prevent CV or kidney outcomes. Address contributors (weight, alcohol, fructose, thiazides). Start ULT in gout with ≥2 flares/y, tophi or radiographic damage.

60M w/ suspected PE; CTPA planned. Reports hives after eating shrimp 10 y ago. No prior contrast exposure. Asthma well controlled.

Cr 80 µmol/L

options.label: D

questions.explanation: Shellfish allergy is IgE to proteins (e.g., tropomyosin), not iodine, and doesn't predict reactions to iodinated contrast any more than other allergies. Don't premedicate, switch tests or delay imaging. The relevant history is a prior reaction to contrast itself.

questions.stem:
35M brought in 1 h after drinking an insecticide. Drooling, sweating, pinpoint pupils, diffuse wheeze and crackles.

BP 84/50, HR 48, RR 28, SpO2 88%

Given atropine 2 mg IV 5 min ago; chest still wet, HR 52.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Double the dose every 5 min until atropinized.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitor; worsens toxicity.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Bronchorrhea, not cardiogenic edema; worsens hypotension.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Oximes don't reverse bronchorrhea; atropine comes first.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Repeating fixed doses delays atropinization.

questions.explanation: Atropinize fast: give 1–3 mg IV, then double the dose every 5 min until the chest is clear, HR >80 and SBP >80 mmHg, then infuse about 10–20% of the loading dose per hour. Very large total doses may be needed. Watch for atropine toxicity (delirium, fever, absent bowel sounds). Oximes may be added but don't replace atropine.

references.title: Pharmacological treatment of organophosphorus insecticide poisoning (Br J Clin Pharmacol 2016)
references.supports: Doubling doses q5min to HR >80, SBP >80, clear lungs

references.title: Atropine antidote recommendations (Queensland Poisons Information Centre)
references.supports: Double dose q5min; infusion 20% of loading/h

questions.stem:
84F w/ displaced femoral neck fracture after a fall; IM consulted preop. h/o HTN, CKD G3a, known mild aortic stenosis on TTE 1 y ago. On ASA 81 mg. No chest pain or dyspnea; walks 2 blocks pre-injury.

BP 146/80, HR 82
Hb 118 g/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: Known mild AS without new Sx; shouldn't delay surgery.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Doesn't change management; delays surgery.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Delay beyond 48 h raises mortality; nothing here needs workup.

options.label: D
options.explanation: ASA shouldn't delay hip fracture surgery.

options.label: E
options.explanation: For nonambulatory or palliative patients only.

questions.explanation: Hip fracture surgery within 48 h of admission, the Canadian benchmark since 2005, is associated with lower in-hospital and 1-y mortality and shorter length of stay. Preop medical assessment should optimize the patient without ordering tests unlikely to change management. Tests like stress testing or a repeat echo for known mild valve disease in a stable patient shouldn't delay surgery.

references.title: Reduced time to surgery improves mortality and length of stay following hip fracture (Can J Surg 2015)
references.supports: 48-h benchmark; surgery within 48 h ↓ in-hospital and 1-y mortality

references.supports: Fixation beyond 48 h ↑ LOS and 1-y mortality

questions.stem:
62M w/ metastatic melanoma on pembrolizumab (cycle 4). Asymptomatic. No new meds or alcohol.

ALT 410 U/L (ULN 40)
AST 350 U/L
Bilirubin 18 µmol/L, INR 1.0
HBV, HCV serology negative
Liver US normal

options.label: A
options.explanation: Grade 2 approach; grade 3 needs steroids now.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Grade 3 (ALT >5–20× ULN): stop ICI, high-dose steroids.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Grade 1 approach; this is grade 3.

options.label: D
options.explanation: No role; ongoing ICI worsens injury.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Avoid infliximab in immune hepatitis (hepatotoxic).

questions.explanation: Grade 3 ICI hepatitis (AST/ALT >5–20× ULN or bilirubin >3–10× ULN), once viral, drug, alcohol and obstructive causes are excluded: stop the ICI, start prednisone (or IV methylprednisolone) 1–2 mg/kg/d with frequent LFTs, and involve hepatology. If no response in 3–5 d, add mycophenolate; avoid infliximab. Grade 1: continue with monitoring; grade 2: hold the ICI.

references.supports: Grading and steroid dosing for ICI hepatitis
