questions.topic: Albuminuric CKD as a statin-indicated condition
questions.stem:
58M, nonsmoker, for annual review. h/o HTN on ramipril. No ASCVD or DM.

BP 128/78
eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m²
Urine ACR 4.5 mg/mmol (repeat 4.1)
LDL 3.1 mmol/L
Framingham risk 9%
questions.lead: Per CCS 2021, most appropriate lipid management?

options.label: A
options.explanation: CKD (age ≥50 with ACR >3 mg/mmol) is statin-indicated regardless of FRS or eGFR.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Low FRS doesn't apply: CKD bypasses risk scoring.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Statin is first line; ezetimibe is add-on.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Lp(a) refines risk; not needed when a statin is already indicated.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Not needed; CKD alone qualifies for a statin.

questions.explanation: CCS 2021 counts non-dialysis CKD in adults ≥50 as statin-indicated if eGFR is <60 mL/min/1.73 m² OR ACR is >3 mg/mmol, so albuminuria alone qualifies even with a normal eGFR; no Framingham calculation needed. Other statin-indicated conditions include clinical ASCVD, AAA, most diabetes and LDL ≥5.0 mmol/L. Statins aren't started for the first time in patients on dialysis.

references.title: Practice guideline update on dyslipidemia for pharmacists, based on CCS 2021 (Can Pharm J)
references.supports: Statin-indicated conditions incl. CKD age ≥50, eGFR <60 or ACR >3

references.title: KDIGO lipid guideline in CKD (National Lipid Association review)
references.supports: Age >50 with eGFR <60, not on dialysis: statin recommended (1A)

issues: Accurate: CCS 2021 lists non-dialysis CKD (age >=50 with eGFR <60 or ACR >3 mg/mmol) as statin-indicated; KDIGO says statins aren't started on dialysis. CCS 2021 is still the current Canadian lipid guideline.

Duplication: bank im-261030-139 (CCS statin-indicated condition, LDL >=5) teaches the same point (a statin-indicated condition bypasses FRS), and its explanation already lists the CKD criteria. The eGFR arm is the well-known one.

questions.stem:
71M w/ HFrEF (EF 30%) on sacubitril-valsartan, bisoprolol, dapagliflozin and spironolactone 25 mg. Routine labs; asymptomatic.

K 6.1 mmol/L (repeat, non-hemolyzed)
Cr 156 µmol/L (baseline 118)
ECG: sinus rhythm, no peaked T waves

options.label: A
options.explanation: Dose reduction is for K 5.5–5.9 mmol/L.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Also K-sparing; would not lower K.

options.label: C
options.explanation: K ≥6.0 mmol/L: stop the MRA and seek advice.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Same class; similar hyperkalemia risk.

options.label: E
options.explanation: K ≥6.0 is a stop threshold, not a tolerate threshold.

questions.explanation: With an MRA in HFrEF: halve the dose (or go to alternate days) for K >5.5 mmol/L or Cr >220 µmol/L; stop it for K ≥6.0 mmol/L or Cr >310 µmol/L. Check K and Cr at 1 wk and after any dose change, avoid NSAIDs and K-containing salt substitutes, and reconsider rechallenge once K normalizes, as the mortality benefit is substantial.

references.title: Practical guidance: MRA use in HFrEF (SIGN 147 Annex 5)
references.supports: K >5.5 reduce; K ≥6.0 stop; monitoring schedule

references.title: Spironolactone monitoring (NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service)
references.supports: K 5.5–6 reduce; >6 stop and seek advice

issues: Accurate: SIGN 147 and SPS say to halve or reduce for K >5.5 or Cr >220 µmol/L, and to stop for K ≥6.0 or Cr ≥310 µmol/L; the monitoring schedule matches.
Options aren't homogeneous: the lead asks about a 'change to spironolactone', but 'Stop dapagliflozin instead' is about another drug.
Sources are UK (SIGN, NHS SPS). They're acceptable, but a CCS HF citation would be better for a Canadian bank.

questions.stem: 62F s/p PCI for NSTEMI 2 d ago, being discharged. On ASA, ticagrelor, high-intensity statin, ramipril, metoprolol. Single-vessel PCI, complete revascularization. EF 50%. Feels well; walks the ward without Sx.
questions.lead: Most appropriate additional intervention at discharge?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Class I after ACS; lowers CV mortality and readmission.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not routinely needed after complete revascularization.

options.label: C
options.explanation: EF is preserved; no routine repeat imaging indicated.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Prolonged rest causes deconditioning; supervised exercise is preferred.

options.label: E
options.explanation: CLEAR SYNERGY: no MACE benefit when started early post-MI; not routine.

questions.explanation: Cardiac rehabilitation (supervised exercise, risk-factor education and psychosocial support) is a Class I recommendation after ACS, PCI or CABG. It reduces cardiovascular mortality and readmissions and improves quality of life, yet it's often underused. The strongest predictor of attendance is an in-hospital referral, so refer before discharge.

references.title: Cardiac rehabilitation: A class 1 recommendation (Cleve Clin J Med via The Hospitalist)
references.supports: Class 1 after MI/PCI; Cochrane: lower CV mortality and readmissions

references.title: Cardiac Rehabilitation: Does it Reduce Morbidity and Mortality? (Clinical Correlations, NYU)
references.supports: In-hospital referral strongly predicts participation

source.book: ACC/AHA secondary prevention; Cleve Clin J Med review

issues: Accurate and appropriate PGY1–2 content: cardiac rehab is Class 1 after MI/PCI, Cochrane shows lower CV mortality (RR 0.74) and readmissions (RR 0.82), and in-hospital referral strongly predicts enrolment.
The 'Exercise stress test before activity' explanation says 'after complete revascularization', but the stem never says revascularization was complete.
The colchicine explanation is outdated. CLEAR SYNERGY (2024; colchicine started within 72 h of MI) found no MACE benefit (HR 0.99), so 'optional' overstates it after ACS.
Both sources are weak: a hospitalist community page and a blog (Clinical Correlations). A guideline citation (CCS or ACC/AHA) would be better.

questions.stem:
76F w/ AF and HFrEF, on digoxin 0.125 mg daily (level 0.9 nmol/L) and bisoprolol. Rhythm control with amiodarone is being started today.

Cr 98 µmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L

options.label: A

questions.explanation: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein and renal digoxin clearance, raising digoxin concentrations by roughly 70–100% over 1–2 wk. When starting amiodarone in a patient on digoxin, cut the digoxin dose by about 50% (or stop it if not essential) and recheck the level in 1–2 wk. Warfarin also needs closer INR monitoring with amiodarone.

K 3.2 mmol/L

options.label: D

options.label: E

questions.explanation: A QTc >500 ms (or a rise >60 ms) on QT-prolonging drugs markedly increases torsades risk. Stop or substitute the offending drugs (fluoroquinolone, ondansetron, haloperidol), replete K to >4.0 mmol/L and Mg, and keep the patient on telemetry. If torsades occurs: IV magnesium, and pacing or isoproterenol for pause-dependent recurrences.

questions.topic: Uncontrolled asthma: check before stepping up
questions.stem: 38F w/ asthma on budesonide-formoterol 200/6 1 puff BID plus PRN. Night waking 2×/wk and reliever use most days for 3 mo. No exacerbations. Spirometry at Dx showed 18% reversibility.

options.label: A

options.label: D

options.label: E
options.explanation: Step up only after technique, adherence and triggers are addressed.

questions.explanation: Before stepping up for uncontrolled asthma, GINA advises confirming the diagnosis, checking inhaler technique (incorrect in most patients) and adherence, and addressing modifiable risk factors and comorbidities (smoking, rhinitis, GERD, obesity). Many 'difficult' patients improve without more medication. Step up only if control remains poor after these are fixed.

The GINA 2021 summary doesn't confirm step-specific MART doses. That's fine, as the explanation doesn't rely on them.

Modern aspiration pneumonia is mostly due to usual CAP and gram-negative organisms, and extended anaerobic coverage increases C. difficile risk without lowering mortality. Sample only if the picture doesn't fit.

questions.topic: Flow-volume loop: fixed upper airway obstruction
questions.stem:
46F p/w 6 mo of progressive exertional dyspnea and noisy breathing. ICU stay w/ prolonged intubation 1 y ago. No response to salbutamol.

Spirometry: FEV1 62%, FVC 88% predicted
Flow-volume loop: flattened plateaus of both inspiratory and expiratory limbs

options.label: A
options.explanation: Variable intrathoracic: flattens the expiratory limb only.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Scooped (concave) expiratory limb; usually bronchodilator responsive.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Fixed central obstruction flattens both limbs; post-intubation is classic.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Variable extrathoracic: flattens the inspiratory limb only.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Restrictive 'witch's hat': small, narrow loop with preserved shape.

questions.explanation: Flattening of both inspiratory and expiratory limbs (a 'box' shape) indicates fixed upper airway obstruction, such as post-intubation tracheal stenosis or a large airway tumor. Variable extrathoracic lesions (vocal cord paralysis) flatten only the inspiratory limb; variable intrathoracic lesions (tracheomalacia) flatten only the expiratory limb. Confirm with CT and bronchoscopy.

questions.stem: 64M w/ T2DM booked for elective laparoscopic colectomy next week. On metformin, empagliflozin 25 mg and semaglutide. HbA1c 7.4%.
questions.lead: When should empagliflozin last be taken?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: E
options.explanation: Longer than needed; worsens glycemic control.

questions.explanation: Hold canagliflozin, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin at least 3 d before scheduled surgery (ertugliflozin at least 4 d) to reduce the risk of perioperative euglycemic DKA. Monitor glucose meanwhile, and restart only once oral intake is back to baseline and other DKA risk factors have resolved. Check ketones and the anion gap if the patient is unwell after surgery.

questions.stem: 66F, postmenopausal, for a periodic health exam. No fractures. Mother had a hip fracture at 78. Nonsmoker, rare alcohol, no glucocorticoids. BMI 24. No falls.
questions.lead: Per Osteoporosis Canada 2023, most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Spine x-ray to screen for fractures

options.label: B

questions.explanation: Osteoporosis Canada 2023: BMD testing at age ≥70 if no risk factors, at 65–69 with ≥1 clinical risk factor, and at 50–64 with a prior fragility fracture or ≥2 risk factors. Parental hip fracture is a risk factor. Then calculate 10-y fracture risk with FRAX (preferred) or CAROC to guide treatment.

questions.stem:
41F p/w 4 mo of fatigue, weight loss, salt craving and darkening of skin creases. Hemodynamically stable.

BP 98/62
Na 128 mmol/L, K 5.4 mmol/L
8 AM cortisol 110 nmol/L
ACTH pending
questions.lead: Best test to confirm the Dx?

options.label: A
options.explanation: For secondary AI; Sx and high K suggest primary.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Screens for hypercortisolism, not deficiency.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.explanation: Random levels are unreliable; stimulation testing needed.

options.label: E

questions.explanation: When suspected clinically and the patient is stable, confirm primary adrenal insufficiency with the standard 250 µg cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test: peak cortisol below ~500 nmol/L (assay dependent) at 30–60 min indicates AI. Measure ACTH (>2× ULN confirms a primary cause), then 21-hydroxylase antibodies. In adrenal crisis, give hydrocortisone first and don't wait for test results.

questions.stem:
45M p/w 12 h of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back after a weekend of heavy drinking. Hemodynamically stable on LR.

Lipase 2400 U/L (ULN 60)
ALT 38 U/L, bilirubin 12 µmol/L
Abdominal US: normal gallbladder, no stones

options.label: A
options.text: No CT now; reassess at 48–72 h
options.explanation: Dx is clear; CT reserved for diagnostic doubt or no improvement.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Early CT doesn't predict severity better and rarely changes care.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Necrosis isn't reliably seen early.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Only for cholangitis; none here.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Normal LFTs and US; low suspicion.

questions.explanation: ACG 2024 suggests against routine CT at admission to assess severity in acute pancreatitis; reserve it for patients in whom the diagnosis is unclear or who fail to improve within 48–72 h of hydration. Necrosis takes days to declare on imaging, and early scans add radiation, contrast and cost without changing management. Do get a transabdominal US for gallstones.

references.supports: No routine CT on admission; image if unclear or no improvement 48–72 h

Options aren't homogeneous: the lead asks about the 'role for CT', but 'Urgent ERCP' and 'MRCP to exclude choledocholithiasis' aren't CT options.
No duplication: the bank's pancreatitis items cover fluids, nutrition and cholecystectomy timing.

questions.stem: 52F w/ typical heartburn, partial response after 6 wk of pantoprazole 40 mg daily, taken at bedtime. No alarm features. No dysphagia or weight loss.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Premature; therapy not yet optimized.

options.label: E
options.explanation: No alarm features; optimize therapy first.

questions.explanation: Delayed-release PPIs work best when taken 30–60 min before a meal, usually breakfast, so they're absorbed as parietal cells are activated; bedtime dosing is less effective. ACG 2021 recommends optimizing PPI therapy (timing, adherence) as the first step for partial response, then considering twice-daily dosing; endoscopy is for alarm features or nonresponse.

references.title: ACG guideline updates recommendations on diagnosis, management of GERD (ACP Gastroenterology Monthly)
references.supports: PPI 30–60 min before a meal rather than bedtime; optimize for refractory

references.title: Highlights of the ACG GERD guideline (Gastroenterology & Hepatology)
references.supports: PPI timing before meals; optimize first

issues: Accurate: ACG says to take PPIs 30–60 min before a meal rather than at bedtime (strong), and to optimize PPI therapy as the first step for refractory symptoms.
Guideline date: the ACG GERD guideline was published Nov 2021 (Am J Gastroenterol 2022). Use 'ACG 2021' or say it consistently.
The option 'Increase to 40 mg BID at bedtime' is odd ('BID at bedtime' doesn't make sense).
Reference failed: cm.healio.com is VPN-restricted. Replacement below.

questions.stem:
58M w/ alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B), abstinent, on furosemide and spironolactone. Recurrent R pleural effusion; thoracentesis 2 wk ago removed 1.5 L transudate, cultures negative. Now dyspneic again.

CXR: large R effusion
Minimal ascites on US

options.label: A
options.explanation: Minimal ascites; won't clear a large effusion.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Sodium restriction and diuretics remain first line.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Usually fails with rapid reaccumulation; high complication rate.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Contraindicated: massive protein/fluid loss, infection, high mortality.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Relieve Sx; refractory hydrothorax → TIPS or transplant evaluation.

questions.explanation: Hepatic hydrothorax is ascites moving through diaphragmatic defects. Manage with sodium restriction and diuretics, and use thoracentesis for symptom relief. Chest tubes are contraindicated (AASLD): they cause massive fluid and protein loss, infection, kidney injury and high mortality. If it's refractory, refer for TIPS and liver transplant evaluation.

questions.topic: Acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease
questions.stem:
24F w/ HbSS admitted 2 d ago for vaso-occlusive pain on PCA hydromorphone. Now fever, pleuritic chest pain and cough.

T 38.6, RR 26, SpO2 91% RA
CXR: new LLL consolidation
Hb 66 g/L (baseline 82)
WBC 16 ×10⁹/L

options.label: A
options.explanation: ACS: CAP-type Abx with atypical cover, O2, spirometry; transfuse for Hb >10 g/L below baseline.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Needs atypical cover; withholding analgesia worsens splinting.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Infection is a common trigger; antibiotics are always given.

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat CXR in 24 h before Tx
options.explanation: ACS is life-threatening; treat immediately.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Overhydration risks pulmonary edema and worsens ACS.

questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome (new infiltrate plus fever or respiratory symptoms) is a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease. Treat with an IV cephalosporin plus a macrolide, oxygen, incentive spirometry, judicious fluids and adequate analgesia, and consult hematology. Give a simple transfusion if Hb has dropped >10 g/L below baseline; urgent exchange transfusion is for rapid progression or persistent hypoxemia.

70M on warfarin for AF (target INR 2–3). Recently started TMP-SMX for cystitis. No bleeding, no planned procedures.

INR 7.2
Hb 138 g/L

options.label: B

options.label: E

questions.explanation: For INR 4.5–10 without bleeding, CHEST suggests holding warfarin without routine vitamin K, which hasn't been shown to reduce bleeding and can cause warfarin resistance. Give oral vitamin K for INR >10 without bleeding; for major bleeding, use IV vitamin K plus PCC. Look for the cause here: TMP-SMX inhibits warfarin metabolism.

68F w/ poor diet and alcohol use p/w fatigue and mild paresthesias in both feet.

Hb 92 g/L, MCV 112 fL
B12 98 pmol/L (low)
Serum folate 4 nmol/L (low)
Smear: hypersegmented neutrophils

options.explanation: Not needed for stable, chronic anemia at Hb 92.

Folic acid alone can correct the anemia while B12-related neurologic damage, such as subacute combined degeneration of the cord, progresses or is unmasked. Her paresthesias make B12 urgent; give IM B12 with neurologic symptoms.

questions.explanation: Incision and drainage is the primary treatment for a cutaneous abscess. In trials, adding TMP-SMX (or clindamycin) after drainage modestly raised cure rates and cut recurrences, so many clinicians add an anti-MRSA agent for abscesses ≥2 cm after shared decision-making. Antibiotics are definitely indicated with systemic signs, extensive cellulitis or immunosuppression.

Biofilm on the old catheter yields polymicrobial, misleading cultures. Remove the catheter entirely if it's no longer indicated.

questions.stem:
36M newly Dx w/ HIV, starting ART this week. No respiratory Sx; CXR normal. No sulfa allergy.

CD4 140 cells/µL
HIV viral load 180 000 copies/mL
Toxoplasma IgG negative
Cr 74 µmol/L

options.label: B

options.label: D

options.label: E

questions.explanation: Start PJP prophylaxis in people with HIV and CD4 <200 cells/µL (or CD4 <14% or oral thrush). TMP-SMX 1 DS (or SS) tablet daily is preferred; DS daily also prevents toxoplasmosis. Stop once CD4 is ≥200 for ≥3 mo on ART. MAC prophylaxis (CD4 <50) isn't needed when ART starts promptly.

issues: Accurate: PJP prophylaxis for CD4 <200 (or <14%); TMP-SMX DS (or SS) daily is first line; DS also covers toxoplasma; stop once CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 mo on ART.
The MAC distractor's explanation gives the wrong main reason. At CD4 140, MAC prophylaxis isn't indicated anyway (threshold <50), and it's also not recommended when ART starts immediately.

Treat with isotonic saline: restoring volume switches off ADH, so watch for a water diuresis and overly rapid correction (limit ≤8–10 mmol/L in 24 h). Fluid restriction and vaptans are for euvolemic or hypervolemic states.

questions.explanation: Gabapentin (and pregabalin) are excreted unchanged by the kidneys, so they accumulate in CKD and cause sedation, ataxia, myoclonus and asterixis. Dose by CrCl; 2700 mg/d is far above the renally adjusted maximum at this level of kidney function. Stop the drug; hemodialysis clears it if toxicity is severe.

Use IV acetaminophen if NSAIDs are contraindicated, then opioids. Antispasmodics don't help.

questions.explanation: ACR 2020 strongly recommends stopping methotrexate before attempting conception, ideally 1–3 mo beforehand, and transitioning to pregnancy-compatible drugs (hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, TNF inhibitors) early enough to confirm control. Leflunomide needs proven undetectable levels or cholestyramine washout.

issues: Accurate: ACR 2020 strongly recommends stopping MTX before attempting conception (1–3 mo); stop MMF ≥6 wk before; leflunomide needs undetectable levels or cholestyramine washout.
Cueing: the keyed option 'Switch to HCQ/SSZ; stop MTX ≥1–3 mo before' is longer and more specific than the distractors, and '≥1–3 mo' is awkward.
Unverified: 'For men, ACR says MTX can be continued' isn't covered by the opened sources and is off the teaching point.

questions.topic: Imaging in acute low back pain
questions.stem: 42M p/w 10 d of low back pain after lifting furniture. Pain worse with bending, no radiation below the knee. No fever, weight loss, cancer history, IV drug use, trauma or bladder/bowel Sx. Neuro exam normal.

options.label: A
options.explanation: No red flags: imaging doesn't change outcome; most improve in weeks.

options.label: B
options.explanation: No indication; high radiation.

options.label: C
options.explanation: No red flags; low yield, radiation, incidental findings.

options.label: D
options.explanation: No red flags for infection or cancer; labs won't change management.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Reserved for red flags or persistent radiculopathy after ~6 wk if intervention considered.

questions.explanation: In acute low back pain without red flags (cancer, infection, fracture risk, cauda equina, progressive neurologic deficit), Choosing Wisely Canada advises against imaging: it doesn't improve outcomes, finds incidental age-related changes and drives further intervention. Reassure, encourage staying active (bed rest delays recovery), use NSAIDs/heat, and reassess if symptoms persist beyond ~6 wk or red flags develop.

references.supports: Do not image LBP unless red flags present

issues: Content is correct and matches Choosing Wisely Canada ('Do not image for lower back pain unless red flags are present'), the red-flag list, and the ≥6-week conservative trial before imaging for suspected disc/stenosis. Heat and NSAIDs are supported by ACP 2017.
Cueing: the keyed option (30 characters, three components) is about twice the length of the others (14-18 characters), and it is the only management option among imaging tests.
Easy for PGY1-2, but high-yield Choosing Wisely content; acceptable.
Reference 1 (PMC6189883) could not be opened (reCAPTCHA wall), so it was not verified. A Choosing Wisely Canada page was added instead.

questions.explanation: Intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective treatment for moderate–severe allergic rhinitis, including congestion, and should be used daily (onset over days). They outperform montelukast, and adding an oral antihistamine to them adds little; an intranasal antihistamine can be added if needed. Allergen immunotherapy is an option for refractory cases.

issues: Accurate in substance: INCS is most effective and preferred over montelukast, and adding an oral antihistamine to INCS adds no benefit (JTF 2017).

The keyed option contradicts its own explanation. 'Add a daily intranasal corticosteroid' (on top of cetirizine) goes against the guideline's INCS monotherapy recommendation, which the explanation cites.

questions.stem: 24F intubated 10 min ago for life-threatening asthma. Volume control, RR 22, VT 450 mL. Now BP 70/40 (was 128/80), HR 132. Peak pressure 52, plateau 34 cmH2O. Breath sounds quiet but equal; trachea midline.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Shortens expiratory time; worsens breath stacking.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Equal breath sounds, midline trachea; try disconnection first.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Dynamic hyperinflation: release trapped gas; BP rises within seconds.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Adds intrathoracic pressure; worsens venous return.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Doesn't address the cause: air trapping.

questions.explanation: Hypotension soon after intubating an asthmatic is usually dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP): trapped gas raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts venous return. Disconnect the ventilator (± gentle chest compression) to let gas escape; BP should recover within 10–30 s. Then lower the RR and tidal volume to lengthen expiration and accept permissive hypercapnia. Consider tension pneumothorax if BP doesn't recover.

references.supports: Disconnect and compress chest; lower RR and VT

questions.stem:
86F, day 2 after hip fracture repair. Nurse reports she was calm this morning but now picks at sheets and can't keep track of the conversation. Alert. Can't recite months backward; speech rambling.

T 37.2, SpO2 95%
Na 136, glucose 6.4 mmol/L
questions.lead: Which findings satisfy the CAM algorithm?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Lacks acute onset and inattention.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Lacks acute onset/fluctuating course.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Lacks acute onset; disorientation and memory aren't CAM features.

options.label: D
options.explanation: CAM: features 1 and 2, plus 3 or 4.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Lacks inattention, which is mandatory.

questions.explanation: The CAM diagnoses delirium when there is (1) acute onset or fluctuating course AND (2) inattention, plus EITHER (3) disorganized thinking OR (4) altered level of consciousness. This patient has features 1, 2 and 3, despite being alert. Next, look for precipitants (pain, opioids, retention, infection, hypoxia) and use nonpharmacologic measures.

references.title: Clarifying confusion: the Confusion Assessment Method (Ann Intern Med 1990)
references.supports: Algorithm: features 1 and 2 and either 3 or 4

references.title: Confusion Assessment Method diagnostic algorithm (QUT)
references.supports: Feature definitions

issues: Accurate: the CAM algorithm needs features 1 and 2 plus either 3 or 4.
Diagnosis given away: the lead names delirium, so this is pure criteria recall.
Cueing: the keyed option 'Acute/fluctuating course + inattention + disorganized thinking' is noticeably longer and is the only one built from all CAM terms.
No duplication with bank im-261030-88 (delirium management).
The PubMed reference (2240918) hit reCAPTCHA; the QUT CAM PDF supports everything.

questions.topic: Palliative RT for uncomplicated bone metastasis
questions.stem: 74M w/ metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer p/w painful L iliac bone metastasis despite regular opioid. No fracture or impending fracture, no neuro deficit, no soft-tissue mass. ECOG 2.

options.label: A
options.explanation: Reserved for selected oligometastatic or reirradiation cases.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Overly protracted for palliation; not recommended.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Equivalent pain relief to longer courses; fewer visits and lower cost.

options.label: D
options.explanation: RT gives durable relief in most; shouldn't be withheld.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Similar pain relief and less retreatment, but more visits; not preferred in Canada.

questions.explanation: For painful uncomplicated bone metastases, a single 8 Gy fraction gives pain relief equivalent to 20–30 Gy in 5–10 fractions with similar or fewer side effects; the trade-off is a higher retreatment rate (about 20% vs 8%), and a single fraction can be safely repeated. Choosing Wisely Canada advises against more than a single fraction for uncomplicated painful bone metastases.

references.title: ASTRO guideline: palliative radiotherapy for bone metastases (Cancer Network)
references.supports: Single fraction equivalent pain control; 20% vs 8% retreatment

references.title: Single-fraction radiotherapy for bone metastases: knowledge translation (PMC9324375)
references.supports: Choosing Wisely Canada: single fraction for uncomplicated bone mets

source.book: ASTRO Bone Metastases Guideline; Choosing Wisely Canada

issues: Single best answer is defensible but needs Canadian sourcing. ASTRO (2017, reaffirmed 2024) treats 8 Gy/1, 20/5, 24/6 and 30/10 as equivalent for pain, so 'E: 30 Gy in 10 fractions' is guideline-acceptable in the US. What makes C the single best answer is Choosing Wisely Canada ('Don't recommend more than a single fraction of palliative radiation for an uncomplicated painful bone metastasis') and the CCO guideline (single 8 Gy recommended). The explanation should cite these.
Wrong attribution: the explanation says 'Choosing Wisely (ASTRO/AAHPM) advises against longer courses'. ASTRO's Choosing Wisely item is only against >10 fractions, which covers option B but not E.
Option E's explanation says 'more visits and toxicity'. ASTRO reports similar toxicity across regimens.

References are dated: the Cancer Network piece covers the 2011 guideline. ASTRO 2024 replaces 2017 (I confirmed on the ASTRO page, but its recommendation text was not on that page). The 20% vs 8% retreatment figures are confirmed.
No duplication: the bank has cord compression (im-261030-59) and bone-pain opioid items, but no RT fractionation item. Stem 32 words, explanation 55 words, options homogeneous.
